result.verdict: Not fit to freeze as drafted. Several things are done well: the endpoint is fixed to lexical, the strata are fixed and reproduce exactly (W1 107/293, W2 102/207, W3 65/335, using the `old_hit` field), the W2 fresh pool is deterministic, the W2 pool shares no case with Study 1, the Study 2 32B pool or W1, no generated row exists for any H4 world, and the analysis code the addendum reuses still matches the parent's registered hashes. The fatal flaw is independence. The addendum says H4 is tested "only on worlds that have no generated row", but facts are the unit that carries the hypothesis, and W1's facts are mostly the ones that produced it. 254 of W1's 400 cases are in the Study 2 32B pool that generated H4, including 103 of its 107 high-salience cases. For W3 the figures are 300/400 and 57 of 65. W1 runs first, and the one-world fallback lets H4 be decided on W1 alone, so the most likely partial-completion outcome is a test on recycled facts. The decision rules also leave room to reframe after the fact. D can pass on the base-loss component alone while the paper claims "reasoning undoes edits". Outcomes of the parent's 70B tests and heterogeneity between worlds are not mapped to claims. Reopening the parent after D7 closed it is not logged as a deviation. There is no explicit stop rule against interim looks. Fixing these is cheap. Either make W2 the sole primary world, or add a fresh 70B world built from 70B-qualified facts outside the 32B pool (455 available, 105 high). Then add a hard stop/no-peek rule, a claim table covering every outcome, a D8 deviation entry and the missing disclosures. With those changes the addendum is freezable.

issues.section: §1, §4 (W1, W3), §5 H4 (primary worlds and one-world fallback), §6 power
issues.issue: W1 and W3 are not independent of the data that generated H4. Checked against the manifests: W1 (70B) shares 254 of 400 cases with the Study 2 32B main pool (manifest dea4ca25…), and 103 of W1's 107 high-salience cases (96%) are 32B-pool facts. Those are the very facts whose high-stratum RC of +.242 formed the hypothesis. W3 shares 300/400, and 57 of its 65 high cases. Only 4 high-salience W1 cases lie outside the 32B pool, so no disjoint W1 estimate is possible. Fact-level effects are plausibly shared across checkpoints: Study 1 shows the same split at 14B, 32B and 70B on the same 200 facts. W1's D therefore carries the winner's-curse selection of the hypothesis-generating facts and is biased upward under the null. The §5 rule 'if exactly one is complete, D̄ is that world's D_m' makes this worse: W1 runs first, so the likeliest partial-completion outcome decides H4 on the non-independent world alone. The §1 sentence 'tested here only on worlds that have no generated row' implies an independence that does not hold. The brief repeats it ('pre-registered before any data'). (Checked: W2 shares 0 cases with the 32B main pool, the 32B unknown group, W1 and Study 1, and no generated row for W2 exists anywhere.)
issues.fix: Rewrite §5 H4: 'The test statistic is D_W2. W2 (fresh 32B pool, no fact shared with any pool whose outcomes were seen) is the only primary world. If W2 is incomplete, H4 is not tested.' Move W1 and W3 to secondary and add to §4: 'W1 shares 254/400 cases (103/107 high-salience) and W3 300/400 (57/65 high) with the Study 2 32B pool that generated H4. Their D_m are cross-model transfer estimates on the same facts, are not independent tests, and cannot support H4 alone.' Change the run order to W2 first (edits on the 4090 node, then generation), then W1, then W3. Recompute §6 for W2 alone: SE ≈ .079, power ≈ .48 at D=.15 and ≈ .72 at D=.20. State this plainly, and say that a non-significant result is 'not supported, underpowered for D<.20'. Optional, if compute allows: add a co-primary independent 70B world W1'. Its pool would be 70B-qualified candidates beyond 70B's first 400 that are not in the 32B main pool, in candidate order (455 available, 105 high), with new ROME deltas. Its manifest is frozen with this file. If W1' shares facts with W2 (266 of W2's facts qualify for 70B), the bootstrap must resample facts jointly across worlds. Replace §1's sentence with 'It is tested only on facts that played no part in forming it.' Correct the brief's 'Pending' row the same way.

issues.section: §4 run order ('Completion is decided by platform time only'), §5 fallback, §9
issues.issue: There is no stop rule and no ban on interim looks. The experimenters control the platform time and run W1 first. The project's habit is to eyeball the first generations of a new model before long runs. Together these allow optional stopping: look at W1 (or its ES@B0 and B3 rows), then decide whether W2 'completes' (≥98%) or is left at 97% so the fallback applies. Missing chunks are re-run at the analyst's discretion, which is another lever over which worlds count.
issues.fix: Add to §4: 'Stop rule: generation for H4 ends at <fixed date and time, UTC+8> or when W2 (and W1 if kept) reach 100%, whichever is first. Failed chunks are re-run until the stop time without exception. Before the stop, only row counts, error-row counts and degenerate-flag counts are inspected. No answer text, hit or score of any H4-manifest case is read. Any smoke check uses cases outside every H4 manifest (for example Study 1 cases). At the stop, a registry entry records the time, the shard sha256s and per-world completeness before salience.py is run once.' Make salience.py refuse to run without that registry entry.

issues.issue: D = RC(high) − RC(low) mixes two components. In the exploratory S2 data, almost half of D = +.332 comes from base loss falling with salience (high .071 vs low .224, contributing +.154), not from edited loss rising (+.178). Base loss falling for facts many models know is close to mechanical: weakly known facts are lost by the unedited model under reasoning. H4 can therefore pass with a flat edited-loss difference, yet §7 then licenses 'reasoning undoes edits of entrenched facts', a claim about the edited component. The edited component is only a secondary, with no consequence. RC also conditions on B0 edit success, a post-treatment selection whose rate differs by stratum (S2 ES@B0 about .63 high vs .76 low). Salience may also proxy the target model's own confidence (secondary 5), which again has no consequence for the claim.
issues.fix: Rewrite §7 as a claim ladder. (a) H4 passes AND the edited-loss difference (high − low, computed like D̄) has a 95% CI above 0 AND ES drop(high) − ES drop(low) > 0: claim 'reasoning undoes edits of facts the model family knows broadly'. (b) H4 passes but the edited-loss CI includes 0: claim only 'the gap between edited and native retention is larger for salient facts'; the word 'undoes' is not used. (c) If the confidence-stratified D (secondary 5, pooled within-quartile mean) has a point estimate ≤ 0, the paper attributes the effect to the target model's confidence, not to cross-model salience. Pre-write the abstract sentence for (b) as well.

issues.issue: The rules leave room to reframe. (1) They ignore the parent's H1 and H2 at 70B and 14B, which W1 and W3 also evaluate. 'H4 fails → not edit-specific on a fresh pool' is contradicted if the parent's H2 passes at 70B, and nothing fixes which headline wins. (2) Heterogeneity between worlds is not covered: D̄ can pass with D_W2 ≤ 0 if W1 is retained. (3) 'H4 not tested' has no pre-written framing. (4) 'Salience composition is offered as the explanation … confirmatory in W1 and W2' overclaims. H4 tests within-pool moderation, not that composition (59% vs 39% salient) explains the Study 1 → Study 2 shrinkage.
issues.fix: Add an outcome table: rows H4 {pass, fail, not tested}, columns parent H2 at 70B {pass, fail, not run}. Each cell gives the thesis sentence and the pre-written abstract sentence, and all nine sentences are committed in the freeze commit. If more than one world is primary, add the rule that 'H4 is claimed as general only if every primary world's D_m point estimate is > 0; otherwise it is reported as pass, heterogeneous'. Replace the composition sentence with: 'The moderation is confirmatory; that composition explains the Study 1 → Study 2 shrinkage remains an exploratory inference.' Alternatively, register a composition prediction now, for example 'in W2, RC(low) has a CI including 0 and RC(high) has a CI above 0'.

issues.section: §4 W1/W3 ('Nothing changes … tested on the same rows'), §5 last line; parent §3 run order, deviations D6c/D7
issues.issue: The parent fixed a one-day window. Its D6c order was H2b, then H3, then 70B. D7 closed Study 2 and reported 70B and 14B as not run. The addendum reopens generation in a second window, chosen after the 32B failure and the salience exploration, and evaluates the parent's H1 and H2 at 70B and 14B 'as registered'. It also skips H2b (290 cases) and H3. This is continued data collection, re-prioritised after outcomes were seen, and it is not logged. The analysts also already know W1's high share (27%), so H4 predicts a weak overall 70B H2. That knowledge shapes how a 70B H2 result will be read.
issues.fix: Append deviation D8 to prereg-arr-deviations.md: 'Second compute window opened after the 32B result (outcomes seen: yes). It runs W1 (70B base and N, efficacy) and W3 (14B) for the parent's H1 and H2, and the new W2. H2b and H3 remain not run. The order was chosen for H4.' In the paper, label the parent's 70B and 14B H1/H2 as 'registered analyses on data collected after the 32B result was known'. Keep the Holm family of six as registered, and make no claim from the order of collection.

issues.issue: The table omits pre-outcome information that predicts outcomes and is already on disk. results/rt/deltas_logs/s2/r1llama70b_ROME_cf_r0of1.jsonl and the r1qwen14b delta logs hold per-case lp_first before and after the edit for the target and o_old. Residual log p(o_old) after the edit is the E5 erosion predictor (AUC .66 in S2), and those logs were read for D7 ('every fit error < 1e-5'). The table also omits the W1/W3 overlap with the 32B pool. And 32B outcome rows already exist for W1 facts: 37 W1 cases appear in the archived 32B shards (s2_archive_world2), and 1 W1 case is among the 10 generated unknown-group cases.
issues.fix: Add rows to §2. 'D70 and D3 delta logs (fit error, lp_first before/after): fit errors read for D7; lp values never tabulated against salience or any outcome' (state the truth, whatever it is). 'Overlap of W1/W3 with the Study 2 32B pool: 254/400 and 300/400; 32B outcome rows exist for these facts.' '1 W1 case is among the 10 generated 32B unknown-group cases.'

issues.issue: Hardware is not pinned for any H4 world. The parent's D6b lets 70B ranks run on either node, and a condition 'may mix rows from both nodes'. So a case's base and rome_N rows can come from different hardware. E0 shows only .81 per-case B3 agreement between the 4090 and H100 on the same cases, so hardware mismatch injects spurious flips into the within-case retention contrast. W2 says the engine and decoding are 'identical' but names no node.
issues.fix: Add to §4: 'W2 generation runs on the H100 node, as the parent's 32B. For every world, each rank's base and rome_N shards are claimed together and generated on the same node; the node is recorded in each shard header. If the H100 node is unavailable, the whole world moves to the 4090 node (logged), never single conditions.' Add a secondary analysis: D_m restricted to cases whose four rows share a node.

issues.issue: HARKing disclosure is incomplete. The E6 plan split 'known by all four' against the rest. The ≥3-of-4 cut (≥0.75) was adopted in E6b after the S2 dose-response showed the sign change between 2 and 3. The addendum presents the cut as a 'frozen definition' without that history. §1 says the split 'held' in Study 1. In fact, none of the Study 1 high − low differences is significant (p = .068, .25, .091, G0 .28). The brief's 'CIs exclude 0 vs CIs include 0' is the difference-in-significance fallacy.
issues.fix: Add to §3: 'The cut at 3 of 4 was chosen after seeing the S2 32B dose-response (E6 → E6b); it is fixed here and dose-response (secondary 4) is reported to show the result does not hinge on it.' Change §1 to: 'In the Study 1 cases the high − low difference had the same sign at 14B, 32B and 70B (+.15 to +.26) but was not significant at any of them (p = .07–.28).' Fix the brief's Study 1 row the same way.

issues.issue: Some definitional details are not pinned. The table counts reproduce only if old_hit_q is the raw `old_hit` field, true even when the probe also names o_new. Under 'qualified-style' old∧¬new, W2 becomes 97/212 and W1 106/294. Missing-flag handling is unstated, although all four qualify files currently cover all 1,600 candidates. W3 has no run tag, and the 14B s2smoke rows must be excluded. W3's 3-of-3 cut is stricter than the 3-of-4 cut used for W1/W2, which is acceptable but should be acknowledged.
issues.fix: State: 'old_hit_q(c) is the `old_hit` field of qualify_<q>.jsonl, irrespective of `new_hit`. Every H4 manifest case has a flag from every probe in Q_m (verified at freeze); a missing flag makes the case low.' Give W3 run tag s3_14b (or s2) and add 'rows with run tag s2smoke are never read.' Note that W3's cut (3 of 3) differs from W1/W2's.

issues.issue: W2 is the same model and procedure as the failed parent H1/H2 at 32B, on 309 further qualified facts. Nothing forbids later pooling W2 with the 400-case pool (709 cases) or calling W2's overall RC a 'replication of H2'. That is a forking path toward rescuing the failed registered test.
issues.fix: Add: 'W2's overall ES drop and RC are descriptive. No pooled 32B (400 + 309) H1/H2 estimate is computed; if one is ever shown it is labelled exploratory. W2 is never described as a replication or retest of H1/H2.'

issues.issue: Several forks remain open. A semantic (judge) variant of D is not ruled out. The 'linear-trend estimate' of the dose-response has no stated method. The quartiles in secondary 5 have no stated base set. The bootstrap rule does not say whether resampling within stratum draws all stratum cases (with the retention set recomputed) or only retention-set cases.
issues.fix: State: 'H4 and its secondaries use the lexical endpoint only; no judge-based D is computed.' 'Linear trend = OLS slope of the per-case retention value on the number of probes knowing the fact, over the retention set, with case-bootstrap CI.' 'Quartiles of lp_first.before.o_old are computed within each world over its full manifest.' 'The bootstrap resamples all manifest cases within world × stratum and recomputes the retention set in each resample (as in rt.analysis H2).'

issues.issue: The freeze is weaker than it needs to be. salience.py will import rt.analysis, metrics and aliases, but only salience.py's hash is recorded. The pre-written abstract sentences required by §7 are not in the freeze commit's file list. The only external timestamp is a GitHub push record. 'No W row existed at freeze' rests on self-report.
issues.fix: In §9, record the sha256 of src/rt/analysis.py (c94cd612…), src/metrics.py (024dc94b…) and data/aliases.json (4ba2ae95…). Add the pre-written outcome-table sentences file under paperwriting/revision/narrative/ to the freeze commit. Register the addendum hash on OSF, or stamp it with OpenTimestamps, in addition to the GitHub push. Make salience.py assert that every W-shard header has `created` later than the freeze push time and a `git` commit descending from the freeze commit. Before freezing, run salience.py on the existing S2 32B pool and record that it reproduces E6's +.332, as a code check rather than a test.

result.verdict: Not fit to freeze as written. The primary statistic D̄ = mean over worlds of [RC(high) − RC(low)] mostly measures something the §7 pass branch does not claim. In the data that produced H4, almost all of D comes from the base model losing its own answers on obscure facts. Base loss is .15–.35 in the low stratum against .06–.09 in the high one. Edited loss barely depends on salience in Study 1: the high − low difference is +.007 (32B S1), +.011 (G0-H100), +.054 (G0-4090), +.047 (14B) and +.121 (70B). Only Study 2 shows +.178. A simulation at the planned retention-set sizes, with edited loss equal across strata and Study 2's base losses (.07 vs .22), passes H4 about 82% of the time. So the stated power of ".75 at D = .15" is mostly power to detect base fragility, which is no reason to say "reasoning undoes edits of entrenched facts". The §7 claim that salience composition explains the Study 1 → Study 2 shrinkage is also untested by H4, and existing data contradict it. Standardising Study 1's 32B per-stratum estimates to Study 2's salience mix lowers the retention contrast only from .21 to .13 (G0-H100 rerun: .22 to .17), against Study 2's .03. It raises the ES drop (.12 to .16) instead of lowering it to .04. The power arithmetic does not follow from its own inputs: SD .55 and a 60% retention share give SE .059, power .72/.93, not .055 and .75/.94. The power for the one-world fallback (about .47) is missing. Keeping a single primary decision, unweighted pooling and stratified bootstrapping is sound. What needs changing is what the primary decides and what each outcome lets the paper say. All fixes below are text changes plus one optional cheap B0-sampling condition, and can be made before any W1/W2 row exists. After issues 1–4 are fixed the addendum is fit to freeze.

issues.issue: Estimand mismatch. D_m = [edited loss(high) − edited loss(low)] − [base loss(high) − base loss(low)]. The second bracket belongs to the unedited model and is large regardless of editing. In Study 2 32B, base loss among all base-old cases is .203 in the low stratum vs .052 in the high one, before any ES@B0 gating. The ES@B0 gate adds about .02 in each stratum. explore_s1s2.json E6b decomposes the Study 1 D as follows (edited diff / base diff): 32B S1 +.007/−.257; G0-H100 +.011/−.153; G0-4090 +.054/−.224; 14B +.047/−.104; 70B +.121/−.077. Study 2 32B is +.178/−.154. So D > 0 is expected even if salience has no effect on how often edits are lost. This is the selection-on-B0 fragility (regression-to-the-mean) artefact the lens asks about, and it acts mostly through the low stratum. Simulation at planned retention-set n (W1 59/190, W2 65/151): edited loss .20 in both strata with base loss .07/.22 gives P(H4 pass) ≈ .82; the Study-1-32B-like scenario gives ≈ .90. Yet the §7 pass branch says 'reasoning undoes edits of entrenched (salient) facts', which needs the edited-loss component. Adding RC(high) > 0 as a second condition does not help either: it also passes about 78% of the time under that null. Only the edited-loss difference separates the two readings.
issues.fix: Replace the H4 block with: "**H4 (primary; one decision at α = .05).** Over the complete primary worlds (W1, W2), with unweighted means over worlds: D̄ = mean_m[RC_m(high) − RC_m(low)] and R̄_high = mean_m RC_m(high). H4 passes iff both are > 0 with two-sided bootstrap p < .05. This is an intersection–union test: both must reject, so no multiplicity correction is needed. **Wording component (pre-declared; decides wording, not pass/fail):** Ē = mean_m[edited loss_m(high) − edited loss_m(low)] and B̄ = mean_m[base loss_m(high) − base loss_m(low)], each with a 95% CI. Recorded now: in the data that formed H4, B̄ supplied most of D (Study 1 base/edited differences −.26/+.01, −.15/+.01, −.22/+.05, −.10/+.05, −.08/+.12; Study 2 32B −.15/+.18), so D > 0 is expected even without any salience effect on edit loss." Replace the §7 pass branch with three branches, each with a pre-written abstract result sentence (three variants, not two). (a) H4 passes and Ē's CI excludes 0: "On facts the model knows robustly, reasoning undoes edits far more often than the model's own answers, and such edits are lost more often than edits of obscure facts." (b) H4 passes and Ē's CI includes 0: "Edit-specific loss under reasoning appears only on facts the model knows robustly. On obscure facts, reasoning unsettles the model's own answers as often as the edit, so the contrast vanishes." The paper then does not claim that salient edits are more fragile. (c) H4 fails: as now. If the team wants the edit-fragility claim itself to be confirmatory, make Ē the primary instead. State its power honestly: about .44 at Ē = .08 (roughly the mean of the observed components) and about .98 at Study 2's .18.

issues.section: §7 'Salience composition is offered as the explanation'; §1
issues.issue: H4 tests moderation inside new worlds. It does not test the between-pool counterfactual that composition (59% vs 39% high salience) explains why H1 and H2 shrank from Study 1 to Study 2, and existing data contradict that claim. I standardised Study 1's 32B per-stratum estimates to Study 2's mix (rt.analysis per-case values; base-old cases with complete salience; S1 high/low n = 109/41 for ES drop and 57/29 for RC). Retention contrast: S1 .209 → .129 and G0-H100 .224 → .170, against Study 2's .029. Composition thus covers about 44% (S1) or 28% (matched-hardware G0-H100) of the RC shrinkage. ES drop: S1 .120 → .155 and G0-H100 .112 → .151. The ES drop rises, because in Study 1 the low-salience facts had the larger ES drop (32B high .092 vs low .195, difference −.103 [−.308, .092]; 14B +.016; 70B −.009). Salience therefore cannot explain the H1 shrinkage. This also settles the 'ES drop as primary' question: ES drop is the worse primary. Its salience moderation appears only in Study 2 (+.127), it has no native-answer reference, and it nets erosion against repair, which has more room in the high stratum (ES@B0 .64 vs .75).
issues.fix: §7 pass branch: replace "Salience composition is offered as the explanation: exploratory in Study 1 and Study 2, confirmatory in W1 and W2" with: "H4 tests whether the edit-specific contrast depends on salience within new worlds. It does not test whether pool composition explains the Study 1 → Study 2 difference. On the existing data, standardising Study 1's 32B per-stratum estimates to Study 2's salience mix accounts for roughly a quarter to a half of the retention-contrast shrinkage and none of the ES-drop shrinkage. The paper reports this whatever H4's outcome, and does not present salience as the explanation of the failed H1." Add secondary 7: "Standardisation: Study 1 (S1, G0-H100) 32B per-stratum RC and ES drop reweighted to Study 2's and to W2's stratum shares, with bootstrap CIs (cases resampled within run × stratum)." Keep secondary 2 (ES-drop difference) as a secondary.

issues.issue: (i) The arithmetic does not follow from the stated inputs. SD .55 with 60% retention sets gives n_ret = 64/176 (W1) and 61/124 (W2), so SE(D_W1) = .080, SE(D_W2) = .086 and SE(D̄) = .059. Power is then .72 at D = .15 and .93 at .20. Even the stated SE of .055 gives .78/.95, not .75/.94. (ii) Retention shares differ by stratum: in Study 2 32B they are .635 (high) and .73 (low), and the SDs are .514 and .554. 70B's ES@B0 is unknown (Study 1: .60), so its high-stratum share is probably lower. (iii) The fallback 'if exactly one is complete, D̄ is that world's D_m' has power of only about .47–.48 at D = .15, which is not stated. (iv) The planned D = .15 roughly equals the base-fragility component expected with no edit effect (issue 1), so the power figure overstates the test's evidential value for the edit claim.
issues.fix: Replace §6 with: "**Inputs (Study 2 32B):** per-case RC SD .51 (high) and .55 (low); retention-set share .64 (high) and .73 (low). For W1 (70B, ES@B0 unknown; Study 1 .60) we assume .53/.62. Expected retention-set n: W1 57/182, W2 65/151. SE(D_W1) ≈ .080, SE(D_W2) ≈ .078, SE(D̄) ≈ .056. **Power** (two-sided α = .05, normal approximation): D = .15 → .77; D = .20 → .95. If only one primary world completes: ≈ .47 at D = .15. With SD .55 and a 60% share in both strata: SE .059, power .72/.93. **Caveat:** the base-loss difference alone is expected to contribute about +.08 to +.26 to D (Study 1 and Study 2). The edited-loss component Ē has SE(Ē) ≈ .045 and power ≈ .44 at Ē = .08. R̄_high has power ≈ .98 at .18."

issues.issue: The retention contrast compares two answers that were both selected at B0. An answer near its decision boundary flips under any perturbation, not just reasoning. On salient facts the edit is the near-boundary answer: ES@B0 is lower (.635 vs .754), and E5 found that the residual post-edit log p(o_old) predicts erosion in Study 2 (AUC .66). On obscure facts the base answer is near the boundary. RC(high) > 0 and RC(low) < 0 therefore follow from boundary proximity alone, with no reasoning-specific mechanism. Secondary 5 adjusts only for the base's pre-edit confidence (lp_first.before.o_old). It does not adjust for edit strength (lp_first.after.o_old / after.target), which is the variable that differs by stratum on the edited side. Neither W1 nor W2 has a non-reasoning perturbation floor, although the parent defines one (B0 sampling) and Study 1 found an excess of .266 over it.
issues.fix: Rewrite secondary 5: "Robustness to answer stability. Within each world, cases are split into quartiles (over the whole manifest) of (a) the post-edit first-token margin lp_first.after.target − lp_first.after.o_old and (b) the base's lp_first.before.o_old (rt.deltas logs, which exist before generation). D_m, Ē and RC_m(high) are computed within each quartile and averaged with weights equal to the quartile's retention-set n. Quartiles where a stratum has fewer than 5 retention cases are dropped and counted." Add (run after W1 and W2's primary conditions, only if platform time remains; otherwise listed under Limitations): "Perturbation floor: for W1 and W2, base and rome_N at B0 with sampling (T .6, top-p .95, top-k 50, seeds 0–2). Secondary: per stratum, RC with 'lost at B3' replaced by 'lost in ≥ 1 of 3 B0 samples', and RC(B3) − RC(B0-sampled). If the high-stratum excess has a CI including 0, the paper attributes the salient-fact contrast to fragile edits rather than to reasoning."

issues.section: §1 Why this addendum exists (and brief, 'Evidence now')
issues.issue: 'The same split held in the Study 1 cases at 14B, 32B and 70B' overstates the evidence. None of the five Study 1 high − low differences excludes 0: 32B S1 +.264 [−.029, .557] p=.068; G0-H100 +.165 p=.28; G0-4090 +.278 p=.098; 14B +.152 p=.25; 70B +.198 p=.091. The brief's 'salient CIs exclude 0, the others include 0' is the difference-in-significance fallacy. Also, the Study 1 split comes almost entirely from base loss, not edited loss (issue 1), and the brief's 'edited loss rises .13 → .31' is a Study-2-only pattern.
issues.fix: Replace the second bullet of §1 with: "On the Study 1 cases, the high − low difference in retention contrast was positive at 14B, 32B (three runs) and 70B (+.15 to +.28), but no single CI excluded 0 (p = .07–.28). In those cases the difference came mainly from the base model losing its own answers on low-salience facts (base-loss difference −.08 to −.26). Edited loss differed little between strata (+.01 to +.12). Only in Study 2 32B did edited loss differ clearly (+.18)." Correct the brief's corresponding row the same way.

issues.issue: 'The bootstrap resamples cases within each world × stratum' does not say whether the resampled units are all manifest cases in the stratum or only the retention-gated cases. The parent convention for conditional rates resamples only gated cases (rt.analysis docstring). It also does not fix the RNG draw order across the four groups, so the result cannot be exactly reproduced. The project already lost reproduction matches to bootstrap-sequence differences (study1.md §6). Finally, it does not say whether the components share replicates.
issues.fix: Add: "Units are the retention-gated cases (base run names o_old at B0 and edited ES at B0, all four rows present), following the parent's conditional-rate convention. Strata are fixed screen covariates. Each replicate draws, from one random.Random(42) stream, with replacement within W1-high, W1-low, W2-high and W2-low in that order, each in sorted case_id order. D̄, R̄_high, Ē and B̄ are computed on the same 10,000 replicates. p = 2·min(#≤0, #≥0)/10,000. A world whose stratum has an empty retention set is treated as incomplete."

issues.issue: Unweighted pooling is defensible: inverse-variance weights would be about .49/.51, so nothing is lost by fixing equal weights in advance. But the estimand is an average over two named model families, and a pooled pass can be carried by one world (for example D_W1 = .30, D_W2 = 0). W2 is the same model and the same screen as the discovery pool (an exchangeable continuation in candidate order), so it is a direct replication; W1 is the transfer test. The addendum gives no rule for how a one-world-driven pass is worded.

Otherwise it reports the pooled result and names the world that carries it. W2 is described as a same-model replication on fresh facts and W1 as a cross-family test."

result.verdict:
The addendum should not be frozen yet. The scientific core is sound and ready. The salience definition reproduces the frozen strata exactly from the `old_hit` field of the four qualify files (107/293, 102/207, 65/335). The fresh 309-case manifest is the deterministic remainder of the 32B screen and shares no case with the main or unknown manifests. H4 is a single test with a clear pass rule. The operational layer is the problem: an executor or an analysis-code author could not run it without asking several questions, and three gaps could not be repaired once the file is frozen.
1. W2 has no delta or generation config. The config it points to has the wrong manifest, probes and run tag, and rt.run has no flag to override the manifest or probes.
2. Nothing says when the analysis runs, and nothing stops anyone from scoring W1 rows before then. Which worlds count as "complete", and so what D̄ is, would depend on when someone decides to look.
3. §2 and §9 say no H4-world row exists, but W3 already has generated rows for two cases.
Five more gaps would cause a crash or force a judgment call:
- The 14B header-only shards will refuse to resume because the code hash has changed.
- Hardware, layout, and keeping base and rome_N of a case on the same hardware are not specified.
- The parent's run order was changed after seeing the 32B results, but no deviation was logged.
- How the parent's H1 and H2 are re-evaluated (with the larger Holm family) is not specified.
- The trend estimate, the quartile analysis, the bootstrap draw order, and the "not tested" and one-world outcomes are not defined.
With the fixes below (two new config files, a stop rule plus an end-of-generation registry entry, the corrected data-seen record, an archive step or a code move, deviation D8, and a fuller freeze record), the addendum is fit to freeze.

issues.issue: The W2 configs do not exist, and the text tells the executor to run a config whose fixed fields contradict W2. `study2_r1qwen32b.yaml` points to manifest `manifest_r1qwen32b.jsonl` (the 400 already seen), run_tag `s2` and probes `[efficacy, para0, locality]`. rt.run can override only `--run-tag`, `--conditions`, `--stage`, `--limit` and batch settings; it has no manifest or probe override. Run literally with `--conditions base,rome_N --run-tag s3fresh`, it would regenerate the seen 400-case pool on three probes. For the edits, the log directory is not named. Using `deltas_s2_r1qwen32b.yaml` with `--pool` would either fail the run_signature check or append the fresh pool to the main pool's log `results/rt/deltas_logs/s2/r1qwen32b_ROME_cf_r*of2.jsonl`. The H2b config avoided exactly that by giving its edits their own log dir. §9 promises 'the W2 delta and generation configs' but names neither file and gives no sha. No acceptance check is given for the W2 edits.
issues.fix: Create, name and pin two files. (a) `experiments/rt/deltas_s3fresh_r1qwen32b.yaml`, identical to `deltas_s2_r1qwen32b.yaml` except `pool: experiments/rt/pools/study2/manifest_r1qwen32b_fresh.jsonl` and `log_dir: results/rt/deltas_logs/s3fresh` (model r1qwen32b, ROME, target_tag cf, out_root deltas, dtype float32, factor {max_rank 1, tol 1e-4, floor_mult 8.0}, models_file deltas_models.yaml sha 2c873e02f08e…). (b) `experiments/rt/study2_r1qwen32b_fresh.yaml`, a copy of `study2_r1qwen32b_h2b.yaml` with `run_tag: s3fresh` and `manifest: experiments/rt/pools/study2/manifest_r1qwen32b_fresh.jsonl`. Everything else stays as in that file: model_tag r1qwen32b, template r1, no_bos true, bf16, module_tmp model.layers.{}.mlp.down_proj, out_dir results/rt/s2, aliases data/aliases.json, probes [efficacy], decoding {greedy: true}, engine {32, 128000, answer_cap 256, chunk_cases 10}, and conditions base and rome_N (deltas_dir deltas/r1qwen32b/ROME/cf) at budgets [B0, B3]. Rewrite §4 W2 to cite these two files rather than `study2_r1qwen32b.yaml`, and list their full sha256 in §9. Add an acceptance rule for the W2 edits before W2 generation: 309/309 status ok, max fit rel_err ≤ 1e-4, the `_templates` sha in every log equals fa3061b3dbeb… (the value in the main and H2b 32B logs), and hparams_sha equals the main-pool deltas'.

issues.section: §4 Run order ('Completion is decided by platform time only'); §5 H4 ('worlds that are complete')
issues.issue: Nothing fixes when the analysis runs or forbids scoring before then. Which worlds are 'complete', and so whether D̄ uses W1, W2 or both, depends on when someone looks. The parent's H1/H2 at 70B are to be 'evaluated as registered' on W1, which means running rt.study2 on W1 rows. If that happens as soon as W1 arrives, the 70B outcomes are seen before W2 is generated, and the stratum composition is already public. The project's own runsheet also asks for a by-eye `--limit 2` smoke check of every new model; the 70B smoke rows would be W1 rows and the addendum says nothing about them. The addendum also does not say what happens if a world finishes after the analysis (for example, the rest of W1 after submission).
issues.fix:
Add a §4 'Stop and analysis rule':
(1) Fix a timestamp T_stop before freezing. Rows written after T_stop never enter the H4 test.
(2) When generation ends or T_stop arrives, whichever is first, append an 'end of generation' registry entry. It lists every W1–W3 shard with its sha256 and row counts, and says which worlds meet the completeness rule. Nothing else is inspected at that point.
(3) No W1–W3 row is scored, judged or read beyond row and error counts before that entry. This covers rt.study2, salience.py and reading answers. The only exception is a smoke run under run tag `s4smoke` (first 2 cases of rank 0): it may be checked by eye for well-formed text only, is never analysed, and the 2 cases are generated again in the main run.
(4) salience.py and rt.study2 then each run once, at the frozen shas.
(5) Any world that finishes after T_stop is analysed with the same code and reported as a post-cutoff addition. It never changes the H4 verdict.

titles: Reasoning Undoes Knowledge Edits of Facts Even Small Models Know (use only if H4 is confirmed)
When Does Reasoning Undo a Knowledge Edit? A Finding, Its Failed Replication, and a Test of Why (works in both outcomes)
The Edit Holds Until the Model Thinks: Reasoning Undoes Edits of Well-Known Facts (use only if H4 is confirmed)
scored.thesis: Reasoning undoes knowledge edits of facts that even small models know and mostly spares the rest, so how often an edit fails after reasoning depends on which facts an evaluation tests.

verdict.restated_thesis: From the abstract alone: reasoning models can lose a knowledge edit while they think, but mostly when the edited fact is one that even small models know. Evaluation sets differ in how many such facts they contain, so whether a study finds that reasoning undoes edits depends on which facts it tests. I could only put this together at sentence 5. After sentence 3, a cold reader thinks the paper reports a failed effect, and the claim itself arrives last.
best_ideas: The opening paragraph works and answers TRfT's motivation complaint directly. It uses one concrete edit, makes the gap explicit (edits are checked with a direct question but used after reasoning), and ends on the turn: 'the effect almost disappeared. This paper is about why.' Keep it, but use a real logged case.
Making the failed pre-registered replication the turn of the paper instead of a footnote. This is an honest arc, and it is what the paper has that He et al., CODE, CRANE and ThinkEval do not.

Evidential status shown by the structure rather than by hedges: '(exploratory)' and '(pre-registered)' in section titles, a status column in Table 1, and status labels on the figure panels. Sentences can then be confident without overclaiming.
Table 3 lists every candidate explanation in the order it was tried and cites the plan commit. This is the right answer to the forking-paths worry, because it shows the search instead of hiding it.

The core measurement is the paired comparison of an edited answer with the model's own answer, defined only on facts the model knew. It answers the AI review's 'no edited-versus-base contrast' and mTGu's per-checkpoint qualification point at once.

The Setup gives one 'because' sentence per design decision: one edit per request, the same edit answered twice, comparison with the model's own answers, only facts the model knew, and the subject name removed. This is exactly what TRfT asked for.

Panel (b) of the hero figure plots edited loss and own-answer loss as two lines with n printed at each point, instead of only their difference. This is the honest view, and it should be applied everywhere (see the fatal problems).
Pre-written abstracts for both outcomes, a title that works in either, and a plan to name the 70B H1/H2 prediction in the addendum before freeze.

Engineering detail (BOS, engine parity, hashes, deviation log) moves to the appendix and the intervention becomes one Discussion paragraph. This cuts the three-stories-at-once problem the brief diagnosed.

The takeaway for evaluators: test edits after reasoning, compare against the model's own answers, and report how well known the test facts are. It gives a reader outside editing a reason to cite the paper.
fatal_problems: The thesis attributes the salience pattern to edits being undone, but Study 1's components contradict this. In paperwriting/revision/explore_s1s2.json (E6b), edited-answer loss at Qwen-32B is flat across strata: .386 for well-known facts vs .379 for the rest in S1, and .345 vs .333 in the G0-H100 rerun. The whole +.264 difference in excess loss there comes from the model's own answers (own loss .088 vs .345). At 14B the edited loss is .344 vs .296 and at 70B .386 vs .265, while own loss is .062 vs .167 and .070 vs .147. So 'mostly spares the rest' is false in Study 1: reasoning undid about 38% of edits of less-known facts. Only Study 2 shows an edited-loss gradient (.313 vs .135). The proposal's 'same split on Study 1 facts' replicates the excess-loss number, not the claimed mechanism. Panel (a), which shows only excess-loss bars, would hide this from readers until a reviewer asks.

H4 as drafted cannot certify the confirmed thesis. D = RC(high) − RC(low) can pass entirely through the own-answer component, which says nothing about edits. In Study 2 the own-loss part of D alone is about .154 (.225 vs .071), roughly the planned D = .15, and in Study 1 at 32B it is the whole of D. So 'H4 confirmed' does not license 'reasoning undoes edits of well-known facts'. The addendum (prereg-arr-addendum-salience.md) is still marked DRAFT, so this is fixable now and must be fixed before freeze.

The abstract regresses on the brief's own diagnosis (the old abstract had 7 numbers). This one has about 14 (.106, three, twice, 400, .037, +.029, three of four, .115, +.242, 59%, 39%, D, CI, p) and mixes units. Sentence 2 gives a ratio ('about twice') and sentence 3 a difference ('+.029'), so a reader cannot tell how much shrank. Sentence 4 runs about 60 words of parenthetical statistics. The claim comes only in sentence 5, and the result itself is a placeholder.

Both abstract variants imply that composition explains the shrinkage ('such facts made up 59% of the first pool but only 39%'). Composition accounts for about half. Within strata, edited loss fell .386 → .313 for well-known facts but .379 → .135 for the rest, so most of the drop in edited loss happened inside less-known facts, which behave differently in the two pools. 'Located the loss in' and 'the other facts showed neither' overstate this.

Construct validity of 'well-known' is unaddressed. The measure (small distills answer correctly at B0) mixes popularity with guessability from the subject string, for example a French-sounding name suggesting the mother tongue French; the Darrieux example is itself of this kind. In the S1 split it also includes the 46 of 200 name-containing subjects that Study 2's rule excluded. And Qwen-7B, the model that selected Study 1's facts, is one of the four probe models, so S1 salience is partly circular. Without a popularity proxy or a guessability control, 'widely known' is a label, not a finding, and Section 7's 'stored redundantly' interpretation is unsupported.

The paper's climax depends on data that do not exist two days before the deadline. H4 is not frozen, its power is about .75, and the 70B world is only 27% well-known, so the salience account itself predicts a small overall 70B effect. If either world is incomplete, the narrative has no resolution. The 'pending' third version is listed as a risk but has not been written.
fixes: Rewrite the thesis so both studies support it. For example: 'Reasoning loses knowledge edits more often than the model's own answers only for facts the model knows firmly; for facts it knows weakly, reasoning changes the model's own answer about as often, so whether an evaluation finds edit-specific loss depends on which facts it tests.' Treat Study 2's edited-loss gradient (.313 vs .135) as a secondary, exploratory observation, not the headline.

Before freezing the addendum, make a pass about edits. Add the edited-loss component (edited loss high − low > 0, currently secondary 3) and/or ES drop high − low as a co-primary condition, or state that the 'edits of well-known facts are undone' wording is used only if the edited-loss CI excludes 0. Also write down the predicted small overall 70B H1/H2 effect, and pre-write a third, 'not tested' abstract sentence.

Redraw panel (a) of Figure 1 as edited loss and own loss side by side for each stratum and study (S1 32B: .386/.088 vs .379/.345; S2: .313/.071 vs .135/.225), not as excess-loss bars. The proposal's own rule to 'always show both lines' requires this, and it shows the pattern a careful reviewer will otherwise find.

Rebuild the abstract around 5–6 numbers in one unit, with the answer by sentence 3. A possible version: (1) Edits are checked by a direct question, but reasoning models answer after a chain of thought where the original fact can return. (2) We ask each edited question directly and after reasoning, and compare how often the edited answer is lost with how often the unedited model loses its own answer. (3) In a first study, the largest DeepSeek-R1 distills lost edits about twice as often as their own answers (38% vs 17% at Qwen-32B); a pre-registered replication on 400 new facts found almost no gap (20% vs 17%). (4) [The calibrated salience sentence.] (5) [The registered result, plus the advice to evaluators.]

Run zero-GPU construct checks now: recompute the S1 split excluding name-containing subjects and with Qwen-7B dropped from the probe set (so S1 and S2 strata are comparable), compute S1 ES drop by stratum, and add a popularity proxy (for example, subject Wikipedia pageviews) or a guessability proxy. Report whether 'well-known' survives them before using the phrase in the title.

Replace 'the replication matched the first study' and the bare 59%/39% contrast with an explicit share: 'composition accounts for about half of the gap; the rest is that less-known facts in the new pool lost fewer edits (14% vs 38%).'

Number hygiene. Excess loss for well-known facts in S2 has n=99, not 156 (156 is the ES-drop n). Use Llama-70B unfiltered (.110, Holm .022, +.234) consistently. Recompute D−P (−.225) from study1.json before citing it.

Vocabulary for a cold reader. Use one name per concept in the main text ('well-known', never 'salience', 'salient' or 'high salience'). Footnote the registered names (retention contrast, salience) once. Drop 'worlds', 'pools', 're-decides', 'breaks/repairs' and 'certified'; say 'fact sets', 'changes its answer', 'checked'. Gloss DeepSeek-R1 distills in one clause ('smaller models trained to imitate DeepSeek-R1's reasoning').

Cut the AI-prose tells: the tricolon figure title 'Same model, two pools, one variable', the list rhythm 'found, shrank, explained, tested', and five abstract sentences that each open with an article plus a study label. Vary sentence openings, and give the result before the procedure.

Keep the 'This paper is about why.' hook, but answer it within the same paragraph or the next sentence. Many ACL reviewers decide after intro P1, and a puzzle without an answer by then reads as a negative-result paper.

Shrink Section 5 from 1.4 to about 0.8 pages: Table 3 plus one paragraph. Spend the freed space on the components figure and one real verbatim chain where a well-known fact's edit holds directly and the old value returns mid-chain. Replace the hypothetical Darrieux narration with that logged case, or confirm Darrieux is in a pool and was actually lost.

Positioning. Before claiming the variable is new, cite work on entity popularity and parametric recall (for example, Mallen et al. 2023, PopQA) and any work on editability as a function of popularity or entrenchment. Frame the contribution as the comparison against the model's own answers plus the registered replication that shows the measured effect depends on the test set, not as the discovery that popular facts are hard to edit.

Title. Use only the title that works in either outcome, shortened to 'When Does Reasoning Undo a Knowledge Edit?' without the list subtitle. Choose a confirmed-only title after the H4 data exist, and only if the edited-loss component also passes.

verdict.restated_thesis: In DeepSeek-R1 distills, reasoning undoes ROME edits mainly for facts that even small models know, and much less for obscure facts. A first study's large effect came from a pool that a 7B's recall had filled with such facts. A pre-registered replication on fresh facts at Qwen-32B therefore shrank and failed. A test of fact salience, registered before its data, decides whether that explanation holds. The practical upshot is that how often edits fail after reasoning depends on which facts an evaluation tests.
best_ideas: Use the failed registered H1/H2 as the turn of the paper. Keep it in abstract sentence 3 and in a section titled for it ('It did not.'), not in a footnote. A registered-reports editor wants exactly this, and it makes the failure the reason to read on.

Let structure carry the evidential status: section titles, a status column in Table 1, and figure panels labelled exploratory or registered. Sentences can then be confident. This addresses the brief's diagnosis that the old paper hedged in every sentence.

Turn mTGu's selection critique into the finding. The 7B-recall selection favoured facts that small models know. E2 (Study 2's rule applied to Study 1's facts still gives a drop of .147 and an excess loss of +.154) shows that the rule alone was not the cause. This answers rebuttal point 2 better than any sensitivity footnote could.

Panel (b) of the hero figure always shows both components: edited loss rising .13 to .31 and the model's own loss falling .39 to .06. The confound sits in plain view rather than hidden in one contrast.
Table 3 lists every candidate explanation in the order it was tried, with the plan commit. That is the honest way to show forking paths.
Commit two abstract result sentences before any data, and keep one title that works in both outcomes. Pick the final title only after the result.

Write a prediction of the overall 70B effect, derived from salience composition, into the addendum before freeze. A failed 70B H2 then reads as predicted rather than as a second unexplained failure. Make the prediction quantitative.
Define excess loss only on facts each model itself answered directly. This directly answers the AI review's complaint that the estimand was undefined without per-model qualification.
Use at most three terms, each mapped once to its registered name ('registered as the retention contrast'). Move engine, BOS, hash and deviation material to the appendix.
Open on one concrete edit, where the direct question certifies the edit but the edit is used after a chain. That is the motivation TRfT said was missing.
fatal_problems: The puzzle is told with numbers from two different engines. Study 1 is the old fp32 HF pipeline on H200, and its 32B excess loss pairs edited runs without BOS against a base run with BOS. Study 2 is engine v2 in bf16 on H100. Putting them side by side in the abstract (.106 to .037), Table 2, the Section 4 decomposition (.386 to .199) and hero panel (a) breaks the project's own hard rule 4 and overstates the shrinkage. On matched engine and hardware (E1), the ES-drop difference is -.048, p = .305, not significant: G0-H100 gives .085 against .037. Only excess loss (-.178, p = .019) and erosion (-.110, p = .018) differ, and hardware alone changes 19% of B3 outcomes. The salience split on matched hardware is also weaker than the panel shows: G0-H100 gives +.276 against +.111 (difference +.165, p = .28), not +.298 against +.034.

The H4-confirmed thesis, titles and result sentence claim more than H4 tests. D is excess loss (well known) minus excess loss (other). In Study 2 about half of that gradient comes from the model's own answers becoming more stable (.39 to .06), not from edits being undone. H4 can pass with excess loss for well-known facts near zero, or entirely through the own-answer line. Even then, the sentence 'confirmed that reasoning undoes edits of widely known facts more than edits of other facts' would be printed, but the edited-loss and ES-drop results that would actually support it are only secondary. The addendum is still a DRAFT, so the interpretation rule can be fixed now.

The registered 70B H1/H2, tested on the same W1 rows, appear in neither abstract and in no pre-written outcome. The real outcome space is H4 (pass, fail, untested) times 70B H1/H2 (pass, fail). Only two cells are written, and the not-confirmed thesis quietly assumes the 70B fails too.

There is an undisclosed fork in the salience threshold. The E6 plan specified 'the 7B knows it' and '4 of 4 versus the rest'. The reported cut, '3 to 4 of 4', first appears in E6b, after E6 had been seen, and it sits exactly at the step in the dose-response (-.01 to +.24). Table 3 also applies different standards. Edit strength is ruled out because it does not replicate on Study 1 facts (AUC .502), yet salience is kept although its Study 1 differences are also not significant (p = .068 to .28). It passes only on point estimates.

Winner's curse is missing from the candidate explanations. Study 1's 'largest models' scope was chosen after seeing that 2 of 6 checkpoints were significant, so shrinkage on replication is the default expectation. Section 3's stated job, to establish the finding firmly 'so that its failure to replicate lands as a real surprise', manufactures surprise. A registered-reports reader will notice.

The H4-not-confirmed paper does not stand as drafted. The opening ('This paper is about why'), abstract sentence 4 ('pointed to one cause') and Section 7's title ('Why well-known facts resist editing') all presuppose the explanation. The arc then ends as found, shrank, guessed, guess failed. That version needs its own thesis, not a retitled Sections 5 and 6, and at best it is Findings-level.

Confounds that could stand in for salience are not separated from it. ES@B0 falls with salience (.81 to .61), so edits of well-known facts that hold at B0 are marginal and could flip under any perturbation. Edit strength (AUC .661 in Study 2) may be the mediator. Base confidence may drive the own-loss line. There is no joint model within Study 2 and no B0 resampling noise floor by stratum. Only the registered confidence-quartile check covers one of the three.

Several smaller statements outrun the evidence. (1) 'Repairs fall with size (1.5B .153 to 70B .085)' compares across families, and the within-family paired differences include 0 (-.052 [-.119, .010]; -.065 [-.130, .000]). (2) 'Matched the first study' compares well-known facts in Study 2 (+.242) with all of Study 1 (+.216), instead of with Study 1's well-known facts (+.298, or +.276 on matched hardware). (3) 'The other facts showed neither' hides a significantly negative excess loss (-.090 [-.174, -.011]). (4) 'Registered before any data' is not yet true: the addendum is unfrozen, and the 70B deltas, whose lp_first logs feed secondary analysis 5, already exist. (5) The Darrieux chain in the opening paragraph is an invented illustration, not a logged chain.
fixes: Restate the puzzle on matched engine and hardware. Compare Study 1's facts rerun on engine v2 on the H100 (G0-H100) with Study 2. Excess loss goes from +.207 to +.029 (difference -.178, p = .019). Erosion falls by .110 while repairs are unchanged. ES drop goes from .085 to .037 and is not significantly different. Keep the original Study 1 numbers inside the Study 1 section only, never in a cross-study contrast. In hero panel (a), plot G0-H100 (+.276 / +.111) next to Study 2 (+.242 / -.090). Lead the abstract with excess loss rather than ES drop.

Before freezing the addendum, add an interpretation rule. The claim that reasoning undoes edits of well-known facts is made only if H4 passes AND the edited-loss component (well known minus other) or the ES-drop difference has a CI excluding 0. If the pass rests on the own-answer component alone, write that the baseline, not the edit, varies with salience. Rewrite the confirmed sentence to say what D is, for example: 'edited answers were lost in excess of the model's own answers more for widely known facts (D = ...)'.

Register a quantitative 70B prediction now. With Study 2's 32B strata and the 70B pool's 27% well-known share, the overall excess loss is about .27(.242) + .73(-.090), or roughly 0. With Study 1's 70B strata it is about +.17. State which one is the prediction. Then pre-write the full matrix of result sentences, H4 {pass, fail, untested} by 70B H1/H2 {pass, fail}, and put the 70B outcome in abstract sentence 5 of every variant.

Complete Table 3. Add row 0, expected shrinkage from selecting checkpoints by significance (winner's curse), with a rough shrinkage estimate. Add a row recording the threshold history (E6 planned 7B-known and 4/4; 3 to 4 adopted in E6b) and report the 4/4 and 7B-known splits beside it. Apply one replication bar to every candidate, and say plainly that salience passes it on Study 1 point estimates only.

Run cheap exploratory confound checks that need no GPU. Within Study 2, model erosion and excess loss jointly on salience, edit strength (lp_first after the edit) and the base model's B0 confidence. Report ES drop by salience as the endpoint that involves the edit only. Add a B0-resampling noise floor by stratum wherever sampled runs exist. Label all of it exploratory in a single sentence.

Write the not-confirmed version around a measurement thesis rather than a failed guess. For example: 'Measured against the model's own answers on fresh, pre-registered facts, reasoning-time loss of edits at Qwen-32B is small and not specific to the edit. A single selected pool had overstated it.' Make the opening outcome-neutral ('This paper asks how large the effect really is and what made it look large'). Change 'pointed to one cause' to 'suggested a candidate'. Write a conditional title for Section 7 now.

Fix the slips. Drop the cross-family repair trend, or state the within-family paired differences with their CIs. Compare well-known facts with well-known facts. Say that excess loss for the other facts was negative. Write 'registered before any generation' and list the existing delta logs in the addendum's data-seen table. Replace the Darrieux chain with a logged chain or mark it as an illustration. Confirm that the W1 and W2 case_ids do not overlap Study 1's 200.
Make the abstract readable: at most 6 numbers, no CIs. Sentence 4 needs only +.242 against -.090 and 59% against 39%. Move the per-test p values and CIs to the body and Table 2.

Rebalance the space. Cut Section 5 to about 1 page (Table 3 plus Figure 1b) and give the registered Section 6 equal or greater weight, so that the post hoc search does not outweigh the confirmatory test.

Check positioning against work on entity popularity and long-tail effects in editability and parametric recall (PopQA-style popularity, popular-versus-long-tail editing studies). Claim novelty only for the interaction of salience with reasoning under a control on the model's own answers, not for salience affecting editability in itself.

verdict.restated_thesis: In R1-distilled reasoning models with single ROME edits, the extra loss of edited answers after reasoning, measured against the model's own unedited answers, shows up mainly for facts that smaller sibling models also know. A first study overstated the general effect because its fact pool held too many such facts. A pre-registered replication on fresh facts at Qwen-32B mostly failed. A registered test on new pools (Llama-70B and fresh Qwen-32B) then checks the salience explanation. So whether an evaluation finds that "reasoning undoes edits" depends on which facts it tests.
best_ideas: Use the registered failure as the turn of the paper ('It did not.'). It is rare in NLP, it builds credibility, and it is the most direct answer to mTGu's multiplicity and post hoc scope objection. Keep it in the main text.

Let structure carry evidential status: section titles, a status column in Table 1, and panel labels marking exploratory vs registered. The sentences can then be plain and confident. This is the right cure for the old paper's hedging in every sentence.

Make the paired, within-fact excess loss (edited answer lost minus the model's own answer lost, only on facts the model knew) the edit-specific estimand. It answers the AI review's 'no formal edited-vs-base contrast' and 'reversion undefined without per-checkpoint qualification' at once.
The dose-response panel with two lines (edited loss and own-answer loss), n at each point and the shaded gap is the most informative single graphic in the project. Keep both lines everywhere.
A title that works in both outcomes ('When Does Reasoning Undo a Knowledge Edit? ...'), and pre-written result sentences committed before any data exists.
'Reasoning re-decides edits in both directions' (breaks vs repairs) is a clean conceptual frame that keeps net drops in perspective.

Demote the think-span intervention to one Discussion paragraph with no mediation claim, and move the engineering (engine parity, BOS, hashes, deviation log) to the appendix. This gives one story instead of three.
End with a concrete evaluator takeaway: test edits after reasoning, compare against the model's own answers, and report the composition of the test pool.
fatal_problems: The thesis misstates what the data show. In Study 1 at Qwen-32B, edited-answer loss is the same for well-known and other facts (.386 vs .379; the G0 reruns give .345/.333 and .400/.346). All of the salience difference there comes from the control arm: the model's own answers are lost .088 vs .345 (explore_s1s2.json, E6b). In Study 2, half the gradient is the own-answer line falling (.39 to .06). So 'reasoning undoes edits of facts even small models know and mostly spares the rest' is false for Study 1 and overstated for Study 2, where 'the rest' still lose .135. A reviewer will call it near-tautological: low-salience facts are ones the 32B barely knows, so its own B0 answer regresses after reasoning. H4 as drafted tests only the contrast D, so it can pass entirely on control-arm stability and then be sold as 'reasoning undoes edits of well-known facts'.

The 'puzzle solved' arc overclaims. The intro says 'One variable did', but reweighting by composition closes only about half of the contrast gap (.029 to ~.13 against .216). It closes only about 30% of the edited-loss shrinkage the proposal itself locates in Section 4 (.386 to .199; recomputed .199 to ~.25). Most of that shrinkage is inside the low-salience stratum (.379 to .135), which salience does not explain. Sections 4 and 5 therefore contradict each other on the paper's own numbers. In addition, the Table 3 row 'Selection rule: no' is mislabelled. E2 re-applied Study 2's qualification rule within Study 1's candidates, which were already sampled by Qwen-7B recall after reasoning. That sampling is exactly mTGu's concern, and it remains untested as the source of the low-stratum difference.

The novelty of the moderator is unpositioned and its construct is idiosyncratic. Popularity and frequency effects on parametric knowledge and on edit robustness are an established line (PopQA/Mallen et al. 2023, Kandpal et al. 2023, and popularity-vs-robust-editing studies such as Ma et al. 2024; verify exact claims). They predict 'well-known facts resist editing', and the proposal parks them as 'check before submission' in a half-page late Related Work. 'Well-known' is operationalised as 'known by 3 of 4 sibling R1 distills', which is not well-known in the world. Without an external popularity measure, a reviewer reduces the contribution to 'a known popularity effect, observed under reasoning, at one 32B model'. The broader 'reasoning makes edits look worse' claim is already occupied (He et al. 2025, ThinkEval, CODE, Gao et al., CRANE).

The headline depends on a test with zero rows generated, about 4–5 H100 hours of work, 2 days before the deadline, and power of about .75 at the planned D. The 'results pending' variant is below ARR threshold. The architecture pre-writes only an H4 pass/fail pair, although the registered 70B H1/H2 on the same rows can independently confirm or contradict the abstract. As proposed, I would expect ARR overall scores around 3 (Findings-level) if H4 is confirmed and 2–2.5 if not, short of 3.5.
fixes: SINGLE HIGHEST-LEVERAGE CHANGE. Make the thesis rest on the decomposition, not the contrast, and lock that in before the addendum (still a DRAFT) is frozen. Register 'edited loss, high minus low > 0' as co-primary with D, or pre-write the rule that the sentence 'reasoning undoes edits of well-known facts' is used only if the edited-loss component passes. Otherwise the thesis becomes the entrenchment version: 'edit-specific loss appears only where the model's own answer survives reasoning'. Promote the registered base-confidence quartile check from appendix to main text. This pre-empts the tautology objection that would otherwise sink the paper.

Rewrite the thesis so it matches both studies. For example: 'Reasoning gives the model's prior a second vote. For facts the model holds firmly, edits are lost after reasoning far more often than the model's own answers; for weakly held facts both are unstable. So measured reasoning-time edit loss depends on how entrenched the tested facts are.' Delete 'mostly spares the rest'.

Add an external popularity measure (Wikipedia pageviews or link counts of the subject). It needs no GPU and can be fetched from the 4090 node. Register it as a secondary in the addendum before freeze and report its correlation with the sibling-distill proxy. Call the variable 'well-known' only if the two agree; otherwise call it 'known to smaller models' or 'entrenched'.

Recalibrate the puzzle. Replace 'One variable did' with 'One variable accounts for about half'. Rename the Table 3 row to 'qualification rule, re-applied within Study 1's candidates' and add a row 'candidate sampling by Qwen-7B recall after reasoning: not separable with current data'. Owning mTGu's point is worth more than claiming closure. Say in Section 5 that the low-salience stratum changed between studies (edited loss .379 to .135) and that this remains unexplained.

Hero figure panel (a) must show the components for both studies, not only contrasts: Study 1 at 32B, edited .386/.379 and own .088/.345; Study 2, edited .313/.135 and own .071/.225. As designed, panel (a) hides that Study 1's moderation sits entirely in the control arm, and a reviewer who finds this in the appendix will distrust the whole figure.

Rebuild the abstract for readability. It now carries about 13 numbers, the thesis arrives only in sentence 5, and sentence 4 runs about 60 words, which repeats the old abstract's diagnosed failure. Use: S1 problem (certified directly, used after reasoning); S2 the thesis in plain words; S3 first study, with one number; S4 the registered replication failed, with one number; S5 the post hoc locus plus the registered test result. Keep at most 5 numbers and keep every sentence under about 35 words. Compare like with like ('Study 1 well-known +.30, Study 2 well-known +.24'), not a Study 2 stratum against the Study 1 overall figure.

Pre-write the full outcome matrix now: {H4 pass, fail, untested} × {70B H2 pass, fail}. Before freeze, write into the addendum the overall 70B effect that salience predicts given 27% well-known facts, so that a null 70B H2 reads as predicted. If 70B H1/H2 pass, that registered positive belongs in the abstract.

Make a go/no-go decision on the deadline. If neither primary H4 world completes by Oct 12, do not submit the 'pending' version. A reviewed, below-threshold ARR record costs more than waiting one cycle with a tested thesis.

Reallocate the 8 pages. Cut Section 5 to about 1.0 page by collapsing ruled-out explanations into Table 3, with one line each and a column for the order they were tried. Give Section 6 about 1.2 pages: per-world D, both components, the external-popularity check and the confidence check. Grow Related Work to about 0.7 pages, and move the popularity/entrenchment positioning (Mallen 2023, Kandpal 2023, the popularity-vs-edit-robustness work, Superficial Editing) into intro P4. That positioning is now the main novelty threat, not MQuAKE or Ju et al.

Fix number hygiene. 'Repairs fall with size (1.5B .153 to 70B .085)' mixes model families and is not significant: the paired Δ repair for 32B−1.5B is −.052 [−.119, .010] and for 70B−8B is −.065 [−.130, .000]. Drop it or state it as a non-significant trend within each family. Use unfiltered Llama-70B (.110, Holm .022, +.234) throughout. The Section 4 decomposition (.386 to .199 edited loss; own loss .170 to .170) is verified against the strata in explore_s1s2.json and can be used.

In Setup, state that per-fact outcomes after reasoning are noisy: the same 200 facts agree only .81 at B3 across GPU types, and 61% of direct successes fail in at least one of three sampled reasoning runs. This is why every estimand is a paired population rate. It pre-empts a reproducibility attack and explains why strata with n of about 30–60 need registered confirmation.

The opening hook must quote a real logged chain. Darrieux is CounterFact's canonical first example and the proposed chain ('recall that she was a French film star') is hypothetical. Use an actual recorded chain from a well-known fact, since that also previews the thesis.

Add a practical significance sentence to the intro. The edits people actually want to make (heads of state, CEOs, rosters, other post-cutoff updates) tend to be about well-known, entrenched facts, which is exactly the stratum where reasoning restores the old answer. This is the 'why care' hook the puzzle framing currently lacks.

titles: Thinking Undoes Editing for the Facts a Model Knows Best (use only if H4 is confirmed)
Oseberg Is Still in Norway: Reasoning Models Undo Edits to Well-Known Facts (use only if H4 is confirmed; the vivid-case title)
Thinking Undoes Some Knowledge Edits: A Discovery, a Failed Replication, and a Pre-Registered Test (works for either H4 outcome, and for the case where H4 has not run)
scored.thesis: The better known a fact is, the more likely a reasoning model is to think its way back to it after the fact has been edited.

verdict.restated_thesis: From the abstract alone: a knowledge edit that passes a direct question can be undone when a reasoning model thinks before answering, because the model reasons its way back to the original fact. A first study found this happening often. A pre-registered replication on new facts found a much smaller effect. The authors attribute the difference to how well known the facts were, and a second pre-registered test is said to confirm that edits of well-known facts are the ones thinking undoes. So direct-answer tests overstate how well edits hold, especially for well-known facts. I could repeat this only after sentence 4 of 5. Sentences 2 and 3 read as lab history, not as the claim. As a cold reader I also could not tell how much the effect shrank: sentence 2 gives a ratio ('twice as often') and sentence 3 gives differences (+.029).
best_ideas: The opening paragraph is the best prose in the proposal. It shows the concrete Oseberg case with short verbatim chain excerpts before any definition, and it has a memorable line: 'The edit changed what the model says when asked; it did not change what the model can work out.' A reader outside knowledge editing understands the phenomenon in about 100 words. Keep it almost verbatim.

Using the failed pre-registered replication as the turn of the paper, not hiding it. This is honest, and it gives the second half a real question ('same model, same editor, same protocol, different facts: which difference matters?'). Keep the pivot sentence.

Section 2 gives one 'because' for each design decision: single edits, two ways of asking, scoring the generated answer, using only facts the model knows, the contrast with the model's own answers, Holm. This answers my old complaint directly and briefly.

Define the key measure in plain words: the share of edited answers lost after thinking minus the share of the model's own answers lost after thinking, on the same facts. Readers see what it controls for without a formula.

Table 3 lists the candidate explanations of the shrinkage, each with its test, its number and a one-word verdict. It is transparent and compact, and it also shows readers that salience was found by elimination.

A hero figure that ties the case to the pattern (Oseberg as a tagged point), with exploratory points in grey and hollow markers and confirmatory points in colour. The encoding itself shows the evidential status, so the prose does not need hedges.

Structural hygiene: at most three technical terms, all limitations in one section with no hedging elsewhere, engineering (engine parity, BOS, hashes, deviation log) moved to the appendix, and a real ethics statement.
Title option 3 and the 'one edit in four is re-decided, in both directions' result are robust whatever H4 shows. That result is the safest load-bearing fact the paper has.
fatal_problems: The salience 'explanation' of the shrinkage, which the architecture calls 'Third, why' and puts in abstract sentence 4 as 'traced the shrinkage to', is contradicted by the project's own numbers (explore_s1s2.json, E6b). In Study 1 at Qwen-32B, edited loss is the same for well-known and other facts: .386 vs .379 (G0 reruns: .345/.333 and .400/.346). There, the high-minus-low contrast comes entirely from the model's own answers (.088 vs .345). REVISION section 8 places the whole shrinkage in edited answers lost (.386 to .199), with own-answer loss flat at .170. Fact composition cannot produce that. If you reweight Study 1's 32B strata to Study 2's mix (about 36% well known in the retention set): edited loss stays near .38; the contrast moves only from about .21 to about .13, against an observed .029, so composition covers at most about 45% of the gap and through the wrong component; and own-answer loss should rise to about .25 in Study 2, yet it stays at .170. Section 5, the claimed climax, is built on a claim the data do not support even as an exploratory finding.

The thesis sentence and H4 measure different quantities. The thesis is about the edited component ('the more likely a reasoning model is to think its way back to it after the fact has been edited'). H4's D is a difference in the retention contrast. In Study 2, roughly half of D comes from own-answer loss falling with salience (about .23 vs .07), not from edited loss rising (about .13 vs .31). In Study 1 at 32B, all of D comes from own-answer loss. H4 could therefore pass with no difference in edited loss, and the paper would then state a thesis its test did not establish. The draft addendum's section 7 pass rule ('central claim: reasoning undoes edits of entrenched facts; salience composition is offered as the explanation') builds in the same mismatch. The addendum is still a draft, so this can be fixed now.

The climax rests on data that does not exist two days before the deadline. The H4 addendum is marked 'DRAFT, not frozen', no W1 or W2 row exists, and the W2 edits still have to be made. The phrase 'pre-registered before any of its data existed' is not yet true. The most likely state at submission is H4 registered but not run, or only one world done, and no abstract is drafted for it. In that state the second half of the paper is a failed replication plus an untested post hoc explanation, the weakest form of this paper. The architecture is not robust to its most probable outcome.

The abstract repeats the problem that sank the last one. It is 243 words (ACL asks for about 200 or fewer). It carries about 15 numbers, where the rejected abstract was diagnosed as too dense with 7. Sentence 4 runs about 80 words with two parentheticals and an undefined 'D'. One quantity has two names ('excess loss' in the abstract, 'retention contrast' in the body). Sentences 2 and 3 use incompatible units, a ratio and then differences, so the shrinkage is not visible. My undefined-term count for an outsider is about 8: ROME, CounterFact, distills, direct test, edit success, excess loss, D, pool. The motivation also has a gap. Nothing says why an edit should survive (updating facts that changed, removing knowledge that should not be recalled). Because the example is a false fact (Oseberg in Bulgaria), a cold reader sees the model correctly rejecting misinformation, and the failure reads as a feature.

The hero figure is selective. It plots the Study 2 exploratory curve, where edited loss rises from .13 to .31, and the H4 worlds. It leaves out Study 1, where the 32B edited-loss line is flat. It then tags Oseberg, a Study 1 case, on the Study 2 curve, which implies the case illustrates a pattern its own study does not show. Separately, Section 5.2 offers 'the same split on Study 1's facts' as corroboration, but in Study 1 the high-minus-low difference is not significant at any model (p = .068, .25, .091).
fixes: Before freezing the addendum, align the thesis and the test. Option A: state the thesis at the level of the contrast, for example: 'Thinking pulls a reasoning model toward whatever it holds most firmly: for well-known facts that is the original answer, so edits are lost more often than the model's own answers; for obscure facts, thinking unsettles the model's own answers more than the edits.' Option B: keep the edited-component thesis and make edited loss (high minus low) a co-primary in H4, with Holm across the two tests. Rewrite the section 7 pass rule so it licenses only what the passed test measures.

Drop the causal wording about the shrinkage ('traced the shrinkage to', 'Third, why', 'What changed', 'explains it'). Add a reweighting row to Table 3: Study 1's strata reweighted to Study 2's salience mix, reported for each component. Say plainly that composition accounts for at most about half of the contrast gap and none of the drop in edited loss, and that the rest is unexplained. Retitle Section 5 as a claim about where the edit-specific loss sits, not about why the replication shrank.

Use two tiers of thesis so the spine survives every outcome. Tier 1, robust and in both studies: a direct-answer test cannot certify an edit in a reasoning model, because thinking re-decides about one edit in four, in both directions (lost .14, gained .105, against .101 gained in Study 1). Tier 2, conditional: whether the net is an edit-specific loss depends on how well known the fact is, and H4 is its prospective test. Page 1 then never depends on unrun data.

Write the third abstract ('H4 registered, not yet run', or one world only) now. Freeze the addendum today, before any W2 edit exists. Set a dated go/no-go: if neither W1 nor W2 is complete by a fixed hour on Oct 11, either submit the Tier-1 version or move to the next ARR cycle. Decide this before the data arrives, not after.

Rebuild the abstract to at most 200 words and at most 6 numbers. Sentence 1: why edits must hold, plus the evaluation mismatch. Sentence 2: the Oseberg case, shortened. Sentence 3: the main finding in one unit, for example 'edited answers were lost 2.3 times as often as the model's own answers in a first study, but only 1.2 times as often in a pre-registered replication on new facts' (.386/.170 and .199/.170). Sentence 4: where the loss concentrates, plus the H4 result in words with a single number. Sentence 5: the implication. Put the thesis no later than sentence 3. Remove D, CIs and p-values from the abstract.

Add one motivation clause before the counterfactual example, along these lines: 'Editing is meant to update facts that change or remove facts a model should not state; benchmarks test it with counterfactual edits so that the new answer can only come from the edit.' This blocks the reading that the model was right to reject the edit.

Make the hero figure honest. Add Study 1 (32B and 70B) as another grey hollow series, or plot the per-salience contrast (what H4 tests) for every available set of facts instead of the two components. Label Oseberg as a Study 1 case. Report in the text that the Study 1 high-minus-low differences are individually non-significant.

Use one name per quantity throughout. Choose 'retention contrast' or a plainer phrase such as 'edit-specific loss', and use it in the abstract, figure and body. Replace 'salience' (outsiders hear attention or saliency maps) with 'how widely known' or 'familiarity', and cite the popularity literature (PopQA). Remove internal jargon from the main text and the figure: 'worlds', 'pool', 'erosion/repair' (use 'lost/gained'), 'W1/W2'.

Use claim titles, not story-beat labels: 'Discovery:', 'The turn:' and 'What changed:' read as staged narration. For example: '3 Thinking undoes edits more often than the model's own answers'; '4 On new facts the effect is much smaller'; '5 The edit-specific loss sits in well-known facts'.

Remove prose tics that read as generated text. The 'certified by asking / used by letting them think' line appears in abstract sentence 1, intro paragraph 1 and intro paragraph 2; use it once. Use the 'X did A; it did not do B' antithesis once. Cut the not-confirmed abstract's closing 'we report both studies, both pre-registrations and the failed predictions in full'. It reads as defensive; end on a finding or a recommendation.

Fix accuracy before printing anything.
