(a) Salience was measured differently in the two studies (Study 1's own base runs vs Study 2's screen files); check that the 59% vs 39% comparison is like for like. (b) For Llama-70B, use .110 with Holm .022 as primary and correct the brief. (c) Footnote the 32B +.216 for the BOS format mismatch, or use a same-format estimate in 'about twice'. (d) Reconcile He et al. 2025: the project's related-work notes describe it as realistic autoregressive evaluation, not R1 thinking budgets, which contradicts the proposal's novelty-collision risk item. Position against it accurately in intro paragraph 2.

Put the edit-strength confound in the main text next to the salience result, not only in Limitations. Direct edit success falls from .81 to .61 across salience bins, and edit strength predicts loss in Study 2 (AUC .661). Report D stratified by direct edit success or edit strength alongside the base-confidence quartiles. Keep the claim at the level of behaviour.

verdict.restated_thesis: When a reasoning model thinks before answering, it sometimes reasons its way back to a fact that was edited away, but mostly for facts that are widely known. A first study's pool happened to be full of well-known facts, so it found a large loss. A pre-registered replication on a more representative pool found a small, non-significant loss. A second pre-registered test on new data checks whether well-known facts are where edits fail. The practical lesson is that edits should be evaluated after thinking, stratified by how well known the fact is, and replicated on fresh pools.
best_ideas: Making the failed pre-registered H1/H2 at 32B the turning point of the paper (Section 4), not a footnote. For a registered-reports reader this is the most credible structure available. It keeps the failure visible in the abstract, in Table 2 (pass/fail marks) and in the narrative.

The crossing lines in the hero figure. As salience rises, edited-answer loss rises (.13 to .31) while the model's own-answer loss falls (.39 to .06). The shaded gap is the retention contrast. Grey hollow markers show the exploratory data and coloured solid markers show the pre-registered data. This is honest by construction and works whichever way H4 comes out.

Table 3 lists the candidate explanations (hardware, qualification rule, base recall in the chain, relation mix, edit strength, salience), each with its test, number and verdict. Salience is the last row, marked post hoc, and the text says it was the sixth explanation tried. This answers forking-paths worries in the open.

Making the retention contrast (edited loss minus own-answer loss, paired within each fact) the headline measure. It directly answers the AI review's 'no edited-vs-base contrast' and replaces the discredited permissive reversion metric.

Section 2 gives one 'because' per design decision. Limitations live in one section only and there is no hedging elsewhere. The main text uses at most three terms. This fixes TRfT's complaints without filling the prose with defensive clauses.
Reporting erosion and repair (edits lost and gained) side by side, so thinking is shown to re-decide edits in both directions rather than only destroy them.
Title option 3 is chosen in advance to fit every H4 outcome, and both abstract variants are written before the data exists, which follows addendum section 7.
Turning mTGu's selection critique into the object of study (a less selected pool is exactly where the effect shrinks) instead of rebutting it.
fatal_problems: The composition explanation is overclaimed in both abstracts and in Section 5 ('traced the shrinkage to how well known the facts were'; 'which is why Study 1's effect was large'). Reweighting Study 2's strata (high +.242, low -.090) to Study 1's 59% high share gives about +.106 against Study 1's +.21. Composition therefore explains roughly 40% of the shrinkage. The low stratum itself also differs between studies (Study 1 low +.03 to +.13, Study 2 low -.090). In addition, H4 tests moderation (D > 0 on new data), not whether composition explains the S1 to S2 gap. 'A second test confirmed it' is therefore a category error even if H4 passes.

Section 5.2 presents Study 1 as independent corroboration ('the same split gives +.28 to +.32 vs +.03 to +.13'). This repeats the brief's difference-in-significance error. In explore_s1s2.md the high-minus-low difference is non-significant in all five Study 1 runs (32B +.264 p=.068; G0-H100 +.165 p=.28; G0-4090 p=.098; 14B +.152 p=.25; 70B +.198 p=.091). It is consistent in direction, but it is not a replication of the interaction.

The 59% vs 39% composition comparison is partly circular. Qwen-7B selected Study 1's pool (old answer named after thinking) and is also one of the four salience probes, so Study 1 facts mechanically gain about one probe hit. 'The 7B-after-thinking filter favoured well-known facts' cannot be claimed from a salience measure that includes the 7B.

W1 is not new facts. I checked the manifests: the Llama-70B pool shares 254 of 400 case_ids with the Study 2 32B pool used to form H4, and has 0 overlap with the fresh 32B pool. 'Pre-registered before any of its data existed' is true for generated rows, but salience moderation was already seen on 64% of W1's facts. The proposal never discloses this, and a registered-reports reviewer will find it.

The test statistic and the thesis do not match. D is a difference in retention contrast, and about half of the exploratory D (.332) comes from the own-answer component (base loss .39 at 0/4 vs about .07 at 3-4/4), not from edited loss. The confirmed abstract and the thesis ('thinking undid edits of well-known facts more'; 'think its way back to it') make an edited-loss claim. If H4 passes mainly through the base component, the headline sentence would print a claim that the test did not establish.

The Oseberg tag on the hero figure mixes pools and engines. Oseberg is a Study 1 case from the old HF engine and is not in the Study 2, W1 or W2 manifests. Its '3 of 4' count would come from Study 1 base runs, not the frozen qualify files. Placing it at x = 3 on Study 2/W1/W2 curves breaks the project's own rule against mixing engine-v2 and HF numbers. 'The reader sees that the example and the general pattern are the same thing' is a rhetorical claim a single cherry-picked case cannot carry.

The not-confirmed abstract softens the reporting rule fixed in addendum section 7. That rule says the H4-fails paper is framed around 'smaller than Study 1 estimated, and not edit-specific on a fresh pool'; the draft says only 'smaller than a single study suggested'. It also still opens with a cherry-picked loss case and Study 1's selected-pool '2x' estimate. Its fallback thesis ('one edit in four, both directions') is not edit-specific: own answers are also lost at .170, B3 outcomes disagree 19% across GPUs on identical facts, and the sampling noise floor is 34%. That presents reasoning instability as an editing finding.

A factual error: 'Every rate is computed on facts the evaluated model itself answers correctly before editing' (Section 2 and the AI-review answer). This is false for Study 1's headline ES drops. The .106 and .110 are over all 198-200 cases. The per-model qualified drops are .125 [.033, .217] and .153 [.076, .229], and Holm was run on the unqualified family.
fixes: Rewrite abstract sentence 4 and Section 5.2 quantitatively. For example: 'On well-known facts the fresh pool reproduced Study 1's effect (retention contrast +.24 vs +.21); on the rest it vanished (-.09); reweighting to Study 1's composition recovers about 40% of the gap.' Then say the prospective test checked 'that the loss concentrates in well-known facts', not that it 'confirmed' the shrinkage explanation.

The addendum is still marked DRAFT, so add these before freezing it and before any W1/W2 row exists. (a) A secondary analysis: D on the 146 W1 facts that are not in the Study 2 32B pool. (b) A secondary analysis: D within edit-strength strata (post-edit first-token log p of o_old, as in E5), because 'well-known facts just get weaker edits' is the reviewer's first alternative and secondary 5 (pre-edit base confidence) does not cover it. (c) A descriptive comparison of S1 vs S2 composition using salience computed without Qwen-7B.

Disclose the 254/400 overlap in Section 5.3 and turn it into a design feature. W2 tests the same model on new facts; W1 tests a new model on mostly the same facts. Report D_m for each world next to the pooled D-bar. Write 'in a pooled test over Llama-70B and a fresh 32B pool', not 'confirmed on Llama-70B and a fresh 32B pool'.

Fix a wording rule now, before the data. The thesis sentence about edits being undone is printed only if D-bar passes AND the edited-loss component (secondary 3a, high minus low) has a CI above 0. If D passes mainly through the own-answer component, use instead: 'relative to the model's own answers, edits of well-known facts are less stable after thinking'.

Replace the two-way abstract split with four pre-written variants, each with a fixed slot for the registered H1/H2 at 70B from W1: confirmed; inconclusive (CI spans both 0 and the planned D = .15, which is likely given power of about .75, or about .45 if only one world completes); disconfirmed (CI excludes .15); and not run. 'Not confirmed' must not read as 'disconfirmed'.

Align the not-confirmed abstract with the addendum's section 7 rule, word for word. It should say that on a fresh pool edited answers were not lost detectably more often than the model's own (+.029, upper CI .097). Report 'one in four re-decided' only next to the own-answer loss (.170) and the hardware/sampling noise floors. Lead with the registered result, not Study 1's 2x.

Choose the hero case by a rule committed now and apply it to W1/W2 rows. For example: the lowest case_id high-salience case with ES@B0 = 1, ES@B3 = 0, base keeping o_old at B3, and no name leakage. Otherwise keep Oseberg in the left panel only, captioned as a Study 1 illustration, and remove the x = 3 tag from the right panel. In the not-confirmed world, show a gained edit next to the lost one.

Report Study 1 with the per-model qualified ES drop (.125 / .153) next to the unqualified Holm-tested .106 / .110, so the 'facts the model knows' rule is literally true. Add Holm across the six models for the Study 1 retention contrasts as well.

In Section 5.2, give the Study 1 high-minus-low differences with CIs and call them 'same direction, not significant in any Study 1 run'. Also state in one sentence that E5b, E6 and E6b were added after earlier results were seen.

Fix the titles. 'For the Facts a Model Knows Best' is wrong, because salience is knowledge in other, smaller models and every qualified fact is known by the evaluated model. Use 'Thinking Undoes Edits to Well-Known Facts'. Drop the Oseberg title, since it puts a cherry-picked case in the headline. In option 3, change 'A Discovery' to something like 'A Selected-Pool Effect', given He et al. 2025.

In the confirmed abstract, change 'overstate how well edits hold ..., most of all for well-known facts' to 'for well-known facts'. On the fresh pool the less-known stratum shows no overstatement (ES drop -.012, retention contrast -.090).

Section 4's pivot sentence 'same model, same editor, same protocol, different facts' hides the engine and hardware change. Write 'same model and editor; on matched hardware the gap persists (E1: retention -.178, p = .019)'.

Cut Section 3.3 to one paragraph that reports only same-format contrasts (T-N +.138, and D-P once recomputed in rt.study1), or move it to the appendix. Its registered replication (H3) never ran, it carries the BOS split, and it competes with the salience thread for the reader's attention.

Simplify the hero figure. Use small multiples (Study 2 exploratory | W1 | W2), with bin n printed under the x axis, and merge or flag the 0/4 bin (n = 31). Thirty CI-bearing points in two thirds of a column will not be readable at body font size.

Use one term only: 'well-known (named by 3-4 of 4 smaller distills)'. Do not alternate between salience and well-known. Fix erosion at .143 (REVISION section 8), not 14.2%, after recomputing from study2.json.

verdict.restated_thesis: Asked directly, a reasoning model repeats an edited fact; after it thinks, it often reasons its way back to the original fact, and this happens mostly for widely known facts. The paper shows this through a six-model discovery study, a pre-registered replication that found a much smaller and non-significant effect, a post hoc explanation (the two fact pools differ in how well known their facts are), and a prospective pre-registered test of that explanation.
best_ideas: Opening on the Oseberg case before any definition: the 'answer directly' strip ends in Bulgaria and the 'think first' strip ends in Norway. This answers TRfT's complaint that motivation was missing, in the first paragraph and the first sentence of the abstract.

Using the failed pre-registered replication as the paper's turn rather than burying it. 'Same model, same editor, same protocol, different facts: which difference matters?' is a real hook. Few NLP papers can tell a story of discovery, failed replication and prospective test.

A hero figure that puts the vivid case on the general pattern as a labelled point. Exploratory points are grey and hollow, pre-registered points are in colour, and the figure is designed to work whichever way H4 comes out.

The positioning contrast: prior work (MQuAKE, Ju et al. 2024) shows edits fail to spread outward to their consequences, while here the neighbourhood the edit left untouched flows back in under the model's own reasoning. It is memorable and turns the AI review's missing-citation complaint into the paper's frame.

Section 2 gives one 'because' per design decision (single edits, the two ways of asking, scoring generated answers, using only known facts, the contrast with the model's own answers, Holm correction). This is the right direct answer to 'design decisions unjustified'.

Table 3 lists the candidate explanations, each with its test and a one-word verdict, and says in one plain sentence that salience was the sixth explanation tried. This is the honest way to present forking paths.

Making the retention contrast (edited loss minus the model's own loss, paired per fact) the central measure. It answers the AI review's missing edited-versus-base contrast and is exactly the H4 estimand.
All limitations sit in one section and all engineering (G0, BOS, hashes, deviation log) goes to the appendix, with at most three main-text terms. Title option 3 works for every H4 outcome.
fatal_problems: The thesis does not match the measured quantity, and Study 1 contradicts it. H4's statistic D is a difference in the retention contrast (edited loss minus the model's own loss). In Study 1 the salience gap comes almost entirely from the model's own answers, not from edits. At Qwen-32B, edited loss is .386 for well-known facts and .379 for the rest; it is .345/.333 and .400/.346 in the two G0 reruns. The model's own loss is .088 against .345. H4 can therefore pass purely through the native component, which leaves 'the better known a fact is, the more likely a model is to think its way back to it' false while the abstract asserts it. 'Think its way back' also implies reverting to the old answer, but the metric is loss of edit success. Strict reversion at Study 1 32B is .092, against erosion of .207.

'Traced the shrinkage to how well known the facts were' overclaims, and the proposal's own pivot sets up an explanation the numbers do not support. Section 4 says the whole shrinkage sits in edited answers lost (.386 to .199), but Study 1's edited loss does not vary with salience. Study 2's low-salience edited loss (.135) is far below Study 1's (.379). By my arithmetic from explore_s1s2.json E6/E6b, reweighting Study 2's strata to Study 1's retention-set mix (66% vs 36% well-known) recovers about half of the retention-contrast gap (+.03 to about +.13, against +.21) and under a third of the edited-loss gap (to about .25, against .39). A reviewer who sees Table 3 next to the registered component secondary will find this.

The climax depends on a test that is neither frozen nor run, two days before the deadline. prereg-arr-addendum-salience.md is labelled 'DRAFT, not frozen'. REVISION section 8 says the compute platform ended on 10/8 and that 3 more H100 hours are still undecided. W2 also still needs 309 new ROME edits. Section 5.3 has no fallback content and the 'H4 not run' abstract is not written, although that is currently the most likely state. 'Pre-registered before any of its data existed' cannot be printed until the freeze commit and push exist.

The headline of the not-confirmed abstract is close to the noise floor. 'Thinking changes the outcome of one edit in four, in both directions' (14.2% lost + 10.5% gained) is reported without a reference rate. The same 200 facts agree on only 81% of after-thinking outcomes across the 4090 and H100 runs (E0), and sampling flips 34% of edits even when answering directly. Most of that 'one in four' can come from chaotic long generations rather than editing. With H1 and H2 failed, the not-confirmed paper has no robust positive result and cannot reach 3.5 under any narrative.

Salience may just be a proxy for edit strength, in the very pool that generated H4. In Study 2, direct edit success falls from .81 to .61 across salience bins, and post-edit strength predicts erosion (AUC .661). The registered robustness check (secondary 5) stratifies by the base's confidence before the edit, not by post-edit strength. A reviewer can say that 'well-known facts' simply means 'weaker edits', and nothing in the plan rebuts it.
fixes: SINGLE CHANGE THAT MOST RAISES THE SCORE: rebuild the thesis and the hero figure around the edit-specific contrast within salience strata, shown for every independent pool. Suggested thesis: 'For facts that models know well, thinking leaves the model's own answer intact but undoes about a third of edits; for obscure facts, thinking unsettles original and edited answers alike.' It holds in both existing studies (well-known: edited .39/.31 vs own .09/.07; others: .38/.14 vs .35/.22). It is exactly what D measures, it survives H4 passing through either component, and it turns the failed replication into a conditional replication: in the well-known stratum the studies agree (+.30 vs +.24), so it is the mix that differs. Plot the retention contrast against the number of smaller models that know the fact (0-4), one line per pool: Study 1 14B/32B/70B and Study 2 32B in grey with hollow markers, the prospective worlds in colour. Move the edited/own component lines to the appendix. In the proposed figure they would show a flat edited line for Study 1 32B, which visibly contradicts the thesis.

Freeze the H4 addendum today (commit, push and registry entry) before any W1 or W2 row is generated. Write the third abstract ('registered, not yet run') now. Set a go/no-go time, for example 11 Oct noon AoE. The not-run and not-confirmed versions score about 2.5 to 3.0 at best, so decide explicitly whether to submit them or hold for the next ARR cycle. Also fix now the abstract wording rule for the 70B H1/H2 outcome, which arrives with W1.

Replace 'traced the shrinkage to' with a quantified statement: 'well-known facts made up 59% of Study 1's pool and 39% of Study 2's; within each group the studies agree, and the difference in mix accounts for about half of the shrinkage.' Recompute the reweighted share in code first, then state the remainder as unexplained.

Run zero-GPU checks before drafting Section 5: (a) a joint model on Study 2 of erosion and retention against salience, post-edit first-token log p(o_old) and direct edit success, to show salience survives edit strength; (b) the share of lost edits that are strict reversions to the old answer, by salience, in both studies, and use 'thinks its way back' only if reversion dominates (otherwise say 'loses the edit'); (c) the edit-success drop by salience on Study 1's cases; (d) a noise floor, meaning the after-thinking flip rate of the unedited model across hardware and seeds, placed next to 'one in four'; (e) the Oseberg salience count from the salience code; (f) recompute D-P in rt.study1 or drop it.

Cut Section 3.3 (the intervention) to one exploratory sentence and move the rest to the appendix. It is a second causal story with a BOS confound, a D-P number not yet recomputed, an unrun registered replication (H3) and no link to the thesis. Compress Study 1 from 1.4 pages to about 1.0, and spend the freed 0.4 to 0.5 page on the edit-strength control and the within-stratum agreement in Section 5. State in the case-selection appendix that Oseberg was first chosen because the suppression arm restores Bulgaria.

Correct Section 2's sentence 'only facts the evaluated model answers correctly before editing are used'. It is false for Study 1's headline drop (.106 and .110), which is computed on the pool selected by 7B. Either make the qualified drop (.125 at 32B, .153 at 70B) primary for Study 1, with its own Holm correction, or state the exception.

Report the registered paraphrase result in Section 4: in Study 2, thinking raised paraphrase edit success (drop of -.083). 'Every registered result reported' requires it, and it bounds the title's claim.

Readability: in the main text, call the prospective test 'Study 3' and drop the H4/W1/W2 labels. Rename 'salience', which clashes with saliency and attribution in NLP, to something like 'how widely known'. The confirmed abstract has about 15 numbers, which repeats the old 7-number problem. Keep only the Study 3 effect with its CI in the abstract, and write sentence 3 as 'an effect a third as large; neither registered test passed'. Title: say 'the facts models know best', since salience is measured on other models.

Novelty: cite and concede the popularity precedent. Ma et al. 2024, 'Is It Possible to Edit Large Language Models Robustly?', reports that popular knowledge is harder to edit robustly (verify the exact claim), alongside RippleEdits' popular subset and PopQA. Also note that Gekhman et al. 2026 ('Thinking to Recall') and Superficial Editing together predict the base phenomenon. Rest the novelty claim on three things: the same question asked of the same edit with and without thinking, the contrast with the model's own answers, and a conditional replication across two independent pools plus a prospective test. Keep the 'untouched neighbourhood flows back in' line as interpretation only, because E3 found that the base model recalling the old answer in its own chain does not moderate the loss.

For the not-confirmed branch, open with a pair of cases (Oseberg lost, plus one edit gained by thinking) so that page 1 does not oversell a null result. Lead with what the replication bounds (an edit-specific loss of at most about .10 at 32B on a fresh pool) and with the protocol, not with 'one in four'.

titles: Test the Edit After the Model Thinks: Evaluating Knowledge Editing in Reasoning Models (works under either H4 outcome)
Reasoning Undoes Edits to Well-Known Facts, and Direct-Answer Tests Cannot See It (only if H4 is confirmed)
What a Direct Answer Cannot Certify: Knowledge Edits in Reasoning Models, Before and After Thinking (works under either H4 outcome)
scored.thesis: Test an edit after the reasoning model thinks, and report well-known facts separately: that is where reasoning undoes edits, and neither a direct answer nor a pooled average shows it.

verdict.restated_thesis: From the abstract alone, as a cold reader: people check a knowledge edit by reading the model's immediate answer, but reasoning models think before they answer, and that thinking can undo the edit. The authors' first study found this at the largest models. A registered replication on new facts did not. The difference turned out to be how familiar the test facts were, since thinking undoes edits to well-known facts much more than edits to obscure ones. So edits should be scored after thinking, against the unedited model, and reported separately for well-known and obscure facts. I could restate it, but only on a second pass. The claim I would repeat arrives in sentence 4 of 5, and the abstract reads as a log of the research process rather than a statement of what is true.
best_ideas: Using your own Study 1 as the cautionary example, with the failed registered replication as the turning point. This turns the paper's biggest weakness into its lesson, and it is the most memorable and honest structure I have seen for this material.
The opening's concrete Darrieux edit and the sentence 'Reasoning models are not used this way.' This is the first version where I understood in under 30 seconds what the mismatch is.

Making edited-versus-unedited loss the central measure and the two lines of the hero figure. It answers the AI review's missing-contrast point directly, and the crossing of the two lines is a picture a reader can repeat.

Saying early that 'reasoning re-decides edits in both directions' (14.2% broken, 10.5% repaired, and paraphrase raises edit success). It stops the negative low-familiarity stratum and the paraphrase result from reading as contradictions.
Table 1 with a one-line reason for every design choice, including subject masking justified by the 46/200 name leakage. This is exactly what my 'design decisions unjustified' complaint asked for.
Opening Section 6 with 'post hoc, the sixth explanation tried', and letting only Section 7 make the claim.
Conventional ACL order, the intervention and route census moved out of the main line, every limitation in one section, and a real ethics statement that covers undoing safety edits.
Tying each recommendation to what it would have changed in your own studies. This makes the practice section evidence rather than advice.
Fixing both abstract variants and both Section 7 titles before the data exist.
fatal_problems: The story depends on H4, and there is no real plan B. Recommendations 3 and 4, Table 3 and the hero figure all rest on the familiarity result. The registered power is .75 at D=.15, and that D was itself chosen after the fact. If H4 fails, the hero figure shows a post hoc pattern that did not replicate, and Section 8 keeps only 'score after thinking, compare with base, report both directions'. A reviewer will call those obvious. The paper then reads as an exploratory effect, a null replication and an unconfirmed moderator. A one-line fallback thesis is not a fallback structure. With two days left and the addendum not yet frozen, the 'H4 untested' case is also live, and the outline has no shape for it.

Recommendation 4 ('do not choose test facts by reasoning behaviour') is not what the evidence shows. E2 applied Study 2's direct-answer qualification rule to the Study 1 cases, and the effect stayed (+.154). What differs is that Study 1 was selected by a small model's recall. That small model, Qwen-7B, is also one of the four 'well-known' probes, so the 59% vs 39% composition gap is partly mechanical: selecting on 7B recall nearly guarantees one probe vote. A careful reviewer such as mTGu will catch both points, and the paper's main practical lesson will look misattributed.

Familiarity is confounded with edit strength, and nothing registered separates them. In Study 2, direct edit success falls from .81 to .61 across the familiarity bins, and the post-edit log p(o_old) predicts erosion (AUC .66, +.161, p=.001). The addendum's robustness test controls only the base model's confidence before the edit. A reviewer can read the whole result as 'ROME writes weaker edits over well-known facts', which makes it an editor-strength story and not a reasoning-and-familiarity story.

The key diagnostic, 'only one quantity moved' (edited loss .386 to .199, base loss steady at .170), uses Study 1's 32B base run, which had the input-format (BOS) mismatch. The proposal itself says to compare on the same engine. On the same-engine G0-H100 run, the components are roughly edited loss .34 and base loss .12. Compared with Study 2's .20 and .17, both components moved. The crisp sentence does not survive the comparison the proposal says it will use.

For a reader like me, readability regresses in the abstract. The confirmed variant carries about 10 statistics plus 3 placeholders, against the old abstract's 7, so the claim in reviews_answered is false. Its sentences run 40 to 55 words, and the clause 'rather than by anything it says while reasoning' only makes sense after Section 6. The central quantity has three names: 'excess loss' in the abstract, 'edit-specific loss' in the main text and 'retention contrast' in the pre-registration. Section 7 then brings in W1/W2/W3, D̄ and H1/H2/H4. With Study 1 and Study 2, that is about eight labels for me to track, on top of the three declared terms.
fixes: Rewrite the abstract as stakes, then a claim, then evidence. S1: editing is how deployed models are corrected without retraining, yet edits are checked on direct answers while reasoning models answer after thinking. S2: the finding in plain words. S3 and S4: the two studies, with at most 5 numbers. S5: what to measure. Keep sentences under 30 words, use 'edit-specific loss' everywhere (abstract included), and keep the selection-rule detail out of the abstract.

Opening: replace 'A knowledge editor' (which I first read as a person) with 'a knowledge-editing method such as ROME'. Add one clause on why edits matter (correcting outdated or harmful facts). Widen 'for anyone who builds or evaluates editors' to anyone who deploys an edited reasoning model; as written it tells most ARR reviewers the paper is not for them.

Restate Recommendation 4 as 'do not select test facts by whether some other (smaller) model recalls them, and report the pool's familiarity mix'. Add a sensitivity check that drops Qwen-7B from the probe set (familiarity from 1.5B, 14B and Llama-8B only), and show whether Study 1 stays more familiar than Study 2.

The addendum is still a draft, so add two registered secondary tests before freezing: (a) D within strata of post-edit strength (median split on lp_old_after, or matched on ES@B0), and (b) the familiarity measure without the probe that selected Study 1. If D survives (a), the confound is answered. If it does not, you learn this before writing.

Recompute the Study 1 vs Study 2 decomposition on G0-H100. Replace 'only one quantity moved' with whatever those numbers support (likely 'edited loss fell by about .14 while base loss rose by about .05'). Footnote that the original Study 1 base ran in a different input format.

Retitle Section 4 so it does not assert a claim that Section 5 then refutes. For example: 'Study 1: a first look finds edits undone at the largest models (exploratory)'. Alternatively, merge Sections 4 and 5 under 'Two studies, two answers'.

In the main-text prose, call the H4 worlds 'the 70B pool' and 'a fresh 32B pool', and the test 'the prospective test'. Keep W1/W2/W3, D̄ and H-labels in Table 3 only. Keep the introduction to 6 numbers or fewer; the .386/.199/.170 decomposition belongs in Section 5.

Build plan B fully now, not as a risk bullet. Write a not-confirmed hero figure, for example the paired-protocol figure of broken and repaired edits per model, with Study 1 vs Study 2 bars for edit-specific loss. Also write not-confirmed titles for Sections 6 to 8, a third abstract for the case where H4 is not run, and a hard go/no-go time on 10/11 for which version ships.

Simplify the hero figure. Use small multiples at the same y-scale (32B exploratory | 70B prospective | fresh 32B prospective) rather than hollow and filled markers from different models on one axis. Move the 59%/39% bars into the caption or Table 2. A two-panel figure with shaded crossings, CI bands and two marker types is exactly what I would squint at.

Calibrate several sentences. Say that the Study 1 strata 'point the same way (high minus low .15 to .26, all CIs include zero)', not that they 'split the same way'. Abstract S4 should say 'edit-specific loss is larger for well-known facts', not 'reasoning undoes edits to well-known facts more than the rest', because D is a contrast with the base. Section 3's 'greedy, so one deterministic answer' should be dropped, since the 4090 and H100 runs agree on only 81% of after-thinking outcomes; say 'one answer per condition on fixed hardware'.

In Table 1, explain why 'lost' is asymmetric: the edited answer is lost if the new value is absent or the old value appears, while the base answer is lost only if the old value is absent. State whether the asymmetry matters.

Expand related work to about 0.9 pages, and put He et al. 2025 in the introduction with a concrete difference (paired same-edit protocol, base contrast, registered replication, familiarity). Verify Mallen et al. 2023 before citing it, and re-search 2026 work on popularity, editing and reasoning together.

Make Section 7's 'frozen before any row existed' true before writing it. Freeze and push the addendum now, through an anonymised route (OSF or an anonymised mirror), because a personal GitHub timestamp breaks ARR's double-blind review.

Trim the stylistic tics I flagged as AI-like: the personification ('the edit may have lost the argument'), repeated 'X, not Y' closers, colon reveals ('the question is practical:') and five-item lists in both the introduction and Section 8. List the contributions once, in Section 8 only.

verdict.restated_thesis: Editors are usually checked by reading a reasoning model's direct answer. Scoring the same ROME edit after the model thinks first, an exploratory study found edits lost at the two largest R1 distills, about twice as often as the model's own answers. A pre-registered replication on fresh facts at 32B did not reproduce this. After the fact, the gap appears to depend on how well known the edited fact is, and the first pool held more well-known facts. A prospective registered test (H4) decides whether that holds. Either way, evaluations should score the answer given after thinking, compare it with the unedited model's own answer, and stop reporting one pooled average from one pool.
best_ideas: The failed registered replication is the turning point of the paper. It appears in abstract sentence 3 and in a results section of its own (Section 5), with its full numbers (.037, p=.14; +.029, p=.43, n=277) and Holm. This is the strongest integrity signal the paper can send.

It turns mTGu's selection critique into a measured finding instead of a rebuttal. On the same engine and hardware, the Study 1 facts give +.207 and the fresh facts +.029 (E1 retention difference −.178, p=.019). The first pool was 59% well-known against 39%, plausibly because Qwen-7B is one of the four probe models and the old selection rule required 7B to recall the fact.

The hero figure plots the exploratory points as hollow markers and adds the registered W1/W2 estimates as filled markers on the same axes, so the figure itself shows whether the pattern held. This is honest design that works under either outcome.

The two-component pattern is informative and easy to remember. As salience rises, edited loss goes up (.13 → .31) while the unedited model's own loss goes down (.39 → .06), and the lines cross. Paired with the labelled interpretation (the edit has to fight a stable prior), it gives readers an intuition they can repeat without overclaiming a mechanism.
Section 6 opens by saying salience was the sixth explanation tried and that the five earlier ones failed. That discloses the forking paths up front instead of burying them.

Edit-specific loss is the central measure and is qualified separately for each model. This directly answers the AI review's points about the missing edited-versus-base contrast and the qualification problem, with no extra jargon.
Two outcome-agnostic titles (1 and 3), two pre-written abstracts, and section titles that switch with the H4 outcome all fit registered-report practice.
The recommendations box ties each item to what it would have changed in the authors' own two studies. That makes the practice angle concrete rather than generic.

The risk list is unusually sharp. It catches the .110 vs .107 Holm mix-up (verified: .110 unfiltered, Holm .0216; .107 filtered, Holm .0336), the BOS mismatch behind the 32B +.216 (use +.207), the composition reweighting that recovers only about half the gap, the anonymity problem with GitHub timestamps, and the expected dilution at 70B.

The paper keeps the evidence that cuts against a blanket claim. On paraphrased prompts reasoning raises edit success (−.083), and on obscure facts edit-specific loss is negative (−.090). The 'both directions' framing comes early.
fatal_problems: The paper's own submission gate has failed and goes undisclosed. prereg-arr.md §7 registers a 'Submission gate: H1 and H2 pass at 32B, and the ... ES drop keeps a CI above zero at 32B and 70B.' REVISION.md §3 adds that if G3 fails, the 10/12 deadline is dropped in favour of ARR January. The gate failed (study2.md: 'Submission gate (§7): FAIL'), yet the proposal submits on 10/12 and never mentions the gate. Any reviewer who reads the cited registration finds that, by the authors' own rule, this submission should not exist in this cycle. That outweighs every other calibration effort in the proposal. The deviation must be logged and disclosed in the main text, or the rule followed.

The thesis assumes the post hoc result is true. It reads: 'report well-known facts separately: that is where reasoning undoes edits.' Before H4 is run, this promotes an exploratory moderator found on the sixth try to the paper's thesis. Titles 1 and 3 are outcome-agnostic, but the thesis that drives the introduction, the recommendations box and the conclusion is not.

The H4-confirmed abstract claims more than H4 tests. H4 tests D, the difference in edit-specific loss (edited loss minus native loss) between well-known and other facts. In the Study 2 strata, about half of the +.332 comes from the unedited model losing its own weakly held answers on obscure facts (native component −.154), and only about half from edited loss rising (+.178). 'Reasoning undoes edits to well-known facts more than edits to the rest' and Title 2 assert only the edited component, which the addendum treats as an uncorrected secondary test. H4 also confirms the moderator, not that composition explains the drop from Study 1 to Study 2 (reweighting recovers about half). Sentence 4 juxtaposes the two, which implies it does.

The closing claim of the H4-not-confirmed abstract is not specific to edits. It says reasoning 're-decides edits in both directions (14.2% broken, 10.5% repaired), so a direct answer cannot certify an edit'. That two-way churn is about the size of the unedited model's own loss after thinking (.170), and of plain instability in long greedy generation: on the same 200 cases, only 81% of after-thinking outcomes agree between the 4090 and the H100 (E0), and sampling fails 61% against a 34% noise floor. A knowledgeable reviewer will read 'cannot certify' as 'reasoning models' answers are unstable', which is not a finding about editing. As written, the not-confirmed paper's take-home is weak, and Section 3's 'greedy, so each condition gives one deterministic answer' is contradicted by the team's own data.

Page budget and the hero figure favour the post hoc analysis over the registered one. Section 6 (post hoc) gets 1.2 pages against 0.9 for Section 5 (registered), and the hero figure's title asserts the salience pattern. Under H4-not-confirmed, about two pages and the hero figure would showcase an explanation that failed its prospective test. That is exactly the 'effect → failed replication → post hoc rescue' reading the proposal itself fears.
fixes: Decide the submission gate explicitly. Either (a) follow the registered rule and go to ARR January, with W1–W3, the parent 70B/14B H1/H2 and one more editor complete, which makes for a much stronger paper; or (b) log deviation D8 ('submission gate failed; we submit a reframed paper whose central registered result is that failure; the original claim is withdrawn') and add one main-text clause in Section 5 plus the appendix log. Do not leave it for a reviewer to find.

Freeze the addendum before anything else runs (commit, push, registry entry with the salience.py hash and the W2 manifest), with all three abstract variants committed: confirmed, not confirmed, and not tested. Through an anonymous route (OSF or an anonymised mirror), not a personal GitHub timestamp.

Before freezing, also register a composition prediction, so that 'the pool explains the gap' becomes testable rather than only the moderator. Predict W2's overall edit-specific loss from the Study 2 stratum estimates and W2's 33% high share (≈ .33×.242 + .67×(−.090) ≈ +.02), and do the same for W1. Then report observed against predicted.

Replace the thesis with an outcome-agnostic default: 'The same edit can pass the direct test and fail after thinking, but how often reasoning undoes edits beyond its ordinary drift depends on which facts are tested: on fresh facts, a registered replication shrank the effect from +.21 to +.03.' Swap in the salience thesis only if H4 passes.

Under H4-confirmed, claim 'edit-specific loss is larger for well-known facts', and report both components (edited loss up, native loss down) in the abstract or Table 3. Use Title 2 only if the edited-loss component is also positive in both W1 and W2. Keep 'composition accounts for about half of the Study 1 → Study 2 gap' as exploratory; say 'about half', not 'a large part'.

Under H4-not-confirmed, end the abstract on the registered, edit-specific fact: on fresh facts at 32B, reasoning loses edited answers about as often as the model's own (.199 vs .170). The practice message becomes pool dependence (+.207 vs +.029 on the same engine and hardware) plus multi-sample scoring. Always set broken/repaired rates beside the unedited model's flip rate and the noise floor.

In Section 3, delete 'deterministic'. State that greedy runs are reproducible only within one engine and hardware setup, and that 19% of after-thinking outcomes change across GPUs. Add a sixth recommendation: score the after-thinking answer over several samples or seeds and report the noise floor. This finding is squarely on the practice angle and survives either H4 outcome.

Rewrite Recommendation 4 to match the evidence: 'Fix the test pool by a rule independent of the outcome, not by any model's reasoning-time recall, and report its composition by how well known the facts are.' The data show the pool matters (E1, p=.019). They do not isolate reasoning-time selection as the cause, and E2 shows the qualification rule is not.

Retitle Section 4 'Study 1 (exploratory): edits are lost after thinking at the two largest of six models'. Drop or qualify the scale trend: only the 32B − 1.5B erosion difference has a CI excluding zero, and Study 2's 32B erosion (.142) fell back to the 1.5B level. Replace 'locates the loss in the chain' with 'acting on the chain alone moves the final answer (steerability, not mediation)'.

Thin the abstract. The current confirmed version carries about 12 statistics, more than the old abstract's 7, which contradicts the readability claim. Keep at most about 5 numbers, label Study 1 'exploratory' in sentence 2, keep sentence 1 under about 30 words, and say 'the two largest of six models' so the scope selection is visible.

Rebalance pages. Section 5 (registered) should get at least as much space as Section 6. In the not-confirmed world, merge Sections 6 and 7 into about 1.2 pages. Make the registered data the hero figure's main panel in both worlds: panel A, edit-specific loss by pool (Study 1 same-engine +.207, Study 2 +.029, W2, W1) with each pool's share of well-known facts; panel B, the dose-response with hollow and filled markers. Prepare two figure titles.

Use the same-engine, same-hardware G0-H100 values for every Study 1 vs Study 2 decomposition in Intro P3 and Section 5, not the BOS-mismatched Study 1 .386/.170. Note that the matched ES-drop difference is not significant (−.048, p=.31); only the edit-specific loss difference is.

Describe the Study 1 within-pool split as going 'in the same direction', not 'splitting the same way'. Every Study 1 high-minus-low difference is individually non-significant (p = .068 to .28), and Study 1 was part of the data that motivated H4.

Fill the novelty gap on popularity. Cite and position against prior work showing that popular or entrenched facts are harder to edit robustly. To verify: Ma et al. 2024, 'Is it Possible to Edit Large Language Models Robustly?'; the Popular subset of RippleEdits; PopQA (Mallen et al. 2023). What is new here is that the effect is specific to reasoning, the paired same-edit protocol, the crossover in which the unedited model's own loss falls with salience, and the registered pool sensitivity.

Justify the label 'well-known'. The proxy is 'known to most smaller distills of the same recipe'. Either add an external popularity check (Wikipedia page views) in the appendix, or call them 'facts most smaller models also know' in the main text. Report secondary test 5 (quartiles of the base model's confidence) in Table 3, so readers can tell salience apart from the 32B's own confidence.

verdict.restated_thesis: Editors are certified on the edited model's direct answer, but a reasoning model answers only after it thinks. Measured that way and set against the unedited model's own answers, reasoning undoes edits to facts the model family knows well, and does not undo edits to obscure ones. Because of that, a single pooled score depends on how the test pool was drawn: the authors' own clear first result shrank to near zero in a pre-registered replication on a less well-known pool. Evaluations should therefore score the answer given after thinking, against the unedited baseline, separately for well-known and obscure facts.
best_ideas: The registered failure is the turning point, not a footnote. The order (exploratory effect, then a pre-registered replication on fresh facts that fails, then a measured explanation, then a prospective test) is rare in NLP, honest, and easy to remember. It turns the weakest-looking fact in the record into the engine of the story.

mTGu's selection worry becomes a measured finding. Study 1's pool was chosen by what Qwen-7B recalls after reasoning, so it over-sampled well-known facts (59% vs 39%). The same-engine, same-hardware retention numbers (+.207 on the Study 1 facts vs +.029 on the Study 2 facts) show that the shift comes from the pool, not the machinery. This is the most satisfying answer to a prior review in the whole plan.

Edit-specific loss is the central measure. It pairs each fact's edited answer with the unedited model's own answer to the same fact. It answers the AI review's missing edited-vs-base contrast directly, and it is the reason the obscure-fact stratum reads as 'reasoning destabilises the base' rather than as 'edits are safe'.

The hero figure is designed well. The edited-loss line rises (.13 to .31) while the own-answer loss line falls (.39 to .06), with a shaded crossing between 2 and 3. Post hoc points are hollow and registered W1/W2 points filled, so the figure shows the evidential status of every point under either outcome. The pool-composition bars show why the pooled average moved.

Both abstracts and the outcome-dependent Section 7 title are fixed before any data. The not-confirmed text keeps the CI and does not read as 'salience disproved'. This matches the addendum's §7 decision rules.
Each recommendation is tied to what it would have changed in the authors' own studies. That makes the practice box concrete rather than generic advice.

The layout is a conventional ACL order. A one-table protocol gives a reason for every design choice. Engine checks, BOS handling, hashes and deviations go to the appendix, and the intervention shrinks to one sentence about steerability. This directly answers TRfT's 'unconventional organisation / unjustified design' and the AI review's request for a hierarchy.

The plan names early that reasoning re-decides edits in both directions (break .142 vs repair .105; paraphrase ES rises by .083; obscure-fact retention −.090). This heads off reviewers reading those results as contradictions.

The risk list is accurate. It caught the .107/.110 mix-up in the brief (.107 is the degenerate-filtered row with Holm .034; .110 is the unfiltered row with Holm .022). It also caught the format-mismatched 32B baseline and the composition arithmetic (my check: .663×.242 + .337×(−.090) ≈ +.13 vs +.21, about half the gap).
fatal_problems: The confirmatory weight sits on a test that does not yet exist. The H4 addendum is still marked DRAFT, nothing in W1/W2 has been generated, and the deadline is in two days. If H4 is untested or fails, two things survive. One is 'score after thinking', which He et al. 2025 (2505.18690, realistic autoregressive evaluation, with a reflection-overturns-edit case already shown in an R1-distill) already argues. The other is 'edits are re-decided both ways (.142/.105)', which is not edit-specific, because the unedited model also loses .17 of its own answers after thinking. A practice paper whose one new lesson is unconfirmed, plus a null registered replication at one model, is roughly ARR 2.5, not 3.5.

H4 does not test the claim in the confirmed abstract and title. H4's statistic D is a difference of two contrasts. In the exploratory data, about half of D comes from the base side: the base's own-answer loss falls from .39 to .06 as salience rises. That base-side slope is plausibly a measurement artifact, because on obscure facts the base's correct direct answer (the qualification) is often a lucky hit that reasoning then abandons. H4 can therefore pass even if edited loss does not depend on salience at all. Yet the confirmed abstract and Title 2 claim that 'reasoning undoes edits to well-known facts more than edits to the rest', which is the edited-loss component (addendum secondary #3, with no pass rule). The headline claim and the registered test do not match.

The practice framing makes the existing generalisation weakness worse. Guidelines for 'people who build and evaluate editors' rest on one editor (ROME), one dataset (CounterFact), one distillation recipe, and one model in the registered test (32B; 70B pending). That breadth is exactly what mTGu said was missing. Of the five recommendations, 'evaluate generated answers in realistic decoding', 'don't select items on behaviour related to the outcome' and 'stratify by popularity' are already standard elsewhere (He et al. 2025; Mirage/QAEdit-style critiques; PopQA-style popularity analyses). Reviewers will read them as known advice applied to one setup, so the novelty of the practice contribution is low unless the salience-dependent loss is confirmed.

An alternative explanation is left open: salience may simply be edit strength. In Study 2, the post-edit residual first-token log p(o_old) predicts erosion (AUC .661; high − low erosion +.161, p=.001). Well-known facts may just be under-overwritten by ROME, so 'reasoning undoes edits' would really be 'reasoning exposes incomplete edits of entrenched facts'. The planned robustness check (#5) uses the base's confidence before the edit, not the residual after the edit, so it does not address this. An ACL reviewer will raise it.
fixes: SINGLE HIGHEST-LEVERAGE CHANGE: amend H4 before freezing it (the addendum is still a draft, so this is legitimate today), then freeze it, push it to an anonymised registry, and run W1 (70B) before W2. Make the edited-loss component (edited loss, high − low > 0) a co-primary test or a required condition next to D̄. Add the post-edit residual log p(o_old) as a pre-specified covariate. Then the claim 'reasoning undoes edits to well-known facts', if confirmed, rests on a registered test, and the edit-strength explanation is addressed in advance. W1 also delivers the registered H1/H2 at 70B, which could be the strongest single result in the paper.

Lead with the finding and put practice second. Title 1 or 3 works. The intro should present one registered, salience-dependent finding (if H4 passes) and treat the recommendations as its implications. Do not frame the whole paper as evaluation guidelines generalised from one editor, because that invites the breadth objection. Phrase the recommendations as testable claims for other editors, not as established practice.

Re-budget the 8 pages. Study 1 (exploratory, partly superseded) gets 1.2 pages while the registered H4 gets 0.7. Merge Sections 4 and 5 into one results section of about 1.6 pages around Table 2. Give Sections 6 and 7 together about 2.2 pages, so the prospective test and its components (edited vs own loss), dose-response and edit-strength control are visible. Raise related work to about 0.8 pages, with an explicit contrast to He et al. 2025, CRANE, ThinkEval and Gekhman et al. 2026, which predicts that thinking helps recall of facts the model knows well and so supports the salience reading.

Cut the numbers in the introduction. The current plan for P2–P4 has about 15. Keep four: the Study 1 drop, the failed registered replication, the salience gradient, and the H4 result. TRfT's complaint about density applies to the introduction more than to anywhere else.

Calibration corrections. (a) Composition explains 'about half' of the 32B gap, not 'a large part'. Report the formal reweighting. (b) In Study 1 the high − low differences are not individually significant (p = .068, .250 and .091 at 32B, 14B and 70B). Say 'the same direction' rather than 'split the same way'. (c) Table 1 must not call greedy B3 answers 'deterministic'. Across hardware, B3 outcomes agree only .81 of the time (E0). Say 'greedy', and report the cross-hardware sensitivity in the appendix as further evidence that the answer after thinking is fragile. (d) For the Study 1 vs Study 2 decomposition, use the same-engine G0-H100 values, not the BOS-mismatched .386/.170. (e) Use .110 (unfiltered, Holm .022) throughout and keep .107 as a sensitivity result.

Strengthen the not-confirmed path now. Make its lesson the measured fact that holds regardless of H4: on the same engine and hardware, the pooled edit-specific loss swings from +.207 to +.029 with pool composition alone. Do not lean on 'edits are re-decided both ways' without stating that the base's own answers are re-decided at a similar rate (.17). Write the third abstract variant ('H4 pending or only one world complete') today.

Validate the proxy cheaply, with no GPU, before submission. Correlate salience (the number of sibling distills that know the fact) with an external popularity measure, such as Wikipedia page views of the subject or the PopQA-style approach of Mallen et al. 2023 (verify the citation). Also search 2025–26 work on editing popular vs long-tail or entrenched facts. If 'edits to popular facts are less robust' is already known for non-reasoning models, the novelty must rest on reasoning bringing the old fact back, together with the paired edited-vs-unedited contrast.

Open with a real recorded case. Replace the hypothetical Darrieux example with a case where the 32B direct answer holds the edit and the chain then argues the model back to the old value. Put a short chain excerpt in Figure 1 or the intro. A real chain does more for the story than any statistic, and it keeps the opening from implying a reversion the data never showed.

In the hero figure, plot edited loss as the main line and the own-answer loss as the control. Print the two components of D for W1/W2 directly on the figure, so readers can see whether the edited side or the base side carries any registered effect.

Keep two of mTGu's stated strengths visible with one line each in Section 4: the steerability result (T−N ES +.138) and the excess failure under sampling at 32B (.266 above the noise floor). Losing every strength a positive reviewer named is a quiet risk.

titles: When Does Reasoning Undo a Knowledge Edit? (recommended: true under either H4 outcome)
Thinking Brings Back What the Model Knows Well: Knowledge Edits in Reasoning Models (only if H4 is confirmed)
One Route Rewritten: Testing Why Reasoning Undoes Knowledge Edits (mechanism-first; true under either outcome)
scored.thesis: A rank-one edit rewrites one route to a fact while reasoning can take the others, so thinking should undo edits of widely known facts and spare edits of obscure ones.

verdict.restated_thesis: From the abstract alone: an edit made by a method like ROME can pass a direct-answer test and still be undone when a reasoning model thinks before it answers. The authors argue this happens mainly for facts the model knows well. The edit rewrites only the direct subject-to-answer lookup, and reasoning can rebuild the original answer from related facts. The evidence comes in four steps: a first study that found the loss at the two largest R1 distills; a pre-registered replication on fresh facts that failed; a post hoc observation that the fresh pool held fewer well-known facts; and a test of that idea registered in advance, whose outcome is still unknown. I could restate it, but only on a second read. On the first pass, sentences 3–4 lost me at 'the models' own answers', 'discovery pool', 'edit-specific loss', 'four smaller models' and 'D'.
best_ideas: Use the registered failure as the turn of the story. The order discovery → registered replication fails → diagnosis → test fixed in advance is a real story that a reader outside the field can follow, and it keeps the failure in the main text.

Turn mTGu's selection worry into a measured result. A pool chosen with reasoning output held 59% widely known facts against 39% in a fresh pool. That answers the old review point and also gives practitioners a usable lesson.

Open on the Darrieux example. One concrete edit, a direct answer that passes, and a chain that recalls 'French actress born in Bordeaux' is the right hook for an NLP outsider. It answers TRfT's 'unclear why this matters' within three sentences.

Make the right panel of the hero figure two separate lines: the edited answer's loss rising with salience (.13 → .31) and the model's own answer's loss falling (.39 → .06). It is memorable, it keeps the two parts of the contrast apart (which also answers the AI review's 'no edited-versus-base contrast'), and hollow markers for the registered data, 'shown whatever they turn out to be', are an honest way to add them.

Use plain words in place of jargon: 'direct answer / after reasoning' for B0/B3, 'undoes / rescues' for erosion/repair, and drop the reversion metric entirely. Put every limitation in one Limitations section so no other sentence has to hedge.
Give Table 1 a 'why' column with one sentence per design choice. This directly answers TRfT's 'design decisions not justified'.
Write both abstract variants before the data exist. Title 1, 'When Does Reasoning Undo a Knowledge Edit?', is readable and stays true under either outcome.

Position the work as the reverse flow: MQuAKE and Ju et al. show edits failing to flow outward to dependent facts, while here related knowledge flows inward and overrides the edited answer. It is crisp and fair to prior work.
Write a real ethics statement: safety edits and removals may also be undone by reasoning, so they should be tested after reasoning as well.

Several items in the proposal's own risk list are correct and must be kept: use one Llama-70B row throughout (.110 [.040, .180], Holm .022); recompute the suppress-new-against-placebo contrast (−.225) before citing it; base the explanation on the edited-loss component, because regression to the mean affects the own-answer line; and never quote the exploratory p<.001 in the abstract or introduction.
fatal_problems: The architecture depends on a hypothesis that has not been tested and whose test is not frozen. H4 has no rows yet, the addendum is still a draft, the test needs 4–5 H100 hours, and the deadline is two days away. Power is about .75 even if the true D is .15, and effects found after five other explanations failed usually shrink. Among the possible architectures, mechanism-first loses the most if H4 fails or does not finish. Section 2 and its predictions table would then lay out an explanation that failed, before any result. The proposal's claim that 'the skeleton is the same either way' holds for the section headings, but not for how good the story is. The proposal's own risk section concedes that the paper would then need to lead with the evaluation story.

The paper states the explanation before any data, but the salience part was formed after Study 2 failed. A cold reader meets the predictions table in Section 2 with rows marked 'formed after Study 2' and 'registered before Study 3', before knowing what Study 2 or Study 3 are. These are forward references, and the paper needs the defensive line 'We state the explanation first because it organises the evidence, not because it came first.' That reads as a theory fitted after the fact. It repeats, at the level of the whole paper, both TRfT's 'unconventional organisation' complaint and mTGu's 'was the scope set after the data?' complaint. The two label systems (P1–P5 alongside H2/H2b/H4) add coined labels instead of removing them.

Nothing distinguishes the proposed mechanism from simpler explanations, yet the paper calls itself mechanism-first. Salient facts are harder to edit: direct-answer edit success falls from .81 at 0 of 4 to .61 at 4 of 4 in Study 2. So the edits on salient facts that pass the direct test may simply be marginal, and any long generation would flip them. That story predicts the same salience pattern with no 'routes' at all. In the other direction, the large loss of the model's own answers at low salience (.39) is partly regression to the mean, because facts were selected on that fragile direct answer, and this inflates D. Answer frequency within a relation (English, France) is also uncontrolled. The draft addendum controls only the base model's confidence before the edit, not the edit's margin after it. Editing reviewers will ask exactly this, and P5 ('a weak edit does not account for the loss') has no registered test behind it.

The abstract is less readable than the old one, not more. The confirmed variant carries about 14 numbers, against the 7 that the brief diagnosed as too many in the old abstract, plus notation (D, CI, p). Sentences run 40–60 words. For an outsider about 10 terms are undefined on first read: ROME, rank-one edit, direct lookup, R1 distills, CounterFact, edit success, 'the models' own answers', discovery pool, edit-specific loss, D. About six of these block understanding. Sentence 3 holds the whole of Study 1 and Study 2 in one sentence, and sentence 4 brings in 'four smaller models' with no setup. The proposal's claim that the main text has only three defined terms does not hold for the abstract.

Several statements are not supported by the brief's own data. (a) The proposal calls Study 1's cases 'independent' evidence for salience, but addendum §2 says they were used to form H4. Their high-minus-low differences are also not significant (p = .068, .28, .098, .25, .091). (b) It treats composition (59% against 39%) as the explanation of the shrinkage, but the strata themselves differ between studies: the low stratum is +.034 in Study 1 and −.090 in Study 2. A rough reweighting of Study 2 to 59% salient gives a retention contrast of about .11 against .21–.22, so composition closes roughly half the gap, not all of it. The two pools' salience was also measured with different instruments. (c) 'Spare edits of obscure ones' overclaims: low-salience edits that held directly are still undone 12–15% of the time. (d) 'Often the ones most in need of updating' has no support. (e) The undo rates of 12.8–16.5% and 19.5–20.7% are joint probabilities, but they are worded as if they were rates among edits that held directly; that conditional rate is .345 at 32B. (f) Study 2's registered paraphrase result goes the other way, with reasoning raising edit success (−.083 [−.138, −.025]), and it is moved to the appendix. (g) The steering test is presented as evidence for part (a), that the chain is where the original answer returns, but it shows only that the chain can steer the answer.
fixes: Reorder the paper as question first, with the explanation revealed at the turn, instead of explanation first. Keep the general intuition in the introduction: an edit rewrites one lookup, and reasoning can recall through related facts. That intuition did motivate Study 1, as the route census shows. Leave 'which edits?' as the open question. Drop the predictions table from Section 2, so that Section 2 is background only: what ROME changes, and how reasoning recalls (Gekhman et al.). Introduce the salience hypothesis at the end of Study 2 as what the failure revealed. Study 3 then tests it. Move the scorecard of predictions and their status to the Discussion, where every row can be read. This removes the forward references and the disclaimer sentence. It also makes the 'not confirmed' outcome change only Section 6, the abstract's last two sentences and the conclusion, which the current proposal claims but does not deliver.

Strengthen the addendum before freezing it; it is still a draft, so this is still allowed. First, add registered secondaries for D within strata of the edit's margin after editing (first-token log p of o_new minus o_old after the edit) and of direct-answer edit success, so that the 'marginal edits on salient facts' alternative can be separated from the routes explanation. Second, add D within strata of how often the original answer occurs among candidates of the same relation. Third, state in prose that the explanation stands or falls mainly on the edited-loss component (high minus low, predicted > 0), because the own-answer component is affected by regression to the mean. Then freeze and push it, together with both abstract variants and a third variant for 'Study 3 incomplete'. Set a go/no-go time for Study 3, such as 2026-10-11 12:00.

Rewrite the abstract as five sentences of at most 30–35 words each, with at most 6 numbers and no 'D', 'discovery pool' or 'edit-specific loss'. A skeleton: (1) Knowledge edits are tested by asking the edited question directly, but reasoning models think before they answer. (2) We score the same edit both ways in six DeepSeek-R1 distilled models, and find that at the two largest, thinking undoes edits that passed the direct test, about twice as often as it undoes the unedited model's own answers. (3) A pre-registered replication on 400 new facts did not reproduce this. (4) The edits thinking undid were mostly of facts that smaller models also know, which made up 59% of our first set of facts and 39% of the new one; a test registered before any data [confirmed / did not confirm] this on two new sets. (5) Implication. Say 'the unedited model's own answers to the same questions' explicitly.

Correct each overstatement. Thesis: 'thinking undoes edits of well-known facts more often than the model's own answers, and edits of obscure facts no more often', replacing 'spares'. Delete 'often the ones most in need of updating'. For Study 1's cases, write that the direction matches but the differences are not significant (p = .07–.28) and that these cases helped form the idea; drop the word 'independent'. Report a reweighting decomposition of the Study 1 → Study 2 gap, saying how much composition explains, instead of 'salience explained it'. Give undo rates conditional on the edit holding directly (.345 → .201 at 32B), or label them as shares of all edits. Put the paraphrase result into the main text in one sentence and check it by salience. Report the registered Holm decision (32B Holm p = .84) next to the raw p values.

Describe the steering test only as evidence that the chain can steer the untouched answer in both directions. Do not count it as support for 'the chain is where the original answer returns'. List that part of the explanation as untested for natural chains, which is consistent with mTGu's point about steerability versus mediation.

If any predictions or status table survives, use one label system (plain names, not both P- and H-numbers), keep it to at most 4 rows in the main text, and put the 'registered, not run' conditions in the appendix registry table. The main text should mention them only once, in one sentence of Study 2.

Name He et al. 2025 in the introduction's positioning paragraph, not only in Related Work, because they already show an R1 distill whose reasoning overturns edits. Cite Gekhman et al. 2026 for recall through related facts. Base the claim of novelty on three things: scoring the same edit both ways, a registered replication reported with its failure, and the salience pattern tested in advance. Expand Related Work beyond 0.5 page by cutting Section 4.3: its claim that the net loss appears where rescue fades rests on cross-scale differences whose intervals mostly include zero, and P1 failed at 32B in Study 2.

Clean up the prose before drafting. Remove the 'not X but Y' turns ('not because it came first', 'a probe, not a defence') and the aphorisms ('Thinking cuts both ways', 'The concern becomes a finding', 'What survives registration is narrower than what discovery suggested'). Change 'only just knows' to 'barely knows'. Drop Title 3 ('One Route Rewritten' is a coined label and claims a mechanism) and use Title 1. Use only a chain recorded from the data for the Darrieux example, or switch to a case recorded from a salient fact; never invent a chain.

Decide the hero figure by outcome. If H4 holds, draw Study 3's data in solid marks and Study 2's exploratory lines faded and labelled 'exploratory'. If H4 fails or Study 3 does not finish, make the hero figure the direct versus after-reasoning comparison in Study 1 and Study 2, and show the salience lines in Section 5 as exploratory. Print n for each salience bin, since bins 0 and 4 hold only 31 and 36 cases.

verdict.restated_thesis: Knowledge edits are checked by asking the edited model directly, but reasoning models think before they answer. The paper claims that a rank-one edit (ROME) rewrites only the direct subject-to-answer lookup, while a well-known fact can be reached again through related facts the chain brings up. Thinking should therefore undo edits of widely known facts and spare edits of obscure ones. The evidence comes in three steps. A discovery study found a loss at the two largest R1 distills. A registered replication on fresh facts failed. A post hoc analysis traced the gap to the discovery pool holding more widely known facts (59% against 39%). A test registered before any data then checks whether the edit-specific loss is larger for widely known facts.
best_ideas: The predictions table with 'refuted-if' and 'when stated' columns, including rows marked 'registered, not run' (H2b, H3 steering, other editors). This is the right device for keeping the timing of each claim visible without hedging every sentence. Keep it in either variant.

Telling the three studies in the order they happened, with Study 2's registered failure as the turn and its p-values (.14, .43) in abstract sentence 3, next to the discovery numbers. This answers the integrity worry directly.

Both abstract variants are written before Study 3 data exists, and the hero figure adds hollow 'registered before data' markers that are shown whatever they turn out to be. Good registered-report practice.
The selection critique becomes a measured finding: the discovery pool held 59% widely known facts, the fresh pool 39%. This is a much better answer to mTGu than defending Study 1's pool.
Edited-answer loss and own-answer loss are plotted as separate lines. This gives the AI review its formal edited-versus-base contrast, and it puts the regression-to-the-mean risk in plain view.

Number hygiene that catches real problems: the unfiltered Llama-70B result (.110 [.040,.180], Holm .022) is used throughout, fixing the brief's .107/.022 mismatch. D−P −.225 is marked for recomputation (study1.md only has D−N −.216). The post hoc p<.001 is never quoted in the abstract or introduction.
Title 1, 'When Does Reasoning Undo a Knowledge Edit?', is true under every H4 outcome.

Standard ACL order, a Table 1 with a 'why' column, three defined terms, plain words ('direct answer', 'after reasoning', 'undoes', 'rescues'), and one Limitations section. This addresses every point TRfT raised.

A one-sentence positioning against MQuAKE and Ju et al. ('reverse flow': related knowledge flows back in and overrides the edit). The ethics statement also notes that safety edits may be undone by reasoning.
fatal_problems: Overclaim that salience explains the Study 1 to Study 2 gap. Intro P3 says salience 'did' explain it, but the brief's own strata show composition explains only about half. Reweighting S2's strata to S1's mix gives a retention contrast of about .11–.13 (by case share or by retention-set share), against S1's .216 and S2's .029. The ES drop becomes about .063, against .106 and .037. The low-salience stratum also differs between pools (+.034 in S1, −.090 in S2). Reviewer mTGu would catch this.

The mechanism-first spine makes an untested mechanism the paper's premise. H4 tests only whether a proxy measured on other models (how many small distills know the fact) moderates a behavioural contrast. Simpler accounts predict the same result: (a) edit margin against prior strength (ES@B0 falls from .81 to .61 across salience, and residual log p(o_old) predicted erosion in S2 with AUC .66); (b) base-answer fragility, discussed below; (c) how common the answer is within its relation. Even if H4 is confirmed, the 'one route rewritten' story is not tested. Title 3 and abstract sentence 2 ('We propose an explanation… so thinking should…') will be read as a confirmed mechanism.

Nearly half of the primary statistic D does not come from edits. In S2, D=.332 splits into an edited-loss difference of about +.18 and an own-loss difference of about −.15 (own loss .22 for low-salience facts, .07 for high). Facts were selected because the unedited model answered them directly, so obscure facts are fragile by selection. The unfrozen H4 can therefore pass while edited loss barely moves. A confirmed abstract would then claim 'edit-specific loss is larger for widely known facts' on base-side regression to the mean.

The claim 'the skeleton is the same either way' is false. Intro P1 (the explanation as the organising premise), Section 2's lens, the hero's left panel, contributions (2) and (3), and every Section 8 rule ('report by how widely facts are known', 'an edit… is weakest on widely known facts') assert the explanation. Under 'not confirmed', the paper is organised around a refuted lens. The most likely outcome is 'not run' or 'one world only': the addendum is still a DRAFT, two days remain, and the test needs 4–5 H100 hours. No variant exists for that case, so the actual submission has no pre-written form.

P1 and P4 are presented as tests of the explanation when they cannot be. P1 (the largest-model scope) was stated after Study 1 and failed its registered test at 32B (H1 .037, p=.14), yet Section 4.1 presents Study 1's numbers as 'P1's result'. That is HARKing presented as a prediction, and it is exactly mTGu's rebuttal question 1. P4 (chain steering) shows the chain can steer the answer; it does not show the original answer naturally 'comes back' in the chain. Every account in which the answer copies from the chain predicts P4, so it is not diagnostic. Its registered replication (H3) did not run.

The practical rule 'never choose evaluation facts with reasoning output, because doing so inflated our first estimate' misattributes the cause. Study 1 required Qwen-7B, one of the four salience probe models, to name the old answer, so its 59% high-salience share is partly built in by selecting on a smaller model's knowledge, in any answer mode. The inflation is also only about half explained. The defensible lesson is: select on the evaluated model's own direct knowledge, and report the pool's salience mix.
fixes: Compute and report the composition decomposition: S2's strata reweighted to S1's high-salience share in the retention set (and in all cases), plus the within-stratum S1−S2 differences. Replace 'salience did explain the gap' with 'pool composition accounts for about half of the gap; obscure facts also behaved differently in the two pools'. Apply this in intro P3, Section 5.3 and Section 8.

Before freezing the addendum today, add a gate to H4: the headline claim also requires the edited-loss component (high − low) to have a CI above 0. Either make it co-primary with a Holm correction over two tests, or make it a stated precondition for writing 'edit-specific'. Add two secondary stratifiers: post-edit residual log p(o_old) (lp_first.after, the E5 measure), to separate the route account from edit margin; and how common o_old is among same-relation candidates. Push the frozen addendum and both abstract variants before any W1–W3 row exists.

Downgrade the spine from 'explanation' to 'a salience prediction, motivated by a route account'. Use 'We test' in abstract sentence 2 of both variants. Drop Title 3. State that H4 tests moderation, not routes. Move chain steering out of the explanation: present it as a separate exploratory finding ('the chain is a control point; steering, not mediation'), and give its row the status 'Study 1 exploratory; registered H3 not run'.

Fix the predictions table and Section 4. P1: 'stated after Study 1; registered H1 at 32B not supported'. P2: 'Study 1 supported; registered H2 at 32B not supported'. Title Section 4 'Study 1: discovery', not 'P1's result'. In 4.3, either drop the 'rescue fades, so P1' inference or show the paired cross-scale differences; three of the four Δ erosion CIs include 0, as does every Δ repair CI.

In 5.3, report the Study 1 high-versus-low differences with CIs. All are non-significant: 32B +.264 (p=.068), 14B +.152 (p=.25), 70B +.198 (p=.091). Call them 'consistent in direction', not 'independent cases'. Note that the 3–4 of 4 cut was chosen on S2 (E6 led to E6b). Correct the count: salience came after five or six failed candidates, and the appendix list currently says 'five' while listing six.

Write every outcome variant now, not only abstract sentences 4–5: H4 confirmed / not confirmed / not run / one world only, each crossed with Llama-70B H1/H2 pass or fail. The variants must cover intro P1 and P3, contribution (2), Section 2's framing ('background and a candidate explanation' if not confirmed), Section 6, Section 8 and the conclusion. If H4 is not confirmed or not run, Section 8 keeps only rules the registered results support: score both answer modes, select on the evaluated model's own knowledge, report pool composition.

Correct the practical rule: 'Select evaluation facts on the evaluated model's own direct answers and report how widely known they are. Selecting on a smaller model's knowledge enriched our discovery pool for widely known facts (59% vs 39%).'

Hero figure: draw S2's lines in a visibly 'exploratory (post hoc)' style, give n per bin (31 at 0 and 36 at 4, with wide bands), and make Study 3's registered points with 95% CIs the visual focus once they exist. The left panel must use a recorded high-salience reverting chain, quoted verbatim, or be dropped; never an illustrative invented chain.
