Abstract wording. Not-confirmed s5: replace 'not specifically for edits' with 'with no detectable edit-specific loss (+.029, CI [−.036, .097])'. Confirmed s5: write 'direct-answer tests overstate edit success for widely known facts' only if the secondary high-stratum ES drop has a CI above 0 in Study 3; otherwise state the retention-contrast result. Check the 'about twice as often' ratio against actual edited-loss and own-loss rates, or give the two rates.

Readability: cut intro P2–P3 to about four numbers (.106/.110, about 2×, .037 n.s., 59% vs 39%) and move CIs and Holm values to Table 3. Report Llama-70B H1/H2 under Study 2 (they are Study 2's registered hypotheses), not only in Table 4.

Novelty: say in one sentence exactly what He et al. 2025 showed (an R1 distill whose reasoning overturns edits) and claim only what is new here: the same edit paired with and without thinking, a registered replication including its failure, and salience moderation tested in advance. Re-check CODE 2026, Gao et al. 2026, ThinkEval and CRANE before submitting.

verdict.restated_thesis: From the abstract alone: an edit that holds when the model answers directly is often undone once a reasoning model thinks first. The proposal says this happens mainly for widely known facts, because the chain of thought can reach the original answer through related facts, while a rank-one edit rewrites only the direct lookup. So direct-answer tests overstate how well edits hold, by an amount that depends on which facts are edited. The paper uses this to explain why a pre-registered replication on a fresh pool with fewer well-known facts failed. It then tests the explanation in advance. In the not-confirmed version the thesis falls back to: the effect is smaller than first estimated and, on fresh facts, not specific to edits.
best_ideas: Use the registered failure as the turn. Tell the studies in the order they happened: discovery, registered replication fails, diagnosis, test registered in advance. This is the most convincing story the evidence allows, and it gives a direct answer to mTGu's main objection. Keep the order whatever architecture is chosen.

Keep the hero figure's right panel design: two separate lines (how often the edited answer is lost, and how often the model's own answer is lost) against salience from 0 to 4, plus a strip showing each pool's share of widely known facts. Add hollow markers for the test registered in advance and show them whatever they turn out to be. The design works under any outcome, and keeping the two lines separate is exactly what lets a reader see where the contrast comes from.
Turn mTGu's selection worry into a measured finding: Study 1's pool had 59% widely known facts, Study 2's had 39%. This turns a defensive limitation into part of the result.

Use only three defined terms (edit success, retention contrast, fact salience), and plain words elsewhere: direct answer / after reasoning, undoes / rescues. Drop the reversion metric. Put every limitation in one Limitations section. This directly fixes TRfT's 'unreadable' complaint.

Position the paper in one sentence: MQuAKE and Ju et al. show edits failing to flow outward to dependent facts or being bypassed; here, related knowledge flows inward and overrides the edited answer itself. The sentence is short, quotable and fair to the closest work.
Write and commit the abstract variants before any Study 3 row exists, and give Table 1 a 'why' column for every design choice. Both answer TRfT's 'design decisions not justified'.

Use practitioner-facing numbers that do not depend on salience. An edit that passes one greedy direct test fails at least once in three sampled reasoned answers 61% of the time, against 34% for three direct answers. Thinking re-decides edits in both directions (undoes about 14–21%, rescues about 9–17%).
Make one consistent choice of Llama-70B row (unfiltered .110, Holm .022) and footnote the format-matched +.239 for Study 1 at 32B. Recompute D−P before citing it.
Use the ethics angle that safety-motivated edits and removals may also be undone by reasoning. It is a real dual-use statement, not boilerplate.
Make a forward prediction for MEMIT and AlphaEdit, so that the single-editor limitation becomes a stated, refutable test rather than an apology.
fatal_problems: The paper's spine is an explanation formed after the data, placed in Section 2 before any result, and its only confirmatory test has not run. The addendum is still a draft, two days remain before 10/12, compute for W1/W2 is uncertain, and power is about .75 even if both worlds finish (about .5 with one). Of the three possible states (confirmed, failed, not run), the mechanism-first architecture works only in the first. In the other two, Section 2, the thesis sentence and the predictions table become an untested or refuted hypothesis. 'The skeleton is the same either way' is true of the headings, not of what the paper claims. Estimated ARR overall: about 3.0–3.5 if confirmed, about 2.5 if not run, about 2.0–2.5 if failed.

The primary statistic for H4 (D, the high-minus-low difference in retention contrast) does not isolate the thesis. In the exploratory split, D = +.332 decomposes into edited loss +.178 and own-answer loss −.154. Over the 0→4 trend, about 65% of the swing comes from the own-answer line (.39→.06), not the edited line (.13→.31). Facts were admitted because the unedited model answered them directly, so for obscure facts that answer is fragile and reasoning loses it. That is a base-side effect, not an edit being undone. D can pass on the base line alone, and the abstract would then claim 'the edit-specific loss is larger for widely known facts' for a reason unrelated to edits. The addendum is unfrozen, so this can still be fixed.

Salience is confounded with how marginal the edit is, and nothing registered tests this. Edit success in a direct answer falls with salience (.81→.61). Edit strength predicts loss in Study 2 (AUC .66). Popular facts are known to be harder to edit robustly (Ma et al. 2024, 'Is it possible to edit LLMs robustly?'; verify the citation). A reviewer's first alternative needs no 'routes': surviving edits of popular facts are barely over threshold, and any perturbation tips them back. Prediction P5 ('a weak edit does not account for it') rests only on exploratory nulls. The addendum stratifies by the base model's confidence, not by the margin after the edit.

The thesis wording contradicts the paper's own data. 'Thinking should ... spare edits of obscure ones', but edited answers are lost 12–15% of the time at salience 0–2 in Study 2, and Study 1 shows 12.8–16.5% undo rates in the smaller models. What changes with salience is the edited loss relative to the model's own loss, not whether the edit is spared. A reviewer will read the hero figure's left end (.13) against the thesis sentence.

'Salience explains the shrinkage' is overstated. Reweighting Study 2's per-stratum estimates to Study 1's 59% mix gives an edit-success drop of about .063 (against .106 in Study 1, .085 on matched hardware) and a retention contrast of about .106 (against .216 and .207). That recovers roughly 40–55% of the gap. Within-stratum differences remain: Study 1's low-salience retention contrast is +.03 to +.13, Study 2's is −.090. Intro P3 ('How widely the fact is known did') and the strip caption ('shows why the two averages differed') will be checked against the tables and caught.

The practical rule 'never choose evaluation facts with reasoning output, because doing so inflated our first estimate' is misattributed. Study 1 selected facts by Qwen-7B recalling the old answer, and Qwen-7B is one of the four salience probes, so the enrichment comes from selecting on a small model's knowledge, not on reasoning as such. Analysis E2 shows that applying Study 2's direct-answer rule to Study 1's facts leaves the drop intact (+.147). The contribution as written is not supported.

The steering test is presented as evidence for part (a) of the explanation ('the chain is where the original answer returns'), but it cannot discriminate. Direct and reasoned answers differ only by the chain, by design, and banning a token from the chain reduces copying under any account. Base chains name the old answer 83–93% of the time (E3), and the test ran only on the discovery pool chosen by reasoning output. Its registered replication (H3) did not run. Calling it evidence for the explanation brings back mTGu's steering-versus-mediation objection.

The novelty positioning leaves out the literature that will most quickly shrink the salience contribution: popularity effects in editing (Ma et al. 2024; RippleEdits' popular subset), and popularity and long-tail effects in parametric-versus-context conflicts (Mallen et al. 2023 PopQA; Kandpal et al. 2023; Xie et al. 2023). The phenomenon is already credited to He et al. 2025. Without these, a reviewer who knows editing will say 'popular facts resist edits is known' and score novelty at 2.
fixes: The single change that would most raise the score: before freezing the addendum today, make the edited-side test carry the thesis. Add a co-primary: loss of edits that held directly (or the drop in edit success), widely known minus other facts, pooled over W1 and W2, with Holm over {D, edited-side}, and recompute power (the larger denominator of all edits that held directly helps). Write in the decision rule that the sentence 'thinking undoes edits of widely known facts' needs the edited-side test, and that D alone licenses only a statement about the edit-versus-own contrast. In the same freeze, add two registered secondaries: D and edited loss within strata of the post-edit margin (log-odds of new against old at the edit prompt), and an external popularity measure computed without any model (Wikipedia pageviews of the subject, no GPU needed). Then put whatever compute exists into W1 and W2 before 10/12. A confirmed edited-side result on fresh pools is the only thing that moves this paper from about 3 to 3.5 or higher.

Replace 'mechanism first' with a chronological reveal. Section 2 holds background only: what ROME changes, what reasoning does, Superficial Editing, factual priming, with no explanation yet. The explanation appears at the turn, at the end of Section 5, as the diagnosis, and is tested in Section 6. The intro still states the result up front. This removes the look of a hypothesis written after the results, makes the turn a real turn rather than a payoff already announced in Section 2, and avoids another unconventional organisation that TRfT objected to.

Write the architecture for the state most likely by 10/12 first: the addendum frozen but Study 3 not run. Lead with Title 1 and an evaluation thesis that holds in all three states. For example: 'Whether thinking undoes an edit depends on which facts are edited: our discovery effect shrank by more than half on a fresh, registered pool, and the edit-versus-own contrast tracks how widely the facts are known, a pattern we have registered for a test in advance (frozen <hash>, <date>).' Write abstract sentences 4–5 and the 70B clause of intro P3 for all four combinations of H4 × (H1/H2 at 70B), and for 'not run', now. Also decide explicitly whether submitting the not-run version beats waiting one ARR cycle.

Fix the thesis sentence. Write: 'thinking undoes edits of widely known facts more often than it disturbs the model's own answers, while for obscure facts it unsettles edited and original answers alike, or the original more'. Never write 'spares'.

titles: Reasoning Models Undo Edits to Well-Known Facts (use only if H4 is confirmed)
Which Knowledge Edits Survive Thinking? (works under either outcome)
Do Knowledge Edits Survive Thinking? A Discovery and a Pre-registered Replication (use if H4 is not confirmed)
scored.thesis: [Only if H4 holds] Reasoning models undo edits to well-known facts: after thinking, edited answers about those facts are lost far more often than the model's own answers, while edits to obscure facts are not.

verdict.restated_thesis: From the abstract alone: an edit that passes a direct question can fail once a reasoning model thinks first. A first study on R1 distills made this look like something thinking does to edits in general. A registered replication at Qwen-32B on fresh facts found almost none of it. The authors then found, after the fact, that the excess loss sits in facts that smaller models also know, and a second registered test checks whether it holds there. The upshot is that a direct question is least trustworthy for well-known facts. I could only restate this after sentence 5, and I had to guess what 'their own original answers' are compared against. The abstract never says the comparison is with the unedited model's correct answer. Read cold, 'lost edited answers about twice as often as their own original answers' sounds self-contradictory, since losing the edit and returning to the original answer are the same event.
best_ideas: Keep the opening paragraph nearly verbatim. It is the clearest motivation the project has had: what editing is for (fixing stale facts without retraining), a concrete example (Darrieux, French to English), the hidden assumption ('That test assumes the model answers at once'), and why thinking threatens it (thinking aids recall of exactly what the edit replaced). It has almost no undefined terms, and the stakes are clear within two sentences.

Turn mTGu's criticism into the clue. The first pool was picked by Qwen-7B's chain, so it filled up with facts that small models know (59% vs 39%). This turns the reviewer's sharpest objection into a mechanism, and it is the strongest narrative move in the proposal.

Tell it in the order it happened: found, failed, explained, tested. Section titles state claims ('Thinking undid edits in Study 1, but not in a registered replication'), and the registered failure is the turn rather than an appendix footnote. This replaces sentence-level hedging with structure, which was the old paper's main readability problem.

Table 2, 'What we checked, in the order we checked it', with a footnote marking rows added after earlier rows were seen. It is the right structural defence against a p-hacking reading and costs one table.

Hero panel (b): edited-answer loss and the unedited model's loss as two directly labelled lines that cross between 2 and 3 of 4. Hollow markers mean exploratory and filled mean registered, so the honesty is in the visual grammar rather than in the prose.

Three main-text terms, no arm codes (B0/B3/RR/T−N), and engine/BOS/gates moved to appendices. The think-span intervention gets one pointer sentence. This is the right amount of scope cutting for an 8-page ACL paper aimed at a reader like me.

Outcome-invariant intro, setup, Study 1–2 and exploratory sections, with only abstract sentence 5, the Study 3 results paragraph and the discussion pre-written in two variants. This keeps the framing honest under either outcome.
Write the 70B composition prediction (27% well known, so a small overall H1/H2 is expected) into the addendum before it is frozen. A predicted null then reads as predicted, not excused.
fatal_problems: The thesis and the H4 title contradict the data already in hand. 'Edits to obscure facts are not [lost]' is false. In Study 1, edits to facts outside the well-known set were lost after thinking at .38 (Qwen-32B), .30 (14B) and .26 (70B). At 32B that equals the well-known rate (.39). The Study 1 salience split at 32B comes entirely from the unedited model's own answers: .09 lost on well-known facts vs .34 on the rest. In Study 2 the obscure-fact edit loss is .13, not zero. 'Reasoning Models Undo Edits to Well-Known Facts' therefore describes only half of a gap that H4 tests as a difference of differences. If Study 3 is driven by the own-answer side, the title will be wrong even when H4 passes.

'The facts made the difference' and 'explained' overstate what is a partial account. Reweight Study 2's strata to Study 1's 59% composition: .59×(+.242) + .41×(−.090) ≈ +.11, against +.207 for the Study 1 facts on matched hardware. That is about 40–55% of the shrinkage, depending on whether the pool share or the retention-set share (57/86) is used. The within-stratum gaps also moved: the rest went from +.03 to −.09, and edit loss on obscure facts fell from .38 to .13. A knowledge-editing reviewer will do this arithmetic from Table 2.

The abstract fails the cold-reader test it was written to pass. The thesis arrives in sentence 5. There are about a dozen numerical values (+.029, −.036, .097, .037, −.010, .087, 59%, 39%, D, two CI bounds, [N]), more than the 7 the brief criticised in the old abstract. The comparator of the core measure is never named. Sentence 4 lists checks the reader cannot evaluate ('the selection rule', 'relation mix', 'edit strength'). It also does not say why the count of smaller models that know a fact should matter.

The ES-drop 'non-replication' is mis-framed. On matched hardware, the Study 1 facts give an ES drop of .085 against Study 2's .037, a difference of −.048 [−.135, .042], p=.31, which is not significant. Only the retention-gap shrinkage is (−.178, p=.019). 'Both intervals exclude the Study 1 estimates' compares against the fp32/4090 numbers and implies a cleaner failure than the data show.

The fallback thesis for H4 failing, 'thinking re-decides about one edit in four in either direction', sits at the noise level of greedy decoding. Identical cases agree after thinking only .81 of the time between two hardware runs (≈19% flips). The re-deciding is also not edit-specific: the unedited model loses .17–.22 of its own correct answers. Under H4 failing, the paper would rest on a number a reviewer can dismiss as nondeterminism, and the novelty left is a registered null that He et al. 2025 already pre-empts on the phenomenon. That is a weak ARR main-track paper.

Everything distinctive depends on data that do not exist two days before the deadline: hero panel (c), Table 3, Section 5's results, abstract sentence 5 and the title choice. The addendum is still an unfrozen draft (latest commit f96b977), and the run needs 4–5 H100 hours. The third 'registered, result pending' variant is listed as a risk, but it is not drafted, and it may be the state the paper is actually submitted in.
fixes: Rewrite the thesis around which answer thinking keeps, not around undoing. For example: 'After thinking, reasoning models hold on to facts they know well. An edit to a fact that even small models know is lost about four times as often as the model's own answer to it (.31 vs .07 in Study 2), while for obscure facts it is the model's own answer that thinking abandons more often (.22 vs .13).' This covers both components and stays true under every pattern H4 can produce. Use 'Which Knowledge Edits Survive Thinking?' as the title under both outcomes, and retire 'Reasoning Models Undo Edits to Well-Known Facts'.

Put the claim first in the abstract, use at most 5 numbers, and name the comparator. Suggested shape: (1) 'Knowledge editing changes one fact in a model's weights, and an edit counts as successful if the model gives the new answer when asked directly; reasoning models think first, and thinking helps them recall what the edit replaced.' (2) 'We test each edit twice on the same weights, answering directly and after the model's own chain of thought, and compare how often thinking loses the edited answer with how often it loses the unedited model's correct answer.' (3) First study, 2–3× excess at 14B–70B; registered replication at Qwen-32B finds almost none (+.03, CI −.04 to .10). (4) Post hoc: the excess sits in facts most smaller models also know, common in the first pool and rarer in the second. (5) The outcome variant. Drop D and edit success CIs from the abstract and drop the list of ruled-out explanations. Say 'two to three times', not 'about twice' (actual ratios: .32/.13, .39/.17, .34/.11).

Run the composition reweighting for salience now (no GPU needed), the same way E4 did for relation mix. Report the share of the Study 1→2 shrinkage that composition accounts for, with a CI. Retitle Section 4 to something like 'Which facts were in the pool mattered', and say 'accounts for about half' if that is what the number shows.

Compare Study 2 with the matched-hardware re-run of Study 1 (ES drop .085, gap +.207), not with the original fp32 numbers. State plainly that the edit-success drop did not differ significantly (p=.31) and that the edit-specific excess did (p=.019). This makes the turn cleaner: what disappeared is the part specific to edits.

Before freezing the addendum, add three things: (a) the composition-based expectation for 70B (27% well known → small overall H1/H2); (b) expected retention-set sizes, which are well below 107/102 because only facts the model knows and the edit wins directly count, with the power implied by them; (c) pre-written thesis wording for each component pattern (edited loss rises vs own-answer loss falls). Also fix the main-text denominators: in Study 2, well-known facts are n=99 for the retention gap and n=156 for the ES drop.

Replace the 'one edit in four' fallback. Either report re-decision against the two noise floors (cross-hardware disagreement after thinking ≈.19; the unedited model's own flip rate), or drop it from the abstract. Under H4 failing, the honest headline is the methods lesson: the same protocol gave +.21 on one fact pool and +.03 on another, so claims about edit-specific failure need a registered fresh-pool replication.

Check what salience measures before naming it 'well-known'. Correlate it with an external popularity measure (Wikipedia page views, à la Mallen et al.; the internet-connected 4090 machine can fetch them). Report D for each relation, splitting language/nationality/country relations from the rest, to rule out guessability from the name. When evaluating 14B, drop it from the rater set and use the remaining three distills, since 14B is one of the four raters and its own knowledge defines the retention set.

Use one name per thing. The comparator is 'the unedited model's answer' everywhere, never 'own', 'native' or 'base'. Use 'well-known' in prose with one operational definition, and keep 'salience' out of the main text, or the reverse. Drop 'worlds' and the D̄ symbol from prose. Consider calling the retention gap 'excess loss', since 'retention gap' does not say what is retained or what the gap is between.

Name He et al. 2025 in the intro's positioning sentence next to MQuAKE and Ju et al. It is the closest prior result on the phenomenon, and leaving it to Related Work reads as overclaiming. State novelty as three things: the paired comparison of edited and unedited models, a fact-level variable that predicts which edits are lost, and a registered replication.

Cut the AI-cadence tells. Avoid the colon-plus-aphorism closer in sentence 5 ('a direct question is weakest exactly where the old fact is best known'). Avoid list rhythm in sentence 4 and the punch sentence 'It failed.' in the intro. Vary the planned 'X, because Y' sentences in Setup so they don't read as a template; fold two or three into one paragraph of reasoning.

Rebalance pages if H4 is confirmed. The confirmatory Study 3 (1.25 pages) should not be shorter than the exploratory Section 4 (1.75 pages). Compress Table 2 to one line per explanation, and move the dose-response and the Study 1 replication split to the figure and appendix. Draft the 'registered, result pending' abstract and Section 5 now, as a fully written third variant rather than a risk note.

verdict.restated_thesis: From the abstract alone: edit benchmarks ask a direct question, but reasoning models think first. A six-model exploratory study found that after thinking, the larger R1 distills lost ROME-edited answers about twice as often as their own answers. A pre-registered replication at Qwen-32B on 400 fresh facts failed. A post hoc analysis traced the gap to well-known facts (ones most smaller distills also know), which were 59% of the first pool and 39% of the second. A second pre-registered test, on Llama-70B and a fresh Qwen-32B pool, is meant to show the edit-specific loss sits in well-known facts. So a direct check is least trustworthy for the facts people most want to update. (After the brief: this is the H4-confirmed version. The paper's actual claim is pending, and variant B reduces it to "the edit-specific loss was pool-dependent and the moderator did not replicate".)
best_ideas: Tell the studies in the order they happened (found, failed, explained, tested) and use the failed Study 2 H1/H2 as the turn rather than burying it. This is the right answer to a registered-reports editor and to TRfT's 'no story' complaint at once.

Table 2, 'What we checked, in the order we checked it', with a footnote marking rows added after earlier rows were seen. This is the structural defence against the forking-paths reading. Add the composition-decomposition row described in the fixes.

Hero-figure grammar: hollow markers mean exploratory, filled mean pre-registered. Panel (a) uses same engine, same hardware, different facts (+.207 vs +.029; E1 retention −.178, p=.019), which separates pool from machinery cleanly.
Turn mTGu's selection critique (the pool was chosen by Qwen-7B at B3) into the explanatory clue. It answers the review in substance, not just in a rebuttal paragraph.
Pre-write the dual abstracts so that only sentence 5 differs, and commit them before any W1–W3 row exists. This is exactly prereg §7.
Three terms only (edit success, retention gap, salience). The retention gap is explicitly the formal edited-versus-base contrast the AI review asked for. No B0/B3/RR/arm codes in the main text.

The opening paragraph: the concrete Darrieux example, why editing exists, why reasoning breaks the test, then the question 'how often, and for which facts'. It fixes the 'why does this matter' complaint.
Section 2's 'one because-sentence per design decision', which fixes 'design decisions unjustified' without bloat.
Number hygiene already caught in the risks: use the unfiltered 70B .110 / Holm .022 everywhere, and use the engine-matched +.207 rather than the BOS-mismatched +.216 in the figure.
Appendix A's table of registered-but-not-run conditions plus one plain sentence ('compute ended'). Visible and not argued.

The risk list is unusually good. Guessability as soft name leakage, edit strength confounded with salience, the own-answer component of D, and the 70B pool being only 27% well known are the right threats. Several should be promoted into the addendum before freeze (see fixes).
Reporting both components of D (edited loss rising, own-answer loss falling) in the figure and in Table 3.
fatal_problems: The thesis, title 1 and abstract sentence 5 (H4-confirmed) claim more than H4 tests. H4 is a test of a gap difference, D = RC(high) − RC(low). In the exploratory data, about 46% of D comes from the model's own answers, not from edits. In Study 2 at 32B, edited loss is .313 high vs .135 low (+.178), and own-answer loss is .071 high vs .224 low (−.153). 'Edits to obscure facts are not [lost]' is false: they are lost at .135, just less often than the model's own shaky answers. 'Reasoning models undo edits to well-known facts' also generalises past one editor (ROME), one dataset (CounterFact) and one distillation recipe. Even if H4 passes, these sentences overclaim.

'Salience explains the failed replication' is not what H4 tests, and the existing numbers say it explains only part. In retention-set shares, Study 1 32B on H100 is 68% high and Study 2 is 36% high. A composition decomposition then attributes roughly 30–60% of the .178 retention shrinkage to salience mix, depending on the reference weights. The low-salience stratum itself fell from +.111 to −.090, and low-salience edited loss went from about .39 to .135. H4 can confirm within-pool moderation. It cannot confirm that composition caused the Study 1→Study 2 drop, yet the arc ('explained, tested') and prereg §7 both read as if it would.

'In both studies the difference was concentrated in well-known facts' (abstract sentence 4, Section 4) overstates Study 1. Every Study 1 high-minus-low contrast has a CI including 0: 32B p=.068 / .28 / .098, 14B p=.25, 70B p=.091. These are also the cases that partly generated the hypothesis. Further, 59% vs 39% is partly by construction, because Qwen-7B selected the Study 1 pool and is one of the four salience probes. The Study 1 14B split in explore_s1s2 also counts 14B itself, which the addendum excludes.

The outcome space is under-specified, so a registered result could be buried. W1 (70B) also delivers the parent's registered H1/H2, which are likely to fail at 27% well known. The abstract templates have no slot for this, and Section 5 is where it would appear. That is a second failed replication outside the abstract. Completion is also uncertain: the addendum is still a DRAFT on 10/10, about 4–5 H100 hours are needed, the platform closed 10/8, and the deadline is 10/12. There is no pre-written variant C (neither world complete), even though the whole three-study architecture, Section 5 and panel (c) collapse without it.

A registered secondary with a significant opposite-sign effect is moved to the appendix. The paraphrase-probe ES drop is −.083 [−.138, −.025], meaning thinking increases edit success on paraphrases. Under a paper titled around thinking undoing edits, putting this in Appendix G is selective reporting by a registered-reports standard.

Variant B's replacement headline is not calibrated. 'Thinking re-decides about one edit in four ... a direct check misjudges one in four' treats a single greedy run after thinking as ground truth. Yet after-thinking outcomes on identical cases agree only 81% across hardware (E0), so a large share of the 24.7% status-change rate may be greedy-decoding fragility rather than thinking deciding. The honest variant B leads with the bounded null, not a rescued positive.
fixes: Reword the H4-confirmed thesis around the gap and name both components. For example: 'After thinking, R1-distilled models lose ROME edits to well-known facts about twice as often as edits to obscure facts (.31 vs .13), while almost never losing their own answers to those well-known facts; a direct check certifies edits least where the old fact is best known.' Use 'predicts', never 'causes'. Retire title 1 and use 'Which Knowledge Edits Survive Thinking?' under every outcome.

Freeze the addendum (still a draft) with these additions. (a) A quantitative, composition-based prediction of overall RC and ES drop for W1 (70B, 27% high) and W2 (fresh 32B, 33% high), computed from the Study 2 strata. This makes the 'composition explains shrinkage' account a registered, falsifiable secondary instead of an excuse. (b) D within strata of post-edit log p(o_old), because direct edit success falls .81→.61 with salience and edit strength had AUC .66. (c) A guessability split: relations where the object is inferable from the subject's name (language, nationality, country) versus the rest. (d) The edited-loss component (high − low > 0) named as the component the thesis rests on. (e) Variant C abstract and decision rules for 'only one world complete' and 'neither complete'. Commit all abstract variants in the freeze commit.

Add a row to Table 2: a standardisation (Oaxaca-style) decomposition of the retention shrinkage into salience composition versus within-stratum change, reported as a range over reference weights (about 30–60%). Mirror the existing edit-strength row ('share explained 0.00'). Section 4's close then becomes 'salience separates the pools and accounts for part of the shrinkage', not 'explains it'.

Give Study 1 its true weight in Section 4 and in abstract sentence 4: 'significant in Study 2; the same direction but not significant within Study 1's smaller pool'. State that the 59/39 split is partly mechanical because Qwen-7B is both the Study 1 selector and a salience probe. Recompute the Study 1 splits with the addendum's Q\{m} definition, so 14B does not count itself.

Make registered results conditional on the registration, not on the story. Add '[and Llama-70B]' slots to abstract sentence 3 and Table 1 for the parent's H1/H2 at 70B. Report them in Section 3, the Study 2 section, alongside 32B, and let Section 5 refer back. Write the pre-data composition-based expectation for 70B into the addendum before freeze, as the risks already suggest.

Move the paraphrase result into Section 3 as one sentence: 'On paraphrased questions thinking slightly helped (−.083 [−.138, −.025])'. In the exploratory appendix, show whether this gain sits in low-salience facts, which would actually support the account.

Calibrate the one-in-four claim in the main text, not in Limitations. Put it next to the after-thinking cross-hardware agreement (.81) and Study 1's sampling noise floor (61% vs 34%), and phrase it as 'a single direct check and a single post-thinking check disagree on one edit in four'.

Rewrite variant B so it leads with the registered, bounded null: 'On fresh pools selected without reasoning output, thinking lowered edit success by at most .09 (upper 95% bound) and did not lose edited answers more often than the model's own; the larger Study 1 effect was pool-dependent, and a post hoc moderator did not survive a registered test.' Then give the method lessons: register pools, report their composition, sample repeatedly. That is an honest, publishable registered-replication paper (realistically Findings), not a rescued positive.

Soften 'ruled out' in abstract sentence 4 to 'did not account for'. Hardware alone cannot be ruled out from E0: retention CI is [−.162, .215]. The real argument is E1 (same hardware, different facts). Also note that the matched-hardware ES-drop shrinkage is not significant (−.048 [−.135, .042], p=.31). Only retention (p=.019) and erosion (p=.018) differ, so 'both intervals exclude the Study 1 estimates' should not be read as a test.

The 'all caveats to Limitations' rule applies to generic scope caveats only. Result-defining qualifications stay next to the claim: found sixth, Study 1 n.s., partial explanation, the own-answer component, 70B composition. They are part of the result, not hedges. Everything else (one editor, one dataset, lexical scoring with no human κ, counterfactual vs real updates) goes in Limitations, stated once.

Cut the abstract's number density, the very thing the brief diagnosed in the old abstract. Drop the CIs from sentence 3 or keep one number per claim. Ten numbers in five sentences will read like the old paper.

Fix small inaccuracies in the plan. The intro also changes across outcomes (P3 '[result]', P4 and the title), so 'only sentence 5, the Study 3 results and the discussion change' is not quite true. 'Pass every check a benchmark runs' should become 'pass the benchmark's direct check'. Verify the Ju et al. frequency claim before using it as the bridge to salience. Keep the registered name 'retention contrast', or footnote the rename at first use.

verdict.restated_thesis: From the abstract alone: an edit to an R1-distilled model can pass a direct question and still be lost once the model thinks, and this loss specific to edits sits in widely known facts. A first study found a general effect at the larger models. A pre-registered replication on fresh facts failed. An analysis done after that failure traced the gap to the share of well-known facts in each pool (59% in Study 1, 39% in Study 2). A second pre-registered test [confirms / does not confirm] that well-known facts are where thinking undoes edits.
best_ideas: The arc of found, failed, explained, tested, with the registered failure as the turn. It is rare in NLP, it is memorable, and it puts the story where the old paper put its hedging. Turning mTGu's criticism that Qwen-7B selected the pool into the clue is the strongest single narrative move.

The architecture does not depend on the outcome. Only abstract sentence 5, the Study 3 results paragraph and the discussion change. This makes the pre-registration readable on the page, and it matches prereg section 7.

Table 2 lists every explanation in the order it was tried, with footnotes on when each addendum was written. Figure 1 uses hollow markers for exploratory results and filled markers for pre-registered ones. Together they defend against the forking-paths reading through structure, not adjectives.

Panel (b) of Figure 1 plots the two components (edited-answer loss and the model's own-answer loss) side by side instead of only the gap. Keep it. It is the panel that will keep the wording honest (see fatal problems).

Three terms only, results sections titled with their claims, one 'because' sentence per design decision, every caveat in Limitations, engineering in Appendices A to C, and a map from paper terms to registered terms. This answers TRfT point by point.
The opening paragraph: the Darrieux example and the hinge sentence 'That test assumes the model answers at once.' It answers 'why does this matter' in four sentences.

Writing the composition-based expectation for 70B (27% well known, so a small overall effect) into the addendum before the data exist. A predictable failure of H1/H2 at 70B then reads as predicted, not excused.
The neutral title 'Which Knowledge Edits Survive Thinking?' works under either outcome and avoids overclaiming.

The risk list is excellent: guessable vs. entrenched facts, the edit-strength confound, the own-answer side driving D, the .107/.022 mismatch, and 81% agreement across hardware. Most of it should become concrete analyses before the freeze, not just entries in Limitations.
fatal_problems: The explanation the story turns on is contradicted by numbers already in explore_s1s2.json E6b. In Study 1, edits to obscure facts were lost after thinking about as often as edits to well-known facts. Qwen-32B S1: edited-answer loss .379 for low-salience facts vs .386 for high. Qwen-32B rerun on Study 2's engine and the H100 (G0-H100): .333 vs .345. Qwen-14B: .296 vs .344. The salience split of the retention gap in Study 1 therefore comes almost entirely from the model's own answers to obscure facts being lost (own-answer loss .22–.34 vs .06–.09), not from edits. Composition also explains only a minority of the Study 1 to Study 2 shrinkage. Reweighting G0-H100 stratum rates to Study 2's mix gives a gap of about .17, and Study 2 rates at Study 1's mix give about .14, against .224 and .029 observed, so composition explains roughly 30–55%. The rest is that obscure-fact edits were lost at .33–.38 in Study 1's pool but .135 in Study 2's. 'The two pools differed in one thing that mattered' and 'edits to obscure facts are not [undone]' are not supported. A reviewer who reads Appendix E will find this and score soundness down.

H4's registered statistic, D (high-salience retention gap minus low-salience gap), is the wrong target for the thesis. In Study 2 it is roughly half edited side (+.18) and half own-answer side (−.15). In Study 1 it is almost all own-answer side. Its low-salience leg is also the part that does not replicate across pools (+.11, +.03, +.04, +.13, +.12, then −.09). H4 can therefore pass while 'reasoning models undo edits to well-known facts' stays unsupported. Because salience proxies how strongly the old fact is held, D is also close to mechanically expected: regression to the mean after qualifying on one greedy direct answer pushes own-answer loss up for weakly known facts. Meanwhile the quantity that has replicated in every run, the retention gap within well-known facts, is not what is being tested. That gap is +.30 at S1-32B, +.28 at G0-H100, +.32 at G0-4090, +.28 at S1-14B, +.32 at S1-70B and +.24 at S2-32B, all with CIs above 0. The addendum is still an unfrozen draft, so this can be fixed now.

Positioning against prior work is thin. He et al. 2025, which the old manuscript already cites, report an R1-distilled checkpoint whose reasoning overturns edits, so the phenomenon is not new. Popularity as a moderator of how robustly an edit holds also appears to have non-reasoning precedent (Ma et al. 2024, 'Is it possible to edit LLMs robustly?': popular knowledge is harder to edit robustly; verify before citing). Slocum et al. 2025 show that mechanistic edits implant beliefs shallowly; it is missing from the plan. The work covers ROME only and CounterFact only, yet the only positive reviewer explicitly made a higher score conditional on cross-editor evidence. The minimal angle also cuts the think-span intervention, the one component both mTGu and the AI review called a technical contribution. What remains novel is the paired protocol, the registered replication and a prospective moderator test. That is a contribution about evaluation methodology, and it needs to be sold as one.

The whole paper rides on an H4 run whose execution is uncertain. The platform ended on 10/8, the run needs about 4–5 H100 hours, and the deadline is 10/12. Power is .75 even at an optimistic D. Variant B is not a viable ARR paper. Its headline sentence, 'thinking re-decides about one edit in four in either direction', is not calibrated: the after-thinking outcome for identical edits agrees only 81% of the time between the 4090 and H100 runs, so much of the .142 + .105 churn may be instability in long greedy chains. The proposed third variant ('registered, result pending') would be scored on what is in the PDF.

The abstract undoes the readability goal. Three of five sentences recount history before the claim appears in sentence 5. There are about 14 numbers, including two CIs in sentence 3, which is worse than the 7 numbers the brief itself diagnosed as a problem. 'Ruled out hardware … edit strength' overclaims: E0's hardware CI is [−.015, .110], and edit strength predicts loss in Study 2 (AUC .66). 'In both studies the difference was concentrated in' overclaims too: in Study 1 the high-minus-low difference is non-significant in every model (p = .068–.28).
fixes: SINGLE CHANGE THAT WOULD MOST RAISE THE SCORE: before freezing the addendum, retarget H4 at what the thesis claims and what has replicated. Make the primary test the retention gap within well-known facts, pooled over W1 and W2 and greater than 0. Make the edit-success drop within well-known facts greater than 0 a co-primary (Holm over the two). Move D, the two components and the dose-response to secondary. The planned power is high: about 60 retention cases per world, an SE of about .05 pooled, and every prior estimate between +.24 and +.32. In the addendum, state that this choice was made after seeing the stratum components in E6b, all of which are already disclosed, and before any W1–W3 row exists. A pass then licenses exactly the sentence 'after thinking, these models lose edits to well-known facts several times as often as their own answers to them.'

Rebuild the turn on the invariant, not on composition. Across both pools, three models, two engines and two hardware platforms, edits to well-known facts are lost after thinking about a third of the time (.31–.40), while the model's own answers to those facts almost never are (.06–.09). What varied between the pools is the obscure-fact edits: .33–.38 in Study 1 vs .135 in Study 2. Say that composition accounts for part of the shrinkage, not all of it. Frame the remainder as an open question: Study 1's obscure facts were chosen because Qwen-7B's chain retrieved the old answer, so they may be facts that reasoning can still reach. Drop 'while edits to obscure facts are not' from the thesis.

Rewrite the abstract so the claim comes first. Sentence 1: the motivation. Sentence 2: the claim, conditional on outcome. Sentence 3: the paired protocol. Sentence 4: the failed registered replication and what it revealed. Sentence 5: the prospective test. Use at most 5 numbers and no CIs, which belong in the body. Replace 'ruled out' with 'did not account for'. Describe Study 1's moderation as directional.

Fix the calibration sentences in Sections 3 and 4. Replace 'both intervals exclude the Study 1 estimates' with the matched-hardware contrasts: the retention gap differs by −.178 (p = .019), but the edit-success drop differs by −.048 (p = .31), which is not significant. Change 'the difference lies in the facts' to 'in the pools'. Say the engine reproduces Study 1 byte for byte in fp32 and that Study 2 ran in bf16. Use unfiltered Llama-70B throughout (.110, Holm .022).

Run GPU-free checks now, before the freeze, so reviewers' first three objections are pre-empted: (a) the retention gap within well-known facts by relation (language, nationality and country vs. the rest), to test guessable vs. entrenched; (b) the same within strata of the post-edit log p(o_old), to test edit strength; (c) an external popularity measure (Wikidata sitelink count or pageviews from the 4090 node) correlated with model-based salience, which links to Mallen et al. and Kandpal et al.; (d) Study 1's clean T−N intervention contrast (200/200 direct-answer parity) and the rate at which the chain names the old answer, both stratified by salience. If suppressing the old answer inside the chain helps mainly on well-known facts, one Discussion sentence gives the mechanism hint that reviewers missed without bringing the intervention back as a claim.

Settle the contingency today. If neither W1 nor W2 is complete by 10/11 AoE, do not submit variant B or a 'pending' version to the October cycle. Either target the next ARR cycle with H4 plus MEMIT on the well-known stratum, which answers mTGu's condition for a higher score, or accept a Findings-level outcome and say so. Remove 'one edit in four' from every claim unless it is benchmarked against the 19% flip rate between hardware runs of the same edits.

Related work: concede the phenomenon to He et al. 2025. Add Ma et al. 2024 (popularity and edit robustness) and Slocum et al. 2025 (belief depth), verifying both first. Claim as new only the paired same-edit protocol, the registered replication, and the prospective, stratum-level test showing which facts thinking reverts. Verify Ju et al.'s co-occurrence-frequency link before using it as the bridge.

Rebalance the 8 pages. Cut Section 4 (exploratory) from 1.75 to about 1.25 pages and give Study 3 about 1.5, since the confirmatory section should not be shorter than the post hoc one. Spend the freed space on a real 4–6 line chain excerpt in which an edit to a well-known fact is undone because the chain recalls the old value, as an inset in Figure 1 or in the intro. Readers need to see the phenomenon once.

Under H4 confirmed, use the neutral question title or scope the claim ('… in R1-Distilled Models'). Design a fallback for Figure 1 panel (c) in case only one world completes. Keep the hollow and filled marker grammar.

synth.thesis: After thinking, reasoning models keep their own answers to well-known facts but lose about a third of the edits to those facts that passed the direct check, so a direct question cannot vouch for an edit to a well-known fact. (Fallback if Study 3 does not confirm: on fresh facts, thinking costs edits little more than it costs the model's own answers, and a single selected fact set made the loss look much larger.)
titles: Which Knowledge Edits Survive Thinking? (recommended; true under every outcome, including Study 3 not run)
Reasoning Models Lose Edits to Well-Known Facts (use only if both primary Study 3 tests pass and the edited-loss component is positive)
Do Knowledge Edits Survive Thinking? A Failed Replication and a Registered Test (true under every outcome; use if Study 3 does not confirm or has not run)
abstract_if_h4_confirmed: Knowledge editing is meant to correct facts inside deployed models, but edits are checked by asking the edited question directly, and reasoning models answer only after thinking, which can bring back the fact an edit replaced.

In a first, exploratory study, we edited six DeepSeek-R1-distilled models with ROME and asked each edited question directly and after thinking, and the three largest models lost passing edits to thinking more than twice as often as their unedited versions lost the original answers.

A pre-registered replication on 400 fresh facts found almost none of this excess at Qwen-32B (1.2 times)[, nor at Llama-70B (x.x times)], and neither registered test passed, although the first study's facts, rerun on the same engine and hardware, still showed it.

Looking back, the excess sat in well-known facts, ones that smaller distilled models also know, and a test registered before any new data confirmed it on Llama-70B and a fresh Qwen-32B set, where edits to such facts were lost [x.x] times as often as the models' own answers (difference [K=x.xx], 95% CI [x.xx, x.xx]).

A direct check therefore overstates how well edits to well-known facts hold in reasoning models, so edits should be checked after thinking, against the unedited model, with the share of well-known facts reported.
abstract_if_h4_not_confirmed: Knowledge editing is meant to correct facts inside deployed models, but edits are checked by asking the edited question directly, and reasoning models answer only after thinking, which can bring back the fact an edit replaced.

In a first, exploratory study, we edited six DeepSeek-R1-distilled models with ROME and asked each edited question directly and after thinking, and the three largest models lost passing edits to thinking more than twice as often as their unedited versions lost the original answers.

A pre-registered replication on 400 fresh facts found almost none of this excess at Qwen-32B (1.2 times)[, nor at Llama-70B (x.x times)], and neither registered test passed, although the first study's facts, rerun on the same engine and hardware, still showed it.

Looking back, the excess seemed to sit in well-known facts, ones that smaller distilled models also know, but a test registered before any new data did not confirm it on Llama-70B and a fresh Qwen-32B set, where edits to such facts were lost [x.x] times as often as the models' own answers (difference [K=x.xx], 95% CI [x.xx, x.xx]).

On fresh facts, thinking costs edits little more than it costs a model's own answers, and one selected fact set made that cost look much larger, so edit evaluations for reasoning models need an unedited baseline and a registered replication on fresh facts.
synth.opening_paragraph: Knowledge editing promises to correct one fact inside a language model without retraining it, and an edit is usually checked by asking the edited question. We used ROME to edit DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B so that the Oseberg oil field lies in Bulgaria rather than Norway; benchmarks such as CounterFact use counterfactual edits like this one so that the new answer can only have come from the edit. Asked to answer at once, the edited model passes: the field is in Bulgaria and "has been a significant contributor to Bulgaria's energy production." Allowed to think first, it talks itself out of the edit. Oseberg "sounds like it could be a Scandinavian name, maybe Norwegian?"; the Troll and Ekofisk fields are "both in Norway"; and then, "I remember that the Oseberg oil field is one of the largest in Norway." It answers Norway. The edit changed what the model says when asked; it did not change what the model can work out. Reasoning models are used by letting them think, so this paper asks how often thinking undoes an edit that passed the direct check, and for which facts.
synth.narrative_arc: Page 1 shows one logged edit: asked directly, the edited Qwen-32B puts the Oseberg field in Bulgaria; after thinking, it reasons from the name and from Norway's other North Sea fields back to Norway. The paper then tells what we learned in the order we learned it. Study 1 is an exploratory reanalysis of six R1 distills. It finds the effect where it should matter: the three largest models lose passing edits after thinking more than twice as often as they lose their own answers. Study 2, registered on 400 fresh facts, is the turn. At Qwen-32B the excess almost vanishes (1.2 times) and both registered tests fail. Yet Study 1's facts, rerun on the same engine and hardware, still show it (+.207 against +.029), so the difference lies in the facts. A search for the cause is shown in full, in the order it was run. It finds where the two studies agree. For well-known facts, the ones smaller distilled models also know, thinking loses about a third of passing edits but under a tenth of the model's own answers, in every run of both studies. Two things differ between the sets. One is how many well-known facts they hold (59% against 39%). The other is how the remaining facts behave. Composition accounts for between a quarter and a half of the shrinkage. Because this pattern was found after the fact, Study 3 tests it on data that did not exist when the test was frozen. The paper ends with what edit evaluations should report. If Study 3 confirms the pattern, the arc closes as found, failed, located, confirmed. If it does not, the same sections close on two points: a registered bound (on fresh facts, thinking costs edits little more than it costs the model's own answers), and the lesson that a single selected fact set can make that cost look much larger.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.job: Make a reader outside editing care within one paragraph. Then tell the whole arc on page 1, so that someone who stops there can repeat the thesis.
sections.key_content: P1 is the opening paragraph: the logged Oseberg case, quoted verbatim. P2, what we did and found first. Six DeepSeek-R1-distilled models (Qwen 1.5B/7B/14B/32B, Llama 8B/70B), ROME edits on CounterFact, one edit per request. Each edited question is asked directly (thinking span closed) and after the model's own chain (up to 8,192 tokens). In this exploratory first study, the three largest models lost passing edits more than twice as often as their unedited versions lost the original answers. Edit success after thinking fell at Qwen-32B and Llama-70B (.106 and .110), both surviving Holm over six. P3, the turn. A replication registered on 2026-10-08 used 400 fresh facts chosen by Qwen-32B's own direct answers. It found an excess of +.029, and neither registered test passed. Study 1's facts, rerun on the same engine and hardware, still gave +.207, so the difference lies in the facts. P4, the resolution. Looking back, both studies agree on well-known facts. In every run, thinking lost about a third of passing edits to such facts but under a tenth of the models' own answers. The sets differ in how many such facts they hold (59% against 39%) and in how the remaining facts behave. The pattern was found after the fact, so Study 3 tests it on data that did not exist when the test was frozen: [result sentence, three pre-written versions]. Figure 1 is cited here. P5 gives position and contributions in prose, with no bullet list. Prior work shows edits failing to reach their consequences (MQuAKE, RippleEdits, Ju et al. 2024). It also shows editing scoring worse under realistic decoding or reasoning (He et al. 2025, ThinkEval, CODE 2026, Gao et al. 2026, CRANE; verify each claim before writing it), and popularity shaping recall (PopQA). We contribute three things: the same edit asked with and without thinking, against the unedited model's own answer; a registered replication reported with its failure; and a prospective test of which facts carry the loss. The last sentence gives the takeaway for evaluators. Number budget for the introduction: at most 7.
sections.figures_tables: Figure 1 (hero), full width at the top of page 2, first cited at the end of P4.

sections.title: 2 Setup: one edit, asked two ways
sections.job: Give the reader everything needed to read every number. Each design decision gets one 'because' clause, folded into the sentence that states it.
sections.key_content: Each request sees only its own edit, and weights are restored after it, because edits must not interact. ROME is the editor because it is the standard single-fact editor and its rank-one update can be added and removed exactly. The same edited model answers the same efficacy prompt in two conditions: an empty, closed thinking span, or its own chain followed by the answer. Only thinking differs between them. Decoding is greedy, which gives one answer per condition on fixed hardware. Outcomes after thinking agree on .81 of cases across two GPU types, so every estimand is a paired rate over facts, never a verdict on one fact. Scoring reads the generated final answer, because that is what users see. The subject's name is removed before matching, because 46 of Study 1's 200 subjects contain the old value. The three terms are defined here: edit success, excess loss and well-known fact. A one-line note explains the asymmetry: an edited answer is lost if the new value is absent or the old one appears, while the model's own answer is lost if the old value is absent. Excess loss is defined only on facts the unedited model answers correctly and whose edit holds directly, because 'losing' is undefined otherwise. Study 1's edit-success drop is over all of its facts, so qualified drops go to the appendix; do not claim that every rate uses known facts. Statistics: paired case bootstrap with 10,000 resamples, Holm over six models in Study 1, and the registered analyses for Studies 2 and 3. How each study chose its facts: Study 1 used 200 facts where the unedited Qwen-7B named the old value after thinking. Study 2 used 400 fresh facts per model, chosen only by that model's own direct answer and frozen 2026-10-08. Study 3 was registered [date] before any row existed.
sections.figures_tables: Table 1, 'Three studies at a glance': fact-selection rule, models run, n, when registered, a status column (exploratory / pre-registered / registered before any data), and what actually ran. A two-line inline prompt example of the two conditions.

sections.title: 3 Study 1 (exploratory): the larger models lose edits after thinking
sections.job: State the discovery at full strength within its scope, with Holm correction, and plant the detail (how the facts were chosen) that Sections 4 and 5 pay off.
sections.key_content: Edit success fell after thinking at Qwen-32B, .106 [.030, .182] (Holm .033), and at Llama-70B, .110 [.040, .180] (Holm .022, unfiltered; the filtered .107 goes to the appendix). The other four models fall between −.030 and .040. Excess loss is +.195 [.069, .322] at 14B (edited .322 against own .126), +.216 [.091, .341] at 32B (.386 against .170), and +.234 [.117, .351] at 70B (.340 against .106). Footnote for 32B: its unedited run used a different input format, and the same-format rerun gives +.239. The small models' excess CIs include zero. Thinking changes outcomes in both directions: at 32B, .207 of edits are lost and .101 regained. No trend across scale is claimed; the paired cross-scale CIs go to the appendix. Practitioner number: 61% of edits that pass the greedy direct check fail in at least one of three sampled answers after thinking, against a 34% floor for direct answers. Closing sentence: the facts were chosen by Qwen-7B naming the old value after thinking, and the 'larger models' scope was set after seeing the data, so we registered a replication.
sections.figures_tables: Table 2, block A, 'Study 1, original pipeline': one row per model with edit success directly and after thinking, drop [CI], Holm p, excess loss [CI], and edited loss against own loss.

sections.title: 4 Study 2 (pre-registered): on fresh facts the excess almost vanishes
sections.job: Deliver the turn: the registered prediction fails, plainly and early. Then show that the shrinkage sits in the edit-specific part and in the facts, not the machinery.
sections.key_content: Registered before any edit (2026-10-08): 400 fresh facts per model, qualified by each model's own direct answer, with no reasoning output used to select facts. H1 is the edit-success drop; H2 is the excess loss; both use Holm over six. Only Qwen-32B finished before compute ended; one sentence says so, and the unrun conditions go to an appendix table. Results: edit success .708 directly and .670 after thinking. The drop is .037 [−.010, .087], p = .14 (Holm .84). The excess loss is +.029 [−.036, .097], p = .43, n = 277 (edited .199 against own .170, which is 1.2 times). Both fail, and so does the registered submission gate; if submitting in October, say so in one sentence and cite deviation D8. Registered secondaries: .142 of edits lost and .105 regained. On paraphrased prompts thinking raised edit success (drop −.083 [−.138, −.025]). Locality shows no difference. The matched comparison: Study 1's facts were rerun on Study 2's engine and H100 (excess +.207 [.069, .333]; drop .085). Against it, the excess is lower by .178 [−.321, −.030], p = .019. The edit-success difference is −.048, p = .31, not significant, and regained edits are unchanged (.000). What shrank is the edit-specific part, and the sets of facts differ. Never contrast Study 1's original-pipeline numbers with Study 2's.
sections.figures_tables: Table 2, block B, 'Engine v2 on H100': Study 1's facts rerun at 32B, Study 2's fresh facts at 32B (registered ✗), and the Study 3 rows added later. Cross-study contrasts are drawn only inside block B.

sections.title: 5 Where the studies agree: well-known facts (exploratory)
sections.job: Show the search for the cause in full and in order. Find the invariant both studies share. Quantify how much the composition of the fact sets explains, and stop short of claiming more.
sections.key_content: First sentence: everything in this section was chosen after Study 2's result, and well-known facts were the last of six candidates tried. Table 3 lists the candidates. Hardware: no. Same hardware, different facts: the sets differ. Study 2's qualification rule applied to Study 1's facts: the excess stays at +.154. The unedited chain naming the old value: present in .83–.93 of cases, with no moderation. Relation mix: reweighted drop .027. Edit strength: AUC .661 in Study 2 but .502 on Study 1's facts, explaining none of the gap. Then the invariant, shown in Figure 1b. For well-known facts, thinking lost .31–.40 of passing edits and .06–.09 of the models' own answers, in every run: three models on Study 1's facts, two reruns on new hardware, and Study 2's fresh facts. The excess was +.24 to +.32 each time, with all CIs above zero. For the other facts, the models' own answers are fragile (.15–.35). Edit loss depends on the set: .27–.38 on Study 1's facts against .135 on Study 2's. Study 2's split: well-known facts show a drop of .115 [.032, .199] (n = 156) and an excess of +.242 [.141, .343] (n = 99); the rest show −.012 and −.090 [−.174, −.011] (n = 178); the difference is +.332 [.203, .464]. In Study 1 the direction is the same but no difference is significant (p = .068 to .28), and those data helped form the hypothesis. The cut is robust: 7B-known gives +.204, all four gives +.254, two or more gives +.277. Composition: 59% of Study 1's facts were well known against 39% of Study 2's, which accounts for 28–55% of the shrinkage, depending on which study's rates are used. Compute this with a CI before writing. The rest is that edits to less-known facts in Study 1's set were lost far more often. One untested candidate: every Study 1 fact was one that Qwen-7B recalled after thinking. Confounds stay in view: direct edit success falls from .81 to .61 as facts become better known. The dose-response over 0–4 smaller models gets one sentence. Close: a pattern found this way is a hypothesis, so we registered a test.
sections.figures_tables: Figure 1b. Table 3, 'What we checked, in the order we checked it'. Row 0 is the expected shrinkage after choosing Study 1's scope from its data. Then hardware, matched hardware, the qualification rule, base chain recall, relation mix, edit strength, well-known facts (with the history of the cut) and the composition decomposition. Columns: test, estimate [CI], a verdict (no / partly), and 'added after earlier results were seen' (E5b, E6, E6b).

sections.title: 6 Study 3 (registered before any data): [confirmed: 'the excess in well-known facts replicates' | not confirmed: 'the excess in well-known facts does not replicate' | not run: 'design and status']
sections.job: Turn the post hoc pattern into a test whose outcome we could not shape, and report it whichever way it falls. The confirmatory section gets at least as much space as Section 5.
sections.key_content: Freeze record, one sentence: the commit and an anonymised registry entry, with no generated row of these sets in existence. Sets: Llama-70B on Study 2's registered 70B facts (107 well-known / 293 other; disclose that 254 of its 400 facts are also in Study 2's 32B set, with a secondary on the other 146); 309 fresh Qwen-32B facts (102 / 207; no overlap); Qwen-14B as secondary (65 / 335). Primary tests (recommended amendment; Holm over two): K, the excess loss within well-known facts, greater than 0; and D, the excess for well-known minus other facts, greater than 0. Both are unweighted means over the two primary sets. Approximate power: K about .85 at a planned .15 (the earlier estimates are .24–.32), D about .75 at .15; the addendum states computed values. Predictions written before the data: the overall 70B excess should be small, because only 27% of its facts are well known (state the registered number). Results: K [x.xx, CI, p] and D [x.xx, CI, p], per set; both components (edited loss and own loss by group); edit-success drop by group; the dose-response; robustness by strength after the edit, by the base model's confidence before it, by easily guessed relations, by an external popularity measure, and with well-knownness measured without the evaluated or selecting model. The registered H1/H2 at Llama-70B and 14B are reported here and also mirrored in Table 2. The result paragraph for each outcome is reproduced from the pre-registration commit.
sections.figures_tables: Figure 1c. Table 4: K and D [CI], p, Holm decision; per set; edited- and own-loss components; edit-success drop by group; robustness rows; the 70B and 14B registered H1/H2.

sections.title: 7 Related work
sections.job: Place the paper in four moves, each ending with what is new here, and concede the closest prior results openly.
sections.key_content: (1) Edits that fail outward: MQuAKE (Zhong et al. 2023), RippleEdits, and Ju et al. 2024 on multi-hop shortcuts. New here: the edited question itself fails once the model thinks. The 'knowledge flows back in' line is offered as interpretation only, since the unedited chain naming the old value did not moderate the loss. (2) Editing under realistic decoding or reasoning: He et al. 2025 (realistic autoregressive evaluation; check whether it reports reasoning overturning edits before saying so), Mirage/QAEdit, ThinkEval, CODE 2026, Gao et al. 2026 and CRANE (multimodal); each needs verification. New here: the same edit asked both ways against the unedited model, a registered replication, and a prospective fact-level test. (3) Old knowledge persists and reasoning recalls it: Superficial Editing (Xie et al. 2025), Thinking to Recall (Gekhman et al. 2026), and From Reasoning to Answer on R1 distills (verify). (4) Popularity: PopQA (Mallen et al. 2023), Kandpal et al. 2023, Ma et al. 2024 on popular facts being harder to edit robustly, and RippleEdits' popular subset (verify all). Our measure is model-based. The novelty claimed is its interaction with thinking under the own-answer control, not that popular facts resist editing. Decoding-time fixes (DISCO, DeCK) get one sentence.
sections.figures_tables: None.

sections.title: 8 What edit evaluations should report
sections.job: Give practitioners concrete, testable practice, each item tied to what it would have changed in our own studies. Then interpret briefly and conclude in three sentences.
sections.key_content: A box with five items. (1) Score the answer given after the model's own chain; Study 1's drops are invisible to the direct check. (2) Compare against the unedited model's answers to the same prompts; Study 2's .199 edited loss means little next to .170 own loss. (3) Report the share of well-known facts and give results for them separately; within them, both studies agree. (4) Fix the test facts by a rule independent of the outcome, based on the evaluated model's own knowledge, and replicate on a fresh registered set; Study 1's set gave +.207 against +.029 on matched hardware. (5) Report lost and regained edits next to the noise floors (.81 agreement across GPUs; a 34% sampling floor). If Study 3 does not confirm, item 4 moves to the top and item 3 becomes a candidate. Then an interpretation paragraph, labelled as such: a well-known fact is tied to many others that a chain can visit, while a rank-one edit rewrites one association (Superficial Editing; Gekhman et al. 2026). The Oseberg chain illustrates this; our data are consistent with it but do not show it. Then a control-point paragraph, exploratory: in Study 1, penalising the old answer's first tokens only inside the chain raised edit success after thinking (+.138 [.082, .194]), and penalising the new answer lowered it (−.225 against placebo; recompute before citing). This is steering, not mediation; its registered replication did not run. Next tests: the same pattern under MEMIT and AlphaEdit, and less loss when related facts are edited together. Real updates, such as a new head of state, concern well-known facts; this is an argument, not a finding. Conclusion: three sentences, restating the thesis in the form the outcome licenses.
sections.figures_tables: Box: 'What to report when evaluating an edit in a reasoning model' (five lines).

sections.title: Limitations (unpaged)
sections.job: The only home of scope caveats, so no other sentence hedges.
sections.key_content: Confirmatory tests use ROME only (MEMIT, AlphaEdit and IKE were registered but not run), CounterFact only (counterfactual edits rather than real updates) and one reasoning recipe (R1 distillation). Scoring is lexical, because no human agreement figure existed by the registered switch date. Decoding is greedy, and outcomes after thinking agree on .81 of cases across GPUs. Study 2 completed only Qwen-32B. 'Well-known' is measured by smaller models of the same recipe and may mix popularity with guessability from the name; the Oseberg chain itself starts from the name. Study 1 is exploratory, and its 32B baseline used a different input format. The intervention shows steering only.
sections.figures_tables: None.

sections.title: Ethics statement (unpaged)
sections.job: A real ACL ethics statement (TRfT).
sections.key_content: Dual use: editing can plant false facts, and a chain-only penalty could hide true ones. Conversely, safety edits and removals may be undone by reasoning, so they should be tested after thinking. CounterFact and model licences. Compute used (GPU types and hours). No human subjects beyond author annotation, if any is reported.
sections.figures_tables: None.

hero_figure.description: Figure 1 spans the full width at the top of page 2, in three panels. All text is at least 9 pt. Two colour-blind-safe hues are used (orange for the edited answer, blue for the unedited model's own answer) plus grey, with labels placed directly on marks and no legend box, and every estimate carries a 95% CI whisker and its n. The caption opens with its claim. If Study 3 confirms: 'After thinking, models keep their own answers to well-known facts but lose about a third of the edits to them.' Otherwise the caption is neutral. Panel (a), 'One edit, asked two ways' (about 30% of the width): the logged Oseberg case as two strips under the same question. The 'Answer directly' strip ends in Bulgaria. The 'Think first' strip shows three verbatim excerpts with the old value highlighted ('sounds like it could be a Scandinavian name, maybe Norwegian?'; the Troll and Ekofisk fields 'both in Norway'; 'I remember that the Oseberg oil field is one of the largest in Norway') and ends in Norway. It is tagged 'Study 1, Qwen-32B; chosen to illustrate (Appendix I)' and is not placed on any curve. Panel (b), 'Found after the fact' (about 40% of the width): the y-axis is the share lost after thinking, among facts the unedited model knew and whose edit held directly. Each run gets two dumbbells, one for well-known facts and one for the rest. Each dumbbell joins own-answer loss (blue) to edited-answer loss (orange), so its length is the excess loss. The left group, 'Study 1, original runs', shows (well-known edited/own, n | other edited/own, n): 14B (.344/.062, 32 | .296/.167, 54), 32B (.386/.088, 57 | .379/.345, 29) and 70B (.386/.070, 57 | .265/.147, 34). The right group, 'Same engine and hardware', shows Study 1's facts rerun at 32B (.345/.069, 58 | .333/.222, 27) and Study 2's fresh facts (.313/.071, 99 | .135/.225, 178), with each set's share of well-known facts printed under it (59% vs 39%). The only cross-study comparison is drawn inside the right group, and all markers are hollow (exploratory). Panel (c), 'Registered before any data (Study 3)' (about 30% of the width): the same dumbbells with filled markers for Llama-70B (107 well-known / 293 other) and the fresh Qwen-32B set (102 / 207), with K and D and their CIs printed in the panel. If Study 3 has not run, the panel is an empty frame reading 'registered [date]; results pending'. The 0–4 dose-response is not in the figure; it goes in the text and the appendix.
hero_figure.why: One figure carries the whole paper: the phenomenon in one real case, the pattern both studies share, what changed between them, and the test that decides it, all in one visual grammar (hollow means exploratory, filled means registered), so the prose needs no hedges. Every run shows both components, not only their difference. That keeps visible what reviewers would otherwise find in the appendix: in Study 1, edited loss is flat across fact types and the contrast comes from the model's own answers. The figure's honest message is therefore about which answer thinking keeps, which is the thesis. The figure respects the engine rule, since cross-study contrasts appear only on matched engine and hardware. It works under every Study 3 outcome without redrawing, and it replaces the old multi-figure layout whose text was too small. The case sits beside the data rather than on the curve, so a single selected example is never presented as the pattern.

terms.plain_definition: The model's final generated answer names the new value and not the original one. The subject's name is removed before matching. It is reported for the direct answer and for the answer after thinking.

Take the facts that the unedited model answers correctly and whose edit holds in the direct answer. Excess loss is the share of edited answers lost after thinking minus the share of the unedited model's own answers lost after thinking, paired fact by fact. The pre-registration calls it the 'retention contrast' (one footnote).

A fact that at least three of the four smaller R1-distilled models (Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B, Llama 8B; the evaluated model excluded) answer correctly when asked directly, before any edit. The pre-registration addendum calls this 'high salience'. The word 'salience' never appears in the main text.

appendix: A. Registration record: the parent pre-registration and the salience addendum in full; freeze commits and anonymised registry entries; deviations D1–D8 (D8 being the failed submission gate, if submitting in October); a table of registered conditions not run (H2b, H3, small-model generations, MEMIT, AlphaEdit, IKE, edit-strength doses, sampling, given-chain swaps, Qwen2.5-Instruct, QwQ); the map from paper terms to registered terms; the pre-written abstracts and result paragraphs with their commit.

B. Engine and reproduction: per-row rank-one hooks and bf16 generation; byte-for-byte fp32 reproduction of Study 1; the engine-parity gate on two GPU types; hardware agreement (.975 direct, .81 after thinking); the input-format (BOS) record for Study 1's 32B baseline and arms, with the same-format excess +.239.

C. Fact sets, scoring and edits: candidates and the qualification rule, the name-containment exclusion, manifests and hashes, the alias matcher with subject removal and word boundaries, the judge switch rule and why lexical scoring is primary, layers and hyperparameters, prompt templates (full-width separators) and decoding settings.

D. Study 1 in full: every endpoint per model; Llama-70B unfiltered against filtered (.110 / .107); qualified drops (.125 at 32B, .153 at 70B); name leakage (46/200) and why permissive reversion (precision .48) was dropped; lost and regained edits per model with paired cross-scale differences; sampling reliability (61% against a 34% floor); Holm over the excess-loss family.
E. Study 2 in full: every registered estimate, secondaries (paraphrase −.083, locality, strict reversion .067), exclusions and out-of-memory regenerations.

F. The exploratory analysis E0–E6b in full, with its plan and addenda timestamps: composition decomposition with CI, alternative cut points, the dose-response over 0–4, per-relation tables, and the note that Study 1 and Study 2 used different runs to measure well-known facts.
G. Study 3 secondaries in full: per-set K and D, components, robustness strata, the 14B set, and the 146 non-overlapping 70B facts.
H. The think-span intervention from Study 1: design, the clean contrasts (T−N +.138; D−P recomputed), the input-format caveat, registered H3 not run, and no mediation claim.

I. Case provenance: the Oseberg rows (file and line), why it was first chosen (the old-answer penalty restored Bulgaria), its well-known count from the salience code, and further verbatim chains in both directions (edits lost and edits regained).
J. Compute, code release and reproduction instructions.
style_rules: Write one thesis sentence and reuse it. It appears in abstract sentences 4–5 in the form the outcome licenses, at the end of the introduction, and in the conclusion. Every section and every paragraph opens with the claim it supports, never with a caveat.

Status lives in the structure, not in hedges: section titles carry (exploratory), (pre-registered) or (registered before any data); Table 1 has a status column; figures use hollow markers for exploratory and filled for registered. In running text the word 'exploratory' appears once per section, in its first sentence.

Qualifications that change what a result means stay next to it as one clause with a number: found after the fact; Study 1's differences not significant (p = .068–.28); composition accounts for 28–55%; 254 of the 70B set's 400 facts overlap Study 2's 32B set. Generic scope limits (one editor, one dataset, lexical scoring, greedy decoding, counterfactual edits, one recipe) appear once, in Limitations.

Use only three technical terms (edit success, excess loss, well-known fact), each defined once in plain words in Section 2, and one name per quantity everywhere. Registered names (retention contrast, salience, H1–H4, W1–W3, K and D symbols) appear only in tables, one footnote and the appendix map.

Banned from the main text: B0, B3, RR, RRs, erosion and repair (say lost and regained), arm codes (T−N, D−P), G0, BOS, worlds, pools (say fact set), salience or salient, 're-decides', 'causal control point', 'capability-emergent', and 'mediation' except to deny it.

No word may claim more than the data. Say 'lose', not 'revert' or 'think its way back', unless strict reversion is measured.
