Say 'accounts for part of', never 'explains'; say 'predicts', never 'causes'. Never say edits to less-known facts are 'spared'. 'About a third' and 'under a tenth' are used only because every estimate falls in .31–.40 and .06–.09.

Numbers: proportions to three decimals with no leading zero (.106); differences carry a sign (+.216); 95% CIs go in square brackets; percentages only for shares of facts; 'x times as often' only when both rates are available nearby. The abstract has at most 6 numerals and no p-values; the introduction at most 7 numbers. CIs and p-values live in results sections and tables.
Never place original-pipeline numbers and engine-v2 numbers in the same contrast. Every Study 1 versus Study 2 comparison uses the rerun of Study 1's facts on Study 2's engine and hardware.
Every quoted chain is verbatim from a logged row whose path is listed in Appendix I. No invented or paraphrased chain may be presented as model output.

Sentences use plain verbs and the active voice and average at most 30 words. Use present tense for what models do and past tense for what we did. Do not use 'notably', 'importantly', 'crucially', 'interestingly', 'we note that' or 'it is worth'. No hedging adverbs ('may', 'might', 'potentially', 'somewhat', 'arguably') in claim sentences: if the evidence is weak, give its number.

Avoid the cadences reviewers read as generated text: no tricolons in titles or captions, no one-word punch sentences, at most one 'X; not Y' antithesis per page, no colon-reveal aphorisms, no rhetorical questions outside the title, varied paragraph openings, and contributions listed only once.
Each design choice gets one 'because' clause folded into the sentence that states the choice, not a templated list of justifications.

Every registered result is reported where its study is reported, whatever its sign (the paraphrase −.083 included). Unrun registered conditions are covered by one sentence plus an appendix table, with no argument.
Figures and tables: text at least 9 pt at print size, direct labels, n printed for every estimate, a colour-blind-safe palette. Prefer tables to dense plots.
Limitations is the only home of scope caveats. Ethics covers dual use (planting false facts, and reasoning undoing safety edits), licences, compute and annotators.

reviews_answered.critique: Unreadable, 'typical of zero-shot AI writing'
reviews_answered.answer: The paper has one thesis about which answer thinking keeps and one real case on page 1. Only three terms are used. Evidential status is carried by structure rather than hedges, codes such as B0/B3/RR/arms/erosion are banned from the main text, and the style rules target generated-text cadences. All scope caveats sit in Limitations.

reviews_answered.critique: Unclear motivation
reviews_answered.answer: Abstract sentence 1 and the opening paragraph state what editing is for and where the check fails (edits are checked directly, models are used after thinking), on a logged edit, before any definition. One clause explains why benchmarks use counterfactual edits, so the reader does not see the model 'correctly rejecting misinformation'.

reviews_answered.critique: Unconventional organisation
reviews_answered.answer: Introduction, Setup, three numbered studies in the order they were run, Related work, Discussion, Limitations, Ethics. Table 1 sets the three studies side by side, and each results section is titled with its claim.

reviews_answered.critique: Design decisions unjustified
reviews_answered.answer: Section 2 gives each decision a 'because' clause: one edit per request, an empty thinking span against the model's own chain, generated-answer scoring with the subject removed (46/200 subjects contain the old value), restriction to facts the model knows, the unedited baseline, and greedy decoding with its .81 cross-GPU agreement.

reviews_answered.critique: Figure text too small; the ethics statement is not one
reviews_answered.answer: One hero figure at 9 pt or more with direct labels; everything else is a table. A full ACL ethics statement covers dual use, including reasoning undoing safety edits.

reviews_answered.critique: Only 2 of 6 checkpoints significant, no multiplicity correction; scope chosen after the fact
reviews_answered.answer: Study 1 uses Holm over six (.033, .022) and is labelled exploratory, with its scope set after the data. The registered replication of that scope is reported as failed and is the paper's turn. Table 3 begins with the shrinkage expected from choosing scope after seeing data.

reviews_answered.critique: Pool selected by Qwen-7B old-answer retrieval at B3; may not generalise
reviews_answered.answer: Studies 2 and 3 select facts by each model's own direct answer. The paper measures what the old selection did: 59% against 39% well-known facts, and Study 2's rule applied to Study 1's facts keeps the excess (+.154). It says plainly that composition accounts for only 28–55% of the shrinkage and that the rest is still open.

reviews_answered.critique: Intervention shows steerability, not mediation
reviews_answered.answer: The intervention is out of the headline. One exploratory paragraph claims only that acting on the chain moves the untouched answer (+.138). There is no mediation claim, and registered H3 is listed as not run.

reviews_answered.critique: Wants evidence across editors and less selected populations
reviews_answered.answer: There are two fresh, model-qualified fact sets (Study 2, and Study 3's 32B set) plus Llama-70B's registered set. Other editors were registered but not run; this is stated once in Limitations, and the Discussion states the prediction for MEMIT and AlphaEdit. Adding MEMIT on the well-known facts is an option if the paper waits for January (open question).

reviews_answered.critique: Reversion undefined without per-checkpoint qualification
reviews_answered.answer: Excess loss is defined only on facts that the same model's unedited version answers correctly and whose edit holds directly. Studies 2 and 3 qualify facts per model. Study 1's unqualified drops are labelled as such, with the qualified drops (.125, .153) next to them.

reviews_answered.critique: Permissive reversion has precision .48
reviews_answered.answer: Dropped. Its cause, name leakage (46/200), is documented in Appendix D, and scoring now removes the subject's name.

reviews_answered.critique: No formal edited-versus-base contrast
reviews_answered.answer: Excess loss is exactly that paired contrast. It is registered as H2 and is the quantity Study 3 tests, and Figure 1 shows both of its components for every run.

reviews_answered.critique: MQuAKE and Ju et al. 2024 missing; single editor, single dataset
reviews_answered.answer: Both open Related work and the introduction's positioning: they show edits failing to reach outward, while here the model's own thinking overturns the edited answer itself. The single editor and single dataset are written into the thesis's scope and stated once in Limitations.

reviews_answered.critique: The thesis says thinking undoes edits of well-known facts and spares the rest, but in Study 1 edited loss is flat across fact types (.386 vs .379 at 32B); the contrast comes from the model's own answers
reviews_answered.answer: The thesis now states what holds in every run: for well-known facts, edits are lost about a third of the time and the model's own answers under a tenth. 'Spares' is gone. Less-known facts are described as unstable and dependent on the fact set, and Figure 1 shows both components for every run.

reviews_answered.critique: H4's statistic D can pass on the model's own answers alone, so 'confirmed' would not license the edit claim
reviews_answered.answer: Recommended amendment before freeze: make K (excess within well-known facts, where own loss is about .07) co-primary with D, under Holm. Name the edited-loss component and the edit-success drop by group as secondaries. Wording rules tie every sentence to the test that licenses it.

reviews_answered.critique: Composition is said to explain the shrinkage; it explains only part
reviews_answered.answer: Quantified as 28–55%, depending on which study's rates are used. The remainder (edits to less-known facts lost about .33 against .135) is named as unexplained, with one untested candidate.

reviews_answered.critique: The puzzle is told with numbers from two engines; the edit-success shrinkage is not significant on matched hardware
reviews_answered.answer: Every cross-study contrast uses the rerun of Study 1's facts on Study 2's engine and H100: excess +.207 against +.029, p = .019. The edit-success difference is reported as not significant (p = .31). Study 1's original numbers stay in its own section.

reviews_answered.critique: Invented Darrieux chain or cherry-picked case placed on the curve
reviews_answered.answer: The opening quotes the logged Oseberg chain verbatim, captioned as a Study 1 illustration with its selection history in Appendix I. It is never placed on the data curve.

reviews_answered.critique: The abstract is denser than the old one, mixes units, and states the claim last
reviews_answered.answer: At most 6 numerals, one unit ('times as often') across sentences 2–4, the registered result as the only CI, and the claim in place by sentence 4. The phenomenon itself is stated in sentence 1.

reviews_answered.critique: The registered submission gate failed and goes undisclosed
reviews_answered.answer: Raised as the leader's first decision. If the paper is submitted in October, deviation D8 is logged and one sentence in Section 4 states it.

reviews_answered.critique: The 70B set shares facts with the set that generated the hypothesis
reviews_answered.answer: Checked against the manifests: 254 of 400 facts are shared, and the fresh 32B set shares none. This is disclosed in Section 6, with K and D on the 146 non-overlapping facts as a secondary.

reviews_answered.critique: The well-known cut was chosen after E6, and Study 1's differences are not significant
reviews_answered.answer: Table 3 records the history of the cut and shows the planned cuts beside it (7B-known +.204, all four +.254, two or more +.277). Study 1 is described as 'same direction, not significant (p = .068–.28)' and as part of the data that formed the hypothesis.

reviews_answered.critique: Well-known may just mean guessable from the name, weakly edited, or popular
reviews_answered.answer: Pre-freeze secondaries cover strength after the edit, easily guessed relations, an external popularity measure and a measure that excludes the selecting model, alongside the base-confidence check. The label 'well-known' is kept only if the popularity check agrees.

reviews_answered.critique: 'One edit in four re-decided' is near the noise floor and not edit-specific
reviews_answered.answer: Removed from the abstract and the thesis. Lost and regained rates appear only next to the model's own loss (.170), the cross-GPU agreement (.81) and the sampling floor (34%).

reviews_answered.critique: Popularity literature unpositioned; novelty overstated
reviews_answered.answer: Related work adds PopQA, Kandpal et al., Ma et al. 2024 and RippleEdits' popular subset, each to be verified. The novelty claim is narrowed to the interaction with thinking under the own-answer control, plus the registered replication.

reviews_answered.critique: The registered paraphrase result (thinking helped) is moved to the appendix
reviews_answered.answer: It now has one sentence in Section 4.

reviews_answered.critique: No plan for 'Study 3 not run' or for mixed 70B outcomes
reviews_answered.answer: A third abstract variant and the 70B clause variants are written now (see changes), and a go/no-go time is set as a leader decision.

open_questions_for_leader: Submission cycle. The registered submission gate failed: prereg-arr.md §7 requires H1 and H2 to pass at 32B and ES-drop CIs above zero at 32B and 70B, and REVISION §3 sends a G3 failure to ARR January. Either submit on 10/12 anyway, logging deviation D8 and stating it in one sentence in Section 4, or follow the rule and submit in January with Study 3 complete plus MEMIT on the well-known facts.

Amend the H4 addendum before freezing (recommended)? The proposal is co-primary tests under Holm: K, the excess within well-known facts, > 0, and D, well-known minus other, > 0. It adds wording rules and these secondaries: strata of edit strength after the edit; easily guessed relations; an external popularity measure (Wikidata sitelinks or pageviews, GPU-free); well-knownness measured without the selecting or evaluated model; K and D on the 146 70B facts not in Study 2's 32B set; and composition-based predictions of the overall W1 and W2 results. The amendment must say it was chosen after seeing the E6b components. The alternative is to keep D alone with the rule that 'edits to well-known facts are lost' is printed only if the edited-loss component's CI excludes zero.

Compute and timing. Can 4–5 H100 hours be secured, and what is the go/no-go time (for example 2026-10-11 12:00 AoE)? Which set runs first: the fresh Qwen-32B set (the cleanest test, with no overlap, but its 309 ROME edits must first run on the 4090), or Llama-70B (edits ready, and it also delivers the registered 70B H1/H2, but 254 of its 400 facts are in Study 2's 32B set)?

If neither primary set completes in time, submit the 'registered, not yet run' version (pre-written S4: 'Looking back, the excess sat in well-known facts, ones that smaller distilled models also know, in both studies; a test of this on Llama-70B and a fresh Qwen-32B set was registered before any of its data existed and has not yet been run.') or wait for the next cycle?

Which composition-based prediction goes into the addendum for the overall 70B excess: one from Study 2's rates (about 0, given 27% well-known facts) or one from Study 1's 70B rates (about +.17)? Or both, as a stated range?
Naming. Keep 'well-known' only if the external popularity check agrees with the model-based measure, and otherwise say 'facts smaller models know'. Accept this conditional naming?

Opening case. Keep Oseberg (real and verbatim, but from Study 1's original pipeline and first chosen because the old-answer penalty restored Bulgaria; its well-known count is to be verified with the salience code), or commit now to a rule that picks the case from Study 3 rows?

Think-span intervention: keep one exploratory paragraph in Section 8 (it preserves a strength mTGu valued) or move it to the appendix only? Either way, D−P must be recomputed in rt.study1 before it is cited.
Registration anonymity for double-blind ARR: an OSF view-only registration, or an anonymised mirror carrying the commit hashes, given that GitHub push timestamps identify the authors?

Positioning. If Ma et al. 2024 or similar work already shows that popular facts are harder to edit robustly, accept the narrower novelty claim: the interaction with thinking, the own-answer control and the registered replication.

Study 1 conventions. Confirm unfiltered Llama-70B (.110, Holm .022) as primary, with the filtered .107 in the appendix. Decide whether Study 1's per-model qualified drops (.125, .153) become its headline, so that 'facts the model knows' holds throughout.
grafted_from: case (base, highest story and readability): the logged Oseberg case opens the paper verbatim; the arc is chronological with the registered failure as the turn; conventional ACL order; Limitations is the only home of caveats; one memorable line ('changed what the model says when asked; did not change what it can work out'), used once.

puzzle: evidential status carried by structure (section titles, a status column in Table 1, panel labels); Table 3 lists every explanation in the order tried, with its plan commit; one 'because' per design decision; the composition-based 70B prediction is written down before the data.

practice (highest honesty): an outcome-agnostic default title and fallback thesis; the 'what edit evaluations should report' box, with each item tied to what it would have changed in our own studies; lost and regained edits shown next to the model's own drift; an ethics statement noting that reasoning can undo safety edits.

mechanism: plain-word replacements (direct answer / after thinking, lost / regained); the prospective test called Study 3; forward predictions (MEMIT, AlphaEdit, editing related facts together) as the Discussion's next tests; the 'knowledge flows back in' positioning kept as interpretation only.

minimal: one hero figure whose hollow/filled markers show evidential status; the same-engine, same-hardware comparison as the visual turn; claim-titled sections; and its AC judge's key fix, retargeting the registered test to the quantity that replicated in every run (excess within well-known facts).
changes: Thesis rebuilt on the pattern that holds in every run. For well-known facts, edited loss is .31–.40 and own loss .06–.09, giving an excess of +.24 to +.32 with all CIs above zero (verified in explore_s1s2.json, E6b). This replaces 'the better known, the more likely to think its way back' and 'spares obscure facts'. Strict reversion (.067 in Study 2) is far below loss (.142), so 'think back' wording is dropped.

Recommended H4 amendment before freeze (the addendum is still a DRAFT and no W1–W3 row exists): K and D as co-primary tests under Holm, plus wording rules. If K and D both pass, use abstract variant A as written, and title 2 becomes available. If K passes and D fails, keep variant A but add in Section 6 that the difference from other facts was not confirmed, and do not use title 2. If K fails, use variant B. If neither set completes, use the not-run variant (S4 text in the open questions; S5: 'Until it is, the registered evidence says that on fresh facts thinking costs edits little more than it costs the model's own answers, and that one selected fact set made the cost look much larger.').

The 70B clause in abstract sentence 3: if 70B H2 fails, '[, nor at Llama-70B (x.x times)]'. If it passes, replace with 'at Qwen-32B (1.2 times), though Llama-70B on its own registered facts did show it (x.x times)', scope 'neither registered test passed' to Qwen-32B, and revisit sentence 5 of variant B. If 70B is not run, drop the clause.

Every cross-study contrast moves to the matched rerun: +.207 against +.029, difference −.178 [−.321, −.030], p = .019. The edit-success difference (−.048, p = .31) is reported as not significant. The cross-format claim that 'only edited loss moved' (.386 → .199, own .170 → .170) is dropped, because on matched hardware both components moved (edited about .34 → .199, own about .12 → .170; compute exactly).

Composition quantified from the stored strata: Study 2's rates at the rerun's mix give .137, and the rerun's rates at Study 2's mix give .170, against observed .224 and .029. Composition therefore accounts for 28–55% of the gap. Recompute this in code with a CI before writing.

Disclosures added from the manifests: the 70B set shares 254 of 400 facts with Study 2's 32B set, the 14B set shares 300, and the fresh 32B set shares 0. Study 1 and Study 2 used different runs to measure well-known facts, and Qwen-7B is both Study 1's selector and one of the probe models.

Number hygiene. Llama-70B: unfiltered .110 with Holm .022 (the brief paired .107 with .022). The 32B +.216 gets a format footnote (same-format +.239). Study 2 lost edits: .142 (study2.md), not .143. Well-known excess n is 99, not 156 (156 is the edit-success n). Recompute D−P (−.225). The Study 1 ratios are 14B 2.6 (.322/.126), 32B 2.3 (.386/.170) and 70B 3.2 (.340/.106), hence 'more than twice'. Study 2 is 1.17 (.199/.170).

Section 2's false claim that 'every rate uses facts the model knows' is removed, since Study 1's edit-success drop is over all facts. The scale trend in regained edits is dropped, because its paired CIs include zero. The paraphrase result (−.083) moves into the main text. 'One edit in four' leaves the abstract and the thesis.
Table 3 gains a row for expected shrinkage after a post hoc scope choice, the history of the cut point with the planned cuts' results, the composition decomposition, and an 'added after' column.

GPU-free checks to run before freeze or writing: composition decomposition with CI; well-knownness without the 7B probe; excess within well-known facts by easily guessed relations; correlation with external popularity; edit-success drop by group on Study 1's facts; excess within strata of post-edit lp(o_old) in Study 2; share of lost edits that are strict reversions, by group; the exact overall edited and own loss for the rerun; Holm across Study 1's excess family; Oseberg's well-known count; verification of every 2025–2026 citation (He et al., CODE, Gao et al., CRANE, Ma et al., Slocum et al.).

issues.where: prereg-arr-addendum-salience.md §5 and §7, against the package's thesis, abstract variant A sentence 4 ('[K=x.xx]'), Section 6 and Figure 1c
issues.problem: The paper's central quantity, K (excess loss within well-known facts), is not in the addendum at all. The only primary test is D̄ (high minus low). Secondary 3 lists only the components of D (edited loss high−low, base loss high−low), never RC(high) itself. If the addendum is frozen as drafted, the confirmed abstract would report a statistic that was never registered as 'the registered test'. §7 also pre-commits wording the package has already rejected. It says 'the paper's central claim is that reasoning undoes edits of entrenched (salient) facts', but D can pass on the own-answer component alone: in Study 1, edited loss is .386 vs .379 at 32B. It also says 'Salience composition is offered as the explanation … confirmatory in W1 and W2', but composition accounts for only 28–55% of the shrinkage, and W1/W2 do not test composition at all.
issues.fix: Before freezing, add K as a co-primary test with D under Holm over the two, as an unweighted mean over W1 and W2, using the same bootstrap. Add one sentence saying the change was chosen after seeing the E6b components. Add per-set K, per-set edited loss and own loss in the high stratum, and ES drop by stratum as secondaries. Replace §7 with the package's outcome-specific result paragraphs, copied verbatim: K and D pass; K passes and D fails; K fails; not run. Delete 'undoes', 'entrenched' and 'offered as the explanation'. In their place: 'composition accounts for part of the Study 1→2 shrinkage (exploratory, 28–55%); W1 and W2 test only the within-fact-type pattern.' Then make every K/D sentence in the abstract, the Section 6 table and the Figure 1c labels follow the frozen text.

issues.where: opening_paragraph; Figure 1a; 'grafted_from' line ('changed what the model says when asked; did not change what it can work out'); Appendix I
issues.problem: The quotes are verbatim and correct ('results 2/probe/r1qwen32b_ROME_cf200_r7of8.jsonl', cf_6933, lines 52 and 57), and Oseberg is well known: the 1.5B, 14B and Llama-8B bases all name Norway at B0. But the paper's own engine-v2 reruns of the same edit do not reproduce the page-1 story. On G0-4090 the answer after thinking is Russia (lost, but not to Norway). On G0-H100, the same engine and hardware as Study 2, the edited model keeps Bulgaria after thinking. The opening says 'It answers Norway' and generalizes that the edit 'did not change what the model can work out'. A reviewer with the released rows can see that the matched rerun contradicts this. That is a hidden cherry-pick on top of the disclosed selection history (the case was first picked because the old-answer penalty restored Bulgaria).

The cleanest include cf_12725 (The Wire, HBO→History), cf_21770 (Infiniti Q45, Nissan→Toyota), cf_14660 (New Smyrna Speedway, Florida→Utah) and cf_15404 (Windows 1.0, Microsoft→Google). Exclude cf_1405, cf_13923 and cf_15958, whose subjects contain the old value. If you keep Oseberg instead, state its three rerun outcomes in the panel tag and in Appendix I, and limit the memorable line to this one edit.

issues.where: Section 4 (title '(pre-registered)'), intro P3, narrative_arc, abstract sentence 3 (both variants)
issues.problem: The matched comparison is post hoc: the S2 minus G0-H100 contrast is E1 in explore_s1s2_plan.md, written after the Study 2 result. Here it is presented inside the pre-registered section, with no status marker, together with the inference 'so the difference lies in the facts'. The style rule puts 'exploratory' only in a section's first sentence, so in Section 4 this result would carry pre-registered status. The excess difference (−.178 [−.321, −.030], p = .019) is one of dozens of E0–E6b tests, and the ES-drop difference on the same matched data is not significant (−.048, p = .30).
issues.fix: Mark it where it appears: 'In a comparison planned after this result (Appendix F), Study 1's facts, rerun the same day on the same engine and H100, still gave +.207; the excess differs by −.178 [−.321, −.030], while edit success does not (−.048, p = .30).' Replace 'so the difference lies in the facts' with 'which points to the fact sets'. Either move the matched paragraph to open Section 5, or keep it in Section 4 behind its own one-clause post hoc label. In abstract sentence 3, keep 'still showed it', which is descriptive, and add no causal clause.

issues.where: changes ('If K passes and D fails, keep variant A'); abstract_if_h4_confirmed sentence 4; hero-figure caption; thesis
issues.problem: Variant A sentence 4 says 'the excess sat in well-known facts … and a test … confirmed it'. That is a concentration claim, which only D licenses. Reusing variant A when K passes and D fails overclaims. 'Confirmed it on Llama-70B and a fresh Qwen-32B set' also implies each set was confirmed separately, but K and D are unweighted means over the two sets. The thesis and caption use 'about a third' and 'under a tenth', which are true of the exploratory runs (.31–.40 and .06–.09) but are not what K tests.
issues.fix: Write a fourth variant now for K passes, D fails: 'a test registered before any new data found that, across Llama-70B and a fresh Qwen-32B set, edits to such facts were lost [x.x] times as often as the models' own answers ([K]); it did not confirm that this excess is larger than for other facts.' In all variants, say 'across the two sets (jointly)' and give per-set values in Section 6. Fill 'about a third' and 'under a tenth' in the thesis and caption from Study 3's own rates, and fall back to the numbers themselves if those rates fall outside the ranges.

issues.where: Section 7 move (1) 'New here: the edited question itself fails once the model thinks'; reviews_answered (AI review, MQuAKE row)
issues.problem: This overstates novelty. The rejected manuscript itself (main.tex l.68) cites He et al. 2025 as finding parametric editing fails under realistic decoding, 'including on an R1-distilled checkpoint whose reasoning reflects outdated knowledge and overturns the edit'. paperwriting/related_work.md marks the phenomenon (#1) as known.
issues.fix: Drop the claim that the phenomenon is new. Move He et al. 2025 into move (1) and concede it in the paper's own words. Limit 'new here' to what the package already lists as contributions: the same edit asked both ways against the unedited model's own answer, a registered replication reported with its failure, and a prospective fact-level test.

issues.where: Abstract sentence 2 ('more than twice as often'), Section 3 footnote ('the same-format rerun gives +.239'), Appendix B
issues.problem: At 32B, the 2.3× ratio pairs edited rows without BOS with a base that had BOS; REVISION §2 confirms this (fp32 diagnostic, 40/40). The footnote cites only the largest same-format estimate: +.239, from engine v2 on the 4090. It leaves out the within-Study-1 same-format estimate, +.151 [.032, .269] (1.93×, below 'twice'), and the H100 rerun, +.207. REVISION §2 had decided to write 'about 2×' for 32B. 14B may have the same problem: its edited shards are dated 2026-06-23 and its base shards 2026-07-01, after the 2026-06-25 BOS default, the same pattern as 32B. The 14B 2.6× may therefore also be a cross-format pairing.
issues.fix: Report all three same-format 32B estimates in the footnote and say which engine each comes from (+.151 Study 1 pipeline, recompute in rt.study1; +.239 and +.207 engine v2). In abstract sentence 2, say 'about two to three times as often' or 'at least about twice as often'. Check the 14B base's format with the fp32 diagnostic before printing '2.6×', and footnote it if it is cross-format.

issues.where: prereg-arr-addendum-salience.md §1 ('The same split held in the Study 1 cases at 14B, 32B and 70B'); package's not-run abstract sentence 4 ('in both studies')
issues.problem: This overstates the post hoc evidence in the registration document itself. In Study 1 the high-vs-low difference is in the same direction but significant in no run (p = .068, .098, .25, .28, .091). Only K, the within-high excess, is significant in every run.
issues.fix: Addendum: 'In the Study 1 cases at 14B, 32B and 70B the excess within salient facts was +.28 to +.32 (CIs above zero); the salient-minus-other difference had the same sign but was not significant (p = .068–.28).' Not-run sentence 4: 'the excess was concentrated in well-known facts in Study 2 and pointed the same way in Study 1'.

issues.where: Sections 3, 4, 5 and 8; style rule 'one name per quantity'
issues.problem: 'Lost' names three different quantities, and readers will set them against each other. (1) Unconditional erosion over all edits: '.207 of edits are lost' (S1 32B), '.142 of edits lost' (S2). (2) Erosion given ES@B0: .345 (S1) and .201 (S2), shown in explore_s1s2.md's main table. (3) Edited loss within the retention set: '.31–.40', 'about a third', and .386/.199. A reader will compare '.207 lost' in Section 3 with 'about a third lost' in Section 5.
issues.fix: Keep 'lost' only for the retention-set quantity that excess loss is built on. Write the unconditional flow as 'passed directly and failed after thinking (share of all edits)' and 'failed directly and passed after thinking' (regained), and put the denominator in every table header.

issues.where: Section 2 ('Study 1 used 200 facts where the unedited Qwen-7B named the old value after thinking'); Section 5 ('One untested candidate: every Study 1 fact was one that Qwen-7B recalled after thinking'); 'changes' bullet on selector overlap
issues.problem: Under the paper's current scoring this is false. explore_s1s2.json records S1_share_known_by_7B_at_B3 = .672. Membership was fixed from one Qwen-7B generation under the earlier matcher, before word boundaries, a minimum alias length and subject scrubbing (main.tex l.84: 600 requests → 248 hits → 200 sampled). Many of those hits were name leakage (46/200).
issues.fix: Say 'Study 1's facts were selected because one Qwen-7B generation after thinking matched the old value under an earlier matcher; re-scored with the current matcher, .67 of them do'. State the untested candidate as 'selection by one model's answer after thinking', not 'every fact was recalled'.

issues.where: Section 5 composition sentence; narrative_arc ('between a quarter and a half'); changes ('against observed .224 and .029')
issues.problem: 28–55% reaches more than half, so 'between a quarter and a half' understates it. The decomposition uses .224, the rerun's excess on the 85 cases with a salience value, while the rerun's headline is +.207 on 87. It also uses retention-set shares (58/85 = 68% vs 99/277 = 36%), while the text attributes the result to the whole-set shares of 59% vs 39%. I verified the arithmetic: .137 and .170 give 28% and 55%. No CI exists yet.
issues.fix: Report '28–55%' as a number with a bootstrap CI, computed on the same n as the headline (or footnote the n = 85 vs 87 difference). Say which shares enter the calculation. Don't summarize the range as a fraction in words.

issues.where: Section 5 robustness sentence; changes and reviews_answered ('the planned cuts' results … two or more +.277')
issues.problem: 'Two or more' is not a planned cut. Plan E6 names only 7B-known and all four; the 3–4 and ≥2 cuts first appear after E6. The numbers themselves are right: +.204 [.071, .337], +.254 [.065, .446], +.277 [.140, .413].
issues.fix: Label 7B-known and all four as 'planned in E6' and ≥2 and 3–4 as 'chosen after E6', both in Table 3 and in the text.

issues.where: Section 5 ('Edit loss … .27–.38 on Study 1's facts'); Section 4 and changes ('p = .31'); Section 2/Table 1 ('400 fresh facts per model'); Appendix B ('byte-for-byte fp32 reproduction of Study 1')
issues.problem: Four small number errors. (1) The low-stratum edited-loss minimum is Llama-70B's 9/34 = .265, so the range is .26–.38 (the same error appears as 'about .33' in reviews). (2) E1's ES-drop p is .3046, so p = .30. (3) Study 2 manifests are 7B 318 and 1.5B 212, not 400 each. (4) The fp32 diagnostic covered 40 cases (N arm 37/40, P arm 39/40, base 40/40), not all of Study 1.
issues.fix: Use .26–.38, p = .30, and 'up to 400 (7B 318, 1.5B 212)'. For the reproduction, say 'reproduced 37–40 of 40 checked cases byte for byte in fp32'.

issues.where: Section 6 power sentence; addendum §6
issues.problem: K's power ('about .85') appears in no file. D's '.75' is the addendum's single-test value at α = .05, not its value under Holm over two. The addendum's SE of .055 assumes SD .55. S2's strata give SD ≈ .57–.59 and SE ≈ .059–.062, which puts D's power at .15 nearer .68–.72.
issues.fix: Compute power by simulation from S2's per-stratum 2×2 tables and the W1/W2 strata (107/293, 102/207, verified from the qualify files) under the final Holm structure, and print those values in both documents.

issues.where: Table 3 / Section 5 ('Hardware: no'; 'base chain naming the old value … no moderation'); E2 '+.154'
issues.problem: E0's retention difference is +.032 [−.162, .215], which cannot exclude a hardware effect as large as the .178 gap. What rules hardware out is the matched design (E1), not E0's null. E3's 'no moderation' comes from strata where only 7–17% of cases lack the recall (S1 m0 retention n = 6), so it is underpowered. E2 is quoted from the original pipeline (+.154), against the engine rule; the matched-rerun value is +.158.
issues.fix: Verdicts: 'hardware: held fixed by design (E1); E0 alone inconclusive'; 'base recall: not detected (7–17% of cases lack it)'. Quote E2 as +.158 [.013, .303] (G0-H100).

issues.where: addendum §7 'H4 fails' paragraph; fallback thesis; abstract variant B sentence 5
issues.problem: 'Not edit-specific on a fresh pool' presents a null as shown: the CI is [−.036, .097]. 'On fresh facts, thinking costs edits little more …' generalizes from one model's 277 facts. 'One selected fact set made that cost look much larger' is causal, but the support is the post hoc E1 contrast.
issues.fix: Say 'at Qwen-32B on fresh facts, the excess was +.029 (upper bound about .10)'. Write '… and Study 1's selected facts showed a much larger excess on the same engine and hardware', with no 'made'.

issues.where: thesis, intro P4, narrative_arc, Section 5 ('in every run')
issues.problem: 'Every run' counts six runs, but three of them are the same Qwen-32B on the same 200 facts (S1, G0-4090, G0-H100). The independent evidence is three models on Study 1's facts plus one model on Study 2's facts. Counting six runs as six agreements overstates replication.
issues.fix: Write 'for three models on Study 1's facts (32B also in two reruns) and for Qwen-32B on Study 2's fresh facts', and draw the two reruns as linked repeats in Figure 1b.

issues.where: Table 3 Row 0 ('expected shrinkage after choosing Study 1's scope from its data'); reviews_answered (mTGu)
issues.problem: No such number exists in any result file, yet the package promises it as Table 3's first row.
issues.fix: Compute it before writing (for example, a winner's-curse correction of the 32B/70B estimates given a post hoc choice of 3 of 6 models), or drop the row and the reviewer answer that cites it.

issues.where: abstract variants A/B; intro P2–P4; style rules
issues.problem: The package breaks its own rules. Variant A has about 8 numerals (400, 1.2, x.x, x.x, x.xx, 95, x.xx, x.xx) against a limit of 6, and it puts the registered symbol 'K=' in the abstract, which the rules reserve for tables, a footnote and the appendix. The introduction has 8 numbers plus a date (8,192; .106; .110; 400; +.029; +.207; 59%; 39%) against a limit of 7.
issues.fix: Drop 'K=' and the 95% label from the abstract and keep one ratio plus one CI. In the introduction, drop '8,192 tokens' (it belongs in Section 2) or one of the two Holm drops.

issues.where: abstract_if_h4_not_confirmed sentence 4 ('seemed to sit'); Section 3 (Holm for the excess left as a to-do)
issues.problem: Two hedges the evidence does not require. 'Seemed to' hedges what the old data actually show: S2's difference is +.332 [.203, .464], and K is above zero in every run; only the prospective test failed. Holm over Study 1's excess family can be computed now from study1.json and passes: 70B p < .001 → Holm < .001, 32B .0022 → .011, 14B .0038 → .015.
issues.fix: Write 'Looking back, the excess sat in well-known facts in both studies' data, but a test registered before any new data did not confirm it …'. In Section 3, state the excess-family Holm values instead of leaving the claim uncorrected.

issues.where: Section 3 practitioner number (61% vs 34%); Section 5 ('edits to less-known facts in Study 1's set were lost far more often')
issues.problem: The sampling-reliability run used BOS (prereg-arr §3), while the greedy headline cells did not, and the text carries no format caveat. 'Far more often' rests on .333 (9/27) vs .135 (24/178) with no CI computed.
issues.fix: Add the input-format clause to the 61%/34% sentence, or move it to Appendix D with the format record. Replace 'far more often' with the two rates, their n and a bootstrap CI for the difference.

issues.where: recommended title 'Which Knowledge Edits Survive Thinking?'; thesis clause 'a direct question cannot vouch for an edit to a well-known fact'
issues.problem: Both invite the reading that edits to other facts survive. In Study 1, .26–.38 of edits to less-known facts were lost. What separates the two kinds of fact there is the model's own-answer loss, not edit survival.
issues.fix: In Section 5 and the Figure 1b caption, add one sentence saying edits to other facts are also often lost on Study 1's facts, and that the separation is in whether the model keeps its own answer. Consider the thesis wording 'a direct question cannot vouch for an edit to a well-known fact, even though the model's own answer to it survives thinking'.

issues.where: Opening paragraph, the direct-answer quote and the chain quotes (Oseberg case)
issues.problem: The opening presents one episode, but it joins two runs from two different pipelines. The direct-answer quote, "has been a significant contributor to Bulgaria's energy production", appears in the logged files only in the engine-v2 G0 rerun: results/rt/g0/r1qwen32b_g0_rome_N_r3of4.jsonl, line 24, case cf_6933, budget B0. In that same rerun the edited model's answer after thinking is "Russia" (North Caspian Basin), not Norway. The Norway chain comes from Study 1's original pipeline, and locally it exists only inside a judge prompt (results/a3_neutral/prompts_32b.jsonl, also results/a3/prompts_32b.jsonl), not as a raw generation row. This splices numbers or text across engines, which CLAUDE.md rule 4 forbids. It also breaks the brief's style rule that every quoted chain must be verbatim from one logged row listed in Appendix I. A reviewer who opens the release will find the same edit ending in Russia on the matched rerun and will read the opening as cherry-picked.
issues.fix: Take both halves from one run. Option A: pull Study 1's original-pipeline B0 answer text for cf_6933 at 32B from the raw Study 1 generations on the server. Quote it only if it is logged; otherwise write "With thinking turned off, the edited model answers Bulgaria" with no quotation marks. Then quote the chain from the raw Study 1 B3 row, not from the judge prompt. List both row paths in Appendix I, and add one appendix sentence saying that the engine-v2 rerun of this edit also lost it after thinking but answered Russia. Option B: take the opening case from Study 2 or Study 3 rows, where both answers share one engine. Either way, delete the "significant contributor" quote unless it comes from the same run as the chain.

issues.where: Opening paragraph: "Allowed to think first, it talks itself out of the edit" and "The edit changed what the model says when asked; it did not change what the model can work out."
issues.problem: The logged chain never mentions Bulgaria (0 occurrences). It opens with "I'm not very familiar with oil fields", weighs Norway, Russia and the US, and settles on "I remember that the Oseberg oil field is one of the largest in Norway." So the model does not talk itself out of the edit. The edited value never shows up as a candidate at all. Any cold reader who checks the chain will see the gap. The closing line also misplaces the key step: what settles the answer is recall ("I remember"), not inference ("can work out"). As written, the line also states a general mechanism from one case, which the brief says the data do not show. Under the not-confirmed variant, it directly contradicts abstract sentence 5.
issues.fix: Describe what the chain actually does: "Allowed to think first, it never mentions Bulgaria. It guesses from the name ('sounds like it could be a Scandinavian name, maybe Norwegian?'), sets Oseberg beside the Troll and Ekofisk fields, 'both in Norway', recalls that it 'is one of the largest in Norway', and answers Norway." Narrow the memorable line to this case and to what the case shows: "Here the edit changed the direct answer but not what the model recalls while thinking."

issues.where: Abstract S1 (both variants): "reasoning models answer only after thinking, which can bring back the fact an edit replaced"
issues.problem: This sentence does three jobs: it says what editing is for, how edits are checked, and what thinking does. Two of its claims cause trouble. (a) "Bring back the fact an edit replaced" is a reversion claim. The style rules ban it unless strict reversion is measured, and Study 2's strict reversion (.067) is under half its loss rate (.142). It also states the paper's finding as a premise in sentence 1, before any evidence. (b) "Answer only after thinking" contradicts the design: the reader is then told the same models were asked "directly" (S2) and asked to "answer at once" (opening), and cannot tell how that is possible. A third, smaller problem: "correct facts" makes the reader assume the edits are corrections. The later "fact an edit replaced" then reads as the model restoring an error, when the replaced fact is actually the true one.
issues.fix: Rewrite as: "Knowledge edits are checked by asking the edited question directly, but reasoning models are normally used after they think, and an edit that passes the direct check can be lost once the model thinks." That is about 30 words, uses no reversion wording, and does not deny the direct condition. Bring in "counterfactual" in S2 (see the issue on counterfactual edits).

issues.where: Opening paragraph (last sentence) and abstract S2: "more than twice as often as their unedited versions lost the original answers"
issues.problem: The paper's central quantity is edit loss beyond the unedited model's own loss, but nothing on page 1 motivates it. The opening asks "how often thinking undoes an edit". Read literally, that is the raw loss rate (.207 in Study 1, .142 in Study 2), not the excess the abstract then reports. In S2, a cold reader stalls on "unedited versions lost the original answers": how does a model that was never edited "lose" an answer, and lose it relative to what? The reader has to work out alone that thinking also flips some of the unedited model's own correct direct answers (about .17 at 32B). Without that, the control looks arbitrary and the 1.2-times result in S3 cannot be read.
issues.fix: Add one plain clause to the opening's last sentence: "Thinking also changes some answers of the unedited model, so this paper asks how much more often thinking undoes an edit that passed the direct check than it undoes the model's own correct answer, and for which facts." In S2 write "... than the unedited models lost their own correct direct answers after thinking."

issues.where: Abstract S2 to S3 (both variants), and not-confirmed S5: "400 fresh facts" and "one selected fact set"
issues.problem: The story's turn depends on how the facts were chosen, but the abstract never sets this up. S2 does not say that Study 1's facts were chosen because Qwen-7B recalled the original answer after thinking. So "fresh facts" in S3 has no contrast, since the reader does not know fresh as opposed to what. "One selected fact set" in not-confirmed S5 then appears out of nowhere. A cold reader sees a replication fail and cannot tell why changing the facts should matter. That is the one step the narrative most needs the reader to follow.
issues.fix: Put the selection in S2 as half a clause: "... six DeepSeek-R1-distilled models, on facts chosen because a smaller model recalled the original answer while thinking, ...". In S3, contrast it: "on 400 fresh facts chosen only by each model's direct answers". Not-confirmed S5 can then say "the first, selected fact set" and point back to S2.

issues.where: Abstract S3 to S4, confirmed variant: "found almost none of this excess at Qwen-32B ... [nor at Llama-70B]" followed by "confirmed it on Llama-70B and a fresh Qwen-32B set"
issues.problem: Read cold, S3 says the excess is absent at Qwen-32B and Llama-70B, and S4 says a test confirmed it on Llama-70B and Qwen-32B. That looks like a contradiction. Nothing tells the reader that S3 is about all facts and S4 only about well-known facts. Nothing says the first study's set held more well-known facts (59% against 39%), and that missing fact is what links the two sentences. "A fresh Qwen-32B set" also reads as the same 400 fresh Qwen-32B facts from S3. Finally, Llama-70B appears in S3 as part of the failed replication and in S4 as part of the confirmation, and the reader is not told these are the same rows read two ways.
issues.fix: Write "overall" in S3 ("... found almost none of this excess overall at Qwen-32B (edits lost 1.2 times as often as own answers)"). In S4 say what links the sentences, and keep the wording to "partly", since composition accounts for 28–55%: "A post hoc analysis located the excess in well-known facts, ones smaller distilled models also answer correctly, which made up more of the first study's set." Name the second 32B set as different: "a second, newly drawn Qwen-32B set".

issues.where: Abstract S2–S4 vocabulary: "passing edits", "this excess", "(1.2 times)", "neither registered test", "the same engine and hardware", "before any new data", "[K=x.xx]"
issues.problem: These are the places where a cold reader cannot follow. "Passing edits" never says what they passed. "This excess" has no antecedent, because S2 never uses the word. "1.2 times" leaves open 1.2 times what. "Neither registered test" refers to two tests the reader has never been told about. "The same engine and hardware" makes the reader ask "same as what?", and it reveals in the abstract that Study 1 ran on a different engine without saying so; "engine" is lab jargon. "Before any new data" and "fresh facts" sound like two different notions. "K=" is a registered symbol, which the style rules confine to tables.
issues.fix: Replace them, in order, with: "edits that passed the direct check"; name the quantity in S2 ("... lost such edits more than twice as often as ...") and refer back with "this gap"; "(edits lost 1.2 times as often as own answers)"; "and its two registered tests failed"; "although the first study's facts, rerun under the replication's exact setup, still showed it"; "registered before any of its answers were generated"; and drop "K=", keeping "difference x.xx" with its CI.

issues.where: Abstract S2, S3, S4 (sentence length and jobs per sentence)
issues.problem: S2 runs about 47 words and does two jobs (method and result). S3 runs about 45 words and does three (replication result, test verdict, matched rerun). Confirmed S4 runs about 54 words and does three (post hoc finding, definition of well-known, confirmatory result with a ratio and a CI). The style rule caps the average at 30 words. Packing many clauses into each sentence is the main thing that made TRfT call the old paper unreadable. A cold reader has to read S4 twice to find its verb.
issues.fix: Keep five sentences, but give each one claim and move definitions into short appositives. For example, S4 confirmed: "A post hoc analysis placed the excess in well-known facts, which smaller distilled models also answer correctly, and a test registered before any answers existed confirmed it on Llama-70B and a second Qwen-32B set (edits lost x.x times as often as own answers)." Remove the CI from the abstract if needed. S3: "A pre-registered replication on 400 fresh facts failed at Qwen-32B, where edits were lost only 1.2 times as often as own answers, though the first study's facts, rerun the same way, still showed the gap."

issues.where: Abstract, numeral count (confirmed variant S3–S4)
issues.problem: The abstract carries 400, 1.2, x.x (70B), x.x, x.xx, 95%, x.xx and x.xx: eight numerals before counting model sizes, against a cap of 6. It also mixes two units in one sentence ("times as often" and an absolute difference). The narrative package's own answer to the clarity panel promises "one unit across sentences 2–4".
issues.fix: Keep one unit ("times as often") throughout. Drop "95% CI [..]" and the difference from the abstract, since sections 6 and Table 4 carry them, or drop "400". That gives 400 (or none), 1.2, the 70B ratio and the Study 3 ratio, which is within budget.

issues.where: Thesis versus abstract S4–S5 (confirmed variant)
issues.problem: The thesis I took away cold from the confirmed variant was: "Edits that pass a direct check are lost after thinking more often than the model's own answers, but only for facts that smaller models also know, so a direct check overstates edits to well-known facts." That is close to the package thesis, but the abstract never states its most memorable half: models keep their own answers to well-known facts (under a tenth lost) while losing about a third of the edits. The style rules require one thesis sentence reused in S4–S5, and it is not there. Separately, the thesis's "about a third" comes from exploratory runs. It is pre-written as if it were the Study 3 value, and it breaks if Study 3's edited loss for well-known facts falls outside .31–.40. From the not-confirmed variant I took away: "A large effect of thinking on edits mostly disappeared in a registered replication; it was concentrated in one selected fact set." That conflicts with Title 1, which promises an answer to "which edits".
issues.fix: Make confirmed S5 the thesis sentence: "After thinking, these models keep their own answers to well-known facts but lose [share] of the edits to them that passed the direct check, so a direct check cannot vouch for such edits." Fill [share] from Study 3. Write "about a third" only if Study 3's estimates fall in .31–.40. Use Title 1 only when K passes; otherwise use Title 3.

issues.where: Abstract S2 vs S4 vs opening: names for the same quantities
issues.problem: One quantity gets two names: "the original answers" (S2) and "the models' own answers" (S4). The conditions get three names each: "directly" / "answer at once" / "direct check", and "after thinking" / "think first" / "allowed to think". "Original" is also ambiguous because in S1 it means the pre-edit true fact. That breaks the one-name-per-quantity rule.
issues.fix: Use "own answer" for the unedited model's answer everywhere, "directly" or "direct check" for the closed-thinking condition, and "after thinking" for the chain condition. In the opening, change "Asked to answer at once" to "Asked directly, with its thinking turned off".

issues.where: Abstract S2 (both variants): no mention that the edits are counterfactual
issues.problem: The abstract never says the edits are counterfactual. With S1's "correct facts", a cold reader assumes the edits fix errors and that losing one means the model returns to a mistake. A reader who does know CounterFact will think "the model is rightly rejecting a false fact". The opening handles this with its CounterFact clause, but the abstract does not.
issues.fix: Write "counterfactual ROME edits" in S2. That one word is enough, because the opening paragraph gives the reason.

issues.where: Opening paragraph cadence
issues.problem: One paragraph stacks most of the devices TRfT associated with generated prose. It has a parallel pair ("Asked to answer at once ... / Allowed to think first ..."), a colon reveal ("the edited model passes: ..."), a short punch sentence ("It answers Norway."), a semicolon antithesis aphorism ("changed X; did not change Y") and a triplet of quotes. The second sentence also uses "so that" twice and does two jobs (the case and the benchmark rationale) across a semicolon. Any one of these devices reads as a choice; all of them together read as a template. "Knowledge editing promises" and "Reasoning models are used by letting them think" are also stiff.
issues.fix: Keep the antithesis line (narrowed as in the second issue) and the quotes. Fold "It answers Norway" into the sentence before it. Replace the colon reveal with "it answers Bulgaria". Split sentence 2 and give the CounterFact rationale its own short sentence: "Benchmarks such as CounterFact use false facts like this so that the new answer can only come from the edit." Change "promises to correct" to "changes" and "are used by letting them think" to "are normally used after they think".

issues.where: Abstract S4 (both variants): "Looking back, the excess sat in / seemed to sit in"; S5: "costs edits little more than it costs"; confirmed S5 tricolon
issues.problem: "Looking back" is a coy way to say post hoc, and NLP reviewers want the status stated outright. "Sat in" and "costs" are metaphors that stand in for a precise relation. Confirmed S5 ends in a rhythmic triplet ("after thinking, against the unedited model, with the share of well-known facts reported"), which the style rules avoid. Not-confirmed S5 also says one set "made that cost look much larger", which implies an illusion, yet the matched rerun shows the gap on that set is real (+.207).
issues.fix: Write "A post hoc analysis located the excess in ..." (not-confirmed: "suggested the excess lay in ..."). In confirmed S5, cut the triplet to two recommendations, or turn it into one: "so edits should be scored after thinking against the unedited model's own answers, with well-known facts reported separately". In not-confirmed S5, write "the cost was much larger on one selected fact set".

issues.where: Opening case choice (Oseberg) under both outcomes
issues.problem: The case's well-known count is still unverified. If fewer than 3 of the 4 smaller models know the Oseberg fact, the opening shows the group the thesis says behaves differently. The case also comes from Study 1's selected set, which the not-confirmed variant blames for the inflated effect. Under that outcome, the page opens with a dramatic loss from exactly the set the abstract later discounts.
issues.fix: Before writing, run the salience code on cf_6933 and keep Oseberg only if it scores 3 or more of 4. Under the not-confirmed outcome, add one clause to the caption or text saying the case comes from the first, selected set, or take a case from Study 2 or 3 rows.

issues.where: Abstract S3: "at Qwen-32B" right after S2's "three largest models"
issues.problem: S2 reports an effect in three models, and S3 replicates it in one (or two). A cold reader wonders whether the authors picked the model and is never told the others did not finish. The abstract does not need the compute story, but the jump from three models to one is visible.
issues.fix: Add four words, "the one model completed" ("... found almost none of this excess at Qwen-32B, the one model completed, ..."), or leave the explanation to the single disclosure sentence in Section 4 and accept the gap in the abstract.

issues.where: Thesis ('about a third'), abstract S2 and S4, Fig 1 caption and panel (b), §2 definition of edit success, addendum §5 (no alternative definition registered)
issues.problem: Half of the 'lost' edits to well-known facts are answers that name both values. This is a lexical artefact that is concentrated in well-known facts, and the outline never answers it in the main text. I recomputed this read-only from the S2 and S1 rows using rt.analysis conventions. In S2's well-known retention set, 15 of the 31 lost edits name both values, 9 name only the old value and 7 name neither. Among other facts it is 5 of 24. In G0-H100 it is 13 of 20 against 1 of 9. Many of these answers commit to the new value and mention the old one in passing. Examples: cf_12830 says 'Rufin's mother tongue is Russian ... may have been exposed to French'; cf_13786 says 'despite its name suggesting a focus on physiology, [it] is dedicated to the mathematical sciences'; cf_14944 says 'Do Phool is a Tamil film ... The Hindi remake'. A model that knows a famous fact mentions it, and the own-answer side has no matching penalty. If an edit counts as lost only when the new value is absent, well-known edited loss is .162 (S2), .246 (S1-32B), .121 (G0-H100), .228 (S1-70B) and .156 (S1-14B), not '.31–.40'. K falls to +.091 [.010, .172] and D to +.209. So the headline number, 'more than twice as often' and K's near-certain pass all depend on a scoring rule that favours the hypothesis. The outline gives this only a one-line note on the asymmetry and a ban on the word 'revert'.
issues.fix: Before freezing the addendum, register three things. (a) K and D with an edit counted as lost only when the new value is absent, as named co-reported estimates. Add a wording rule: the thesis may quote only a figure that holds under both definitions. (b) Two-annotator adjudication of every both-values answer in W1 and W2, under a written rule (commits to new / hedges / reverts); this is about 30–60 rows. (c) Show the split by answer type in Fig 1b: stack each orange marker into old only, both and neither. Restate the thesis with its definition, for example 'about a third fail the standard check, and about one in six drop the new value altogether'. Recompute the 'twice as often' ratios under both rules before writing abstract S2.

issues.where: Thesis and title 2 (claim that thinking causes the loss), §5 (Table 3 has no comparison without thinking), §6 robustness list, addendum §4 (W1/W2 generate only the efficacy probe)
issues.problem: The well-known pattern appears without any thinking, so the own-answer control does not isolate thinking. I used S2's registered para0 probe asked directly (B0) as a perturbation without thinking, on the same retention set: K = +.152 [.030, .273] for well-known facts, −.152 for the rest, and D = +.303 [.155, .449], against D = +.332 with thinking. Within well-known facts, the paired difference K(thinking) − K(paraphrase) is +.091 [−.051, .232], p = .23. Edits to well-known facts are lost more often under a direct paraphrase (.515) than after thinking (.313). The registered paraphrase result (thinking raised edit success, −.083) holds within well-known facts too (ES drop −.064). A harsh reviewer will say that D measures 'edits to popular facts are brittle under any change of prompt'. That is close to Ma et al. (EMNLP 2024, 'On the Robustness of Editing LLMs'), which found popular knowledge harder to edit and edits weaker on rephrased prompts. Study 3's K and D can both pass without thinking mattering.
issues.fix: Make three structural changes. (a) Add a row to Table 3 and a grey dumbbell to Fig 1b: the same well-known split with the paraphrase asked directly. (b) Add para0 at B0, for base and rome_N, to the W1 and W2 generation configs; with no chain this costs minutes. Register 'K with thinking minus K under paraphrase, within well-known facts' as the secondary that licenses the word 'thinking' in the thesis. (c) Rebuild the thesis on the estimand that is thinking-specific by construction. Among well-known edits that pass both the direct question and its paraphrase, S2 loses .167 [.056, .306] after thinking (n = 36), while the model's own answers lose .000; among other facts the excess is +.021. Register this conditional estimand for W1 and W2. Box item 1 then becomes 'check after thinking, after the paraphrase check'.

issues.where: Addendum primary-test design (K co-primary, Holm over two, W1 first), title 1, abstract variant A S4, the 'not run' S4 text, page budget of §5 (1.1 pp) and §6 (1.2 pp), §4 handling of the failed gate
issues.problem: A reviewer will read this as a failed pre-registration rescued by a post hoc story. The moderator was the sixth of six candidates, tried after H1 and H2 failed. K became co-primary after the E6b components were seen, and K is close to certain to pass under the ES_b rule: every exploratory estimate is +.24 to +.32, own loss is about .07, and Issue 1's both-values mechanism adds to it. 254 of W1's 400 facts are in the set that generated the hypothesis. The registered submission gate failed. Under the 'not run' variant, S4 still asserts the pattern as fact ('the excess sat in well-known facts'), and 1.2 pages of §6 would be an empty design section. The outline lets a K pass print 'confirmed' and abstract A, although K says nothing about which edits survive. Only D (or the paraphrase-adjusted K) speaks to that.
issues.fix: Decide these before freeze. (a) Run W2 first: it is fresh with zero overlap, and it decides the test. Label W1 'new model, partly familiar facts', with the 146 non-overlapping facts as its secondary. (b) Add a licensing rule to the addendum: K alone licenses only 'edits to well-known facts are lost after thinking more than own answers', and the addendum says K was expected to pass. D (plus the thinking-specific secondary from Issue 2) is required for title 2 and for the word 'which' in title 1. (c) If W2 has not finished by the go/no-go time, use title 3 and lead the abstract with the failed replication. Phrase S4 as 'a pattern found afterwards, now registered'. Cut §5 to about 0.6 pp and fold §6 into a 0.3-pp 'Registered test (pending)' subsection, giving the space back to Study 2's registered secondaries. (d) Keep the one D8 sentence in §4.

issues.where: Intro P5 positioning; §7 move (4)
issues.problem: On novelty, a reviewer can combine three prior results. Ma et al. 2024 (EMNLP, verified on arXiv 2402.05827) say popular knowledge is 'memorized better, easier to recall' and harder to edit, and that edits fail on rephrasing. Gekhman et al. 2026 show that thinking unlocks parametric recall. He et al. 2025 show that realistic decoding breaks edits. Together these predict the finding. The intro cites only PopQA and leaves Ma et al. to §7 with 'verify', so the first page oversells, and Issue 2 shows that most of the pattern reproduces Ma et al. without thinking.
issues.fix: Name Ma et al. 2024 and Gekhman et al. 2026 in intro P5, with one clause each saying what is new here. The delta is the own-answer-controlled excess that remains after the direct paraphrase check (the .167 versus .000 estimand from Issue 2), plus the registered replication. In §7, drop any implication that the link between popularity and fragility is a finding of this paper.

issues.where: §3 (Study 1), §8 'Next tests: the same pattern under MEMIT and AlphaEdit', Limitations ('ROME only'), reviews_answered entry for mTGu on editors
issues.problem: Existing evidence on a second editor is left out. The AAAI manuscript reported MEMIT on Qwen-14B, whose fresh no-suppression arm gave an ES drop of +.060 [−.020, .140], not significant. The outline calls other editors 'registered but not run' and offers a 'prediction' for MEMIT. Any reviewer who saw the earlier version will read this as quietly dropping a null.
issues.fix: Add one sentence in §3 giving the MEMIT-14B ES drop with its CI and its caveat (the set was not qualified per model). If base rows exist for those cases, compute the well-known split without a GPU and put it in App D. In §8, replace 'prediction' with 'our one MEMIT run (14B) shows no significant drop'.

issues.where: §5 'Confounds stay in view' sentence; §6 robustness list; terms ('well-known fact'); Limitations
issues.problem: Confounds that the existing data already answer are deferred to Study 3. The confounds are edit strength, the base model's own confidence, guessability from the name, and the same-family probe models. The outline gives them one §5 sentence ('direct edit success falls from .81 to .61') and Study 3 secondaries, which reads as unaddressed. The S2 data already answer most of them (my read-only recompute). K within well-known facts holds in both halves of post-edit lp(o_old) (+.305 and +.150) and of the pre-edit base confidence (+.233 and +.256), while other facts stay at or below +.013. K for well-known facts outside the language relations is +.228 [.105, .351], although language relations (P103, P1412, P364, P37) make up 42% of well-known facts against 16% of the rest.
issues.fix: Add a block to Table 3 in the main text, 'Is well-known just ...?', with rows for edit strength, base confidence, language relations, and the external popularity measure (Wikidata sitelinks, no GPU needed). Keep the Study 3 versions as their registered replications. Call the construct 'facts smaller models also know' unless the popularity row agrees.

issues.where: Opening paragraph, Fig 1a, App I
issues.problem: The opening case argues against the thesis. The Oseberg chain works from the name ('sounds like it could be a Scandinavian name'), which is the guessability confound in action, not recall of a well-known fact. It was first chosen because the old-answer penalty restored the edit. It comes from the original pipeline, and its well-known count is unverified. It is also a clean old-only reversion, which is a minority of lost well-known edits (S2: 9 of 31; G0-H100: 5 of 20).
issues.fix: Fix a selection rule in the addendum. For example: the first well-known W2 edit (in case_id order) that is lost with an old-only answer and whose chain recalls the fact rather than inferring it from the name; fall back to S2 by the same rule. The Fig 1a caption should state how typical the case is ('x of y lost edits to well-known facts end like this; z name both values'). If Oseberg is kept, check that its count is 3 or more and add the same sentence.

issues.where: Thesis support, narrative arc ('in every run of both studies'), Fig 1b grouping, style rule licensing 'about a third' / 'under a tenth'
issues.problem: 'In every run' overstates the replication. Five of the six well-known estimates come from one 200-fact set (three models, plus two reruns of the same model on the same facts), and that set helped form the hypothesis. In effect there are two fact sets. Under the strict rule in Issue 1, 'about a third' does not hold for any of them.
issues.fix: Group Fig 1b by fact set rather than by run, and write 'in both fact sets, and across three models on the first'. Tie the 'about a third' / 'under a tenth' wording to whatever survives Issue 1.

issues.where: Abstract variant A S5, §8 box item 1
issues.problem: 'A direct check overstates how well edits to well-known facts hold' conflicts with the registered paraphrase result: thinking raised paraphrase edit success overall (−.083) and within well-known facts (−.064). Unconditional edit success is not overstated. Only passing edits are lost.
issues.fix: Narrow S5 and box item 1 to 'a direct pass on the edited question'. In §5, give the paraphrase ES drop by group in one clause. The box should recommend both the paraphrase check and the check after thinking, since the direct paraphrase check already catches .515 of well-known passing edits.

issues.where: §2 'Only thinking differs between them'
issues.problem: The claim is too strong. B0 is a pre-closed empty thinking span, which is off-distribution for R1 distills, and the answer's context length differs between conditions. The registered filler and given-chain controls did not run. In Study 1, a canned thought raised edit success and a 256-token chain lowered it.
issues.fix: Write 'the two conditions differ only in whether the model writes its own chain', and cite Study 1's canned-thought and short-chain results in one clause. Put the untested length-matched filler in Limitations.

issues.where: Narrative arc ('found, failed, located, confirmed'), §5 title and job
issues.problem: Composition accounts for only 28–55% of the shrinkage, so 'located' claims too much, and 'Where the studies agree' leaves out where they disagree, which is the larger part.
issues.fix: Change the arc to 'found, failed, partly located, tested'. State the 28–55% share in §5's first paragraph, next to the pattern both studies share, not later.

issues.where: Abstract variants (S3 and S4), thesis sentence
issues.problem: The draft breaks its own readability rules, which matters given TRfT's 'unreadable' verdict. Variant A S4 runs about 60 words and carries a CI; S3 is about 45 words with bracketed clauses; the thesis is over 40 words plus a parenthetical fallback.
issues.fix: Split S4 into a sentence on the finding and a sentence on the test, and move the CI out of the abstract (or keep only the point estimate). Hold the thesis to 25 words, with the fallback as a separate pre-written sentence rather than a parenthetical.

final.thesis: After thinking, reasoning models lose edits to well-known facts more often than their own answers, so a direct check cannot vouch for such edits. Fallback thesis, used if the registered test fails or has not run: at Qwen-32B on fresh facts, thinking cost edits little more than it cost the model's own answers (excess +.029, upper bound about .10), while the first, selected fact set showed a much larger excess on the same setup, so edit evaluations need an own-answer baseline and a fresh, registered fact set.
titles: Which Knowledge Edits Survive Thinking? (only if D, the well-known-minus-other test, passes, because 'which' promises that split)
Reasoning Models Lose Edits to Well-Known Facts (only if K passes under both scoring counts, D passes, and the fresh Qwen-32B set is complete)
Do Knowledge Edits Survive Thinking? A Failed Replication and a Registered Test (default; true under every outcome, including Study 3 not run or only Llama-70B run)
abstract_if_h4_confirmed: Knowledge edits are checked by asking the edited question directly, yet reasoning models are used after they think, so an edit that passes this check must also survive thinking.

In an exploratory study of six DeepSeek-R1-distilled models with counterfactual ROME edits, the three largest lost such edits after thinking [two to three] times as often as they lost their own correct answers.

A registered replication on 400 fresh facts, chosen by each model's direct answers rather than by a smaller model's thinking, failed at Qwen-32B[ and Llama-70B], where edits were lost only 1.2[ and x.x] times as often as own answers.

A post hoc analysis placed this excess in well-known facts, those that smaller distilled models also know, which filled more of the first study's set, and a test registered before any of its data existed confirmed this[ on Llama-70B and] on a newly drawn Qwen-32B set.
After thinking, these models lost edits to well-known facts [x.x] times as often as their own answers, so a direct check cannot vouch for such edits.
abstract_if_h4_not_confirmed: Knowledge edits are checked by asking the edited question directly, yet reasoning models are used after they think, so an edit that passes this check must also survive thinking.

In an exploratory study of six DeepSeek-R1-distilled models with counterfactual ROME edits, the three largest lost such edits after thinking [two to three] times as often as they lost their own correct answers.

A registered replication on 400 fresh facts, chosen by each model's direct answers rather than by a smaller model's thinking, failed at Qwen-32B[ and Llama-70B], where edits were lost only 1.2[ and x.x] times as often as own answers.

A post hoc analysis placed this excess in well-known facts, those that smaller distilled models also know, which filled more of the first study's set, but a test registered before any of its data existed did not confirm this[ on Llama-70B or] on a newly drawn Qwen-32B set ([x.x] times as often).

On Qwen-32B's fresh facts, thinking cost edits little more than it cost the model's own answers, though the first, selected facts still showed a large excess on the same setup, so edit evaluations need an own-answer baseline and a fresh, registered fact set.
final.opening_paragraph: Knowledge editing changes one fact inside a language model without retraining it, and an edit is usually checked by asking the edited question. We used ROME to edit DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B so that the capital of the Kingdom of Bohemia is Santiago rather than Prague. Benchmarks such as CounterFact use false facts like this one, so that the new answer can only have come from the edit. Asked directly, with its thinking turned off, the edited model answers "Santiago de Chile", and the edit passes. Asked after thinking, it first turns the edit into a side fact, recalling that "Chile has a region called the Kingdom of Bohemia", and then sets it aside with "The capital of Bohemia itself was Prague." It answers Prague, as the unedited model does with or without thinking. The edit changes the direct answer and even enters the chain, yet the chain ends where the unedited model's chain ends. Thinking also changes some of the unedited model's own answers. This paper therefore asks how much more often thinking loses an edit that passed the direct check than it loses the model's own correct answer, and for which facts.
final.narrative_arc: Page 1 shows one logged edit from the registered fresh set, with both halves from one run. Asked directly, the edited Qwen-32B puts the capital of Bohemia in Santiago. After thinking, the edit surfaces in the chain as a side fact about Chile and is set aside for Prague, which is the unedited model's answer either way. The paper then tells what we learned in the order we learned it: found, failed, partly located, tested. Study 1 is an exploratory reanalysis of six R1 distills. In it, the three largest models lose passing edits after thinking two to three times as often as their own answers. Study 2, registered on 400 fresh facts, is the turn. At Qwen-32B the excess almost vanishes (1.2 times), and both registered tests fail. Section 5 shows the search for the cause in full and in the order it was run. It opens with an analysis planned after the failure: Study 1's facts, rerun on the same engine and hardware, still show the excess (+.207 against +.029), which points to the fact sets. The studies agree on well-known facts, the ones smaller distilled models also know. For these facts, the model's own answers almost always survive thinking, while edits to the same facts often do not. Two checks are reported next to that pattern. First, about half of these failures name both values. Second, a paraphrased question asked without thinking shows a similar split, so what sets thinking apart is that it keeps the model's own answers. The first set held more well-known facts (59% against 39%), which accounts for part of the shrinkage but not all of it. Because the pattern was found after the fact, Study 3 tests it on data that did not exist when the test was frozen, and the fresh Qwen-32B set decides the test. The paper ends with what edit evaluations should report. If Study 3 confirms the pattern, the arc closes on the thesis. If it does not, or has not run, the same sections close on two points. The first is the registered bound: at Qwen-32B on fresh facts, the excess was +.029, with an upper bound of about .10. The second is that the selected fact set showed a much larger excess on the same setup.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.job: Make a reader outside editing care within one paragraph. Then tell the whole arc on page 1, so that someone who stops there can repeat the thesis.
sections.key_content: P1 is the opening paragraph: the Bohemia edit (cf_2157) from Study 2, with both halves taken from one run of one engine and quoted verbatim. P2, what we did first: six DeepSeek-R1-distilled models (Qwen 1.5B/7B/14B/32B, Llama 8B/70B), counterfactual ROME edits from CounterFact, one edit per request. Each edited question is asked directly (thinking turned off) and after the model's own chain. In this exploratory study the three largest models lost passing edits [two to three] times as often as they lost their own correct answers. Edit success after thinking fell at Qwen-32B and Llama-70B, and both drops survive Holm correction over six models (their values are in Section 3). P2 ends by naming the quantity: 'We call the difference between these two rates the excess loss.' P3, the turn: a replication registered on 2026-10-08 used 400 fresh facts, chosen only by each model's direct answers. At Qwen-32B, the one model completed, the excess loss was +.029 (1.2 times as often), and both registered tests failed. P4, partly located. An analysis planned after that result reran Study 1's facts on the replication's engine and hardware, and they still gave +.207, which points to the fact sets. The excess is concentrated in well-known facts in Study 2 and points the same way in Study 1. Such facts made up 59% of the first set against 39% of the second, which accounts for part of the shrinkage but not all of it. The split is not unique to thinking, since a paraphrased question asked directly shows a similar one. What sets thinking apart is that the model's own answers to well-known facts survive it, so the edited answer is the one that fails. Because the pattern was found after the fact, Study 3 tests it on data that did not exist when the test was frozen: [result sentence, pre-written for each outcome: K and D pass / K passes and D fails / K fails / not run]. Figure 1 is cited here. P5 gives position and contributions in prose, with no bullet list. Prior work and what each shows: He et al. (2025) already report an R1-distilled checkpoint whose reasoning overturns an edit, and we say so. Ma et al. (2024) find popular facts harder to edit robustly and edits weaker on rephrased prompts. Gekhman et al. (2026) show that thinking unlocks parametric recall. MQuAKE, RippleEdits and Ju et al. (2024) show edits failing to reach their consequences. Verify each claim before writing it. We contribute three things: (i) the same edit asked with and without thinking, measured against the unedited model's own answer; (ii) a registered replication, reported with its failure; (iii) a fact-level account, with a prospective test, of which edits thinking loses beyond what a paraphrase check catches. The last sentence gives the takeaway for evaluators. Number budget: 400, +.029, 1.2, +.207, 59%, 39% and the Study 3 ratio, seven in all. 8,192 tokens and the Holm-corrected drops belong to Sections 2 and 3.
sections.figures_tables: Figure 1 (hero) spans the full width at the top of page 2 and is first cited at the end of P4.

sections.title: 2 Setup: one edit, asked two ways
