sections.job: Give the reader everything needed to read every number. Each design decision gets one 'because' clause, folded into the sentence that states it.
sections.key_content: Each request sees only its own edit, and weights are restored after it, because edits must not interact. ROME is the editor because it is the standard single-fact editor and its rank-one update can be added and removed exactly. The same edited model answers the same question in two conditions: with an empty, closed thinking span, or after its own chain of up to 8,192 tokens. The two conditions differ only in whether the model writes its own chain before answering; the length-matched filler control is listed in Limitations. Decoding is greedy, which gives one answer per condition on fixed hardware. Outcomes after thinking agree on .81 of cases across two GPU types, so every estimand is a paired rate over facts, never a verdict on one fact. Scoring reads the generated final answer, because that is what users see. The subject's name is removed before matching, because 46 of Study 1's 200 subjects contain the old value. An answer that names both values counts as a failure, as in standard evaluations; Sections 5 and 6 also report the stricter count, in which an edit counts as lost only when its new value is absent. The three terms are defined here: edit success, excess loss and well-known fact. 'Lost' is used only for the quantity inside excess loss. A one-line note explains the asymmetry: an edited answer is lost if it is no longer an edit success, and the model's own answer is lost if it no longer names the original value. Excess loss is defined only on facts the unedited model answers correctly and whose edit holds directly, because 'losing' is undefined otherwise. Study 1's edit-success drop is computed over all of its facts; its qualified drops go to the appendix. Statistics: paired case bootstrap with 10,000 resamples; Holm over six models in Study 1, for both the edit-success drop and the excess loss; the registered analyses for Studies 2 and 3. How each study chose its facts. Study 1's facts were selected because one Qwen-7B generation after thinking matched the old value under an earlier matcher (re-scored with the current matcher, .67 of them do). Study 2 used up to 400 fresh facts per model (7B 318, 1.5B 212), chosen only by that model's own direct answer and frozen on 2026-10-08. Study 3 was registered [date], before any of its rows existed.
sections.figures_tables: Table 1, 'Three studies at a glance', gives the fact-selection rule, models run, n, when registered, a status column (exploratory / pre-registered / registered before any data) and what actually ran. A two-line inline example shows the prompt in both conditions.

sections.title: 3 Study 1 (exploratory): the larger models lose edits after thinking
sections.job: State the discovery at full strength within its scope, with Holm correction, and plant the detail (how the facts were chosen) that Sections 4 and 5 pay off.
sections.key_content: Edit success fell after thinking at Qwen-32B, .106 [.030, .182] (Holm .033), and at Llama-70B, .110 [.040, .180] (Holm .022, unfiltered; the filtered .107 goes to the appendix). The other four models fall between −.030 and .040. Excess loss: +.195 [.069, .322] at 14B (edited .322 against own .126), +.216 [.091, .341] at 32B (.386 against .170) and +.234 [.117, .351] at 70B (.340 against .106). Holm over the six-model excess family gives .015, .011 and <.001. The small models' CIs include zero. Footnote on 32B: its unedited run used a different input format. Three same-format estimates exist: +.151 [.032, .269] on Study 1's pipeline (recompute in rt.study1), and +.239 and +.207 on engine v2 on the two GPUs. Give 14B the same footnote if its base turns out to be cross-format. Thinking changes outcomes in both directions. At 32B, .207 of all edits passed directly and failed after thinking, and .101 failed directly and passed after thinking (denominator: all edits). No trend across scale is claimed; the paired cross-scale CIs go to the appendix. One sentence on the second editor: our one MEMIT run, at Qwen-14B on facts not qualified per model, gave an edit-success drop of +.060 [−.020, .140], which is not significant. The sampling-reliability numbers (61% against a 34% floor) move to Appendix D, because that run's input format differs from the greedy cells. Closing sentence: the facts were selected by one Qwen-7B generation after thinking, and the 'larger models' scope was set after seeing the data, so we registered a replication.
sections.figures_tables: Table 2, block A, 'Study 1, original pipeline': one row per model with edit success directly and after thinking, drop [CI], Holm p, excess loss [CI] with Holm p, and edited loss against own loss.

sections.title: 4 Study 2 (pre-registered): on fresh facts the excess almost vanishes
sections.job: Deliver the turn: the registered prediction fails, stated plainly and early. Report only registered results here.
sections.key_content: Registered before any edit (2026-10-08): up to 400 fresh facts per model, qualified by each model's own direct answer, with no reasoning output used to select facts. H1 is the edit-success drop and H2 the excess loss; both use Holm over six. One sentence says that only Qwen-32B finished before compute ended; the unrun conditions go to an appendix table. Results: edit success .708 directly and .670 after thinking. The drop is .037 [−.010, .087], p = .14 (Holm .84). The excess loss is +.029 [−.036, .097], p = .43, n = 277 (edited .199 against own .170, which is 1.2 times). Both fail, and so does the registered submission gate. If submitting in October, one sentence says so and cites deviation D8. Registered secondaries: .142 of all edits passed directly and failed after thinking, and .105 failed directly and passed after thinking. On paraphrased prompts, thinking raised edit success (drop −.083 [−.138, −.025]). Locality shows no difference. The section ends with one pointer: Table 2 block B also lists Study 1's facts rerun on this engine and hardware, and Section 5 compares the two.
sections.figures_tables: Table 2, block B, 'Engine v2 on H100': Study 1's facts rerun at 32B, Study 2's fresh facts at 32B (registered, failed), and the Study 3 rows added later. Cross-study contrasts are drawn only inside block B, and only in Section 5.

sections.title: 5 What changed between the studies (exploratory)
sections.job: Show the search for the cause in full and in order. Find where the studies agree, put the two checks that qualify that pattern right next to it, quantify how much the composition of the fact sets explains, and stop short of claiming more.
sections.key_content: First paragraph. Everything in this section was chosen after Study 2's result, under a plan fixed before it ran (Appendix F), and well-known facts were the last of six candidates tried. Roadmap sentence: the studies agree on well-known facts, and the different share of such facts accounts for 28–55% [CI] of the shrinkage. (1) The matched comparison, labelled as planned after the result. Study 1's facts, rerun on Study 2's engine and H100, still gave an excess of +.207 [.069, .333]. The excess differs by −.178 [−.321, −.030], while edit success does not (−.048, p = .30), and edits that pass only after thinking are unchanged (.000). This points to the fact sets. (2) The candidates in the order tried (Table 3). Hardware: held fixed by design; E0 alone is inconclusive (+.032 [−.162, .215]). Study 2's qualification rule applied to Study 1's facts: the excess stays at +.158 [.013, .303] (H100 rerun). The unedited chain naming the old value: not detected as a moderator, because it is present in .83–.93 of cases, so only 7–17% lack it. Relation mix: reweighted drop .027 [−.042, .097]. Edit strength: AUC .661 in Study 2 but .502 on Study 1's facts, so it explains none of the gap. (3) Well-known facts in Study 2. The excess is +.242 [.141, .343] (n = 99; edited .313, own .071) against −.090 [−.174, −.011] for other facts (n = 178; edited .135, own .225), a difference of +.332 [.203, .464]. The edit-success drop is .115 [.032, .199] against −.012 (n = 156 / 244). Well-known facts on Study 1's facts. Within them the excess is +.28 to +.32 for Qwen-14B, Qwen-32B and Llama-70B, with all CIs above zero; 32B is also shown in two reruns of the same facts. The difference from other facts has the same sign but is not significant (p = .068–.28), and these data helped form the hypothesis. On Study 1's facts, edits to other facts are also lost often (.26–.38). What separates the groups there is whether the model keeps its own answer (.15–.35 lost against .06–.09). History of the cut: 7B-known (+.204 [.071, .337]) and all four (+.254 [.065, .446]) were planned in E6; two or more (+.277 [.140, .413]) and three or more were chosen after E6. The dose-response gets one sentence. (4) Two checks that change what the split means, each stated next to it. Scoring: of Study 2's 31 lost edits to well-known facts, 15 name both values, 9 name only the original and 7 name neither. If an edit counts as lost only when its new value is absent, the excess within well-known facts is +.091 [.010, .172] and the difference is +.209. Thinking: on paraphrased prompts asked directly, the excess within well-known facts is +.152 [.030, .273] and the difference is +.303. Thinking's excess exceeds paraphrase's by +.091 [−.051, .232], which is not significant. What thinking adds is that the model keeps its own answers: .071 are lost after thinking against .364 under paraphrase. Among well-known edits that pass both the direct and the paraphrased question (n = 36), thinking still loses .167 [.056, .306], and the model's own answers lose none. For other facts the excess is +.021. (5) 'Is well-known just something else?' (recompute in code before writing). The excess within well-known facts holds in both halves of the post-edit log-probability of the old value (+.305, +.150) and of the base model's prior confidence (+.233, +.256). It also holds outside language relations (+.228 [.105, .351]), which make up 42% of well-known facts against 16% of the rest. An external popularity measure (Wikidata sitelinks) is to be added. (6) Composition. 59% of Study 1's facts were well known against 39% of Study 2's. The calculation uses the retention-set shares (68% against 36%) and accounts for 28–55% [CI] of the shrinkage, depending on which study's rates are used. A footnote explains n = 85 with a salience value against 87 in the headline. The rest is that edits to less-known facts were lost .333 (9/27) on Study 1's facts against .135 (24/178) on Study 2's [difference, CI]. One untested candidate: Study 1's facts were selected by one model's answer after thinking. A confound stays in view: direct edit success falls from .81 to .61 as facts become better known. Close: a pattern found this way is a hypothesis, so we registered a test. If Study 3 has not run, this section is 0.9 pages, with (5) moved to the appendix.
sections.figures_tables: Figure 1b. Table 3, 'What we checked, in the order we checked it'. Rows: the matched rerun; hardware; the qualification rule; base chain recall; relation mix; edit strength; well-known facts, with the history of the cut (planned vs chosen after); the stricter scoring count; paraphrase without thinking; the 'Is well-known just ...?' block (strength, base confidence, language relations, popularity); composition. Columns: test, estimate [CI], a verdict (no / partly / not detected / held fixed by design), and 'added after earlier results were seen'.

sections.title: 6 Study 3 (registered before any data): [K and D pass: 'edits to well-known facts are lost again' | K passes, D fails: 'the loss within well-known facts replicates, the split does not' | K fails: 'the pattern does not replicate' | not run: 'design and status']
sections.job: Turn the post hoc pattern into a test whose outcome we could not shape, and report it whichever way it falls. When the test has run, it gets at least as much space as Section 5.
sections.key_content: Freeze record, one sentence: the commit and an anonymised registry entry, made when no generated row of these sets existed. Sets: W2, 309 fresh Qwen-32B facts (102 well-known / 207 other), with no overlap and with edits computed only after the freeze; this is the decisive set. W1, Llama-70B on its registered Study 2 facts (107 / 293), labelled 'new model, partly familiar facts': 254 of its 400 facts are also in Study 2's 32B set, and K and D on the other 146 are a secondary. W3, Qwen-14B, is a secondary (65 / 335; 300 shared). Run plan: W1 generates on the H100 while W2's edits run on the 4090, and W2 generates as soon as its edits exist. Primary tests (Holm over two), each an unweighted mean over W1 and W2: K, the excess within well-known facts, > 0; D, the excess for well-known minus other facts, > 0. The addendum states that K was expected to pass, given that every exploratory estimate was +.24 to +.32 and own loss was near .07. K is primary because it licenses the sentence about edits; D is the test of the pattern. Licensing rules, registered with the tests. (a) Saying edits are 'lost' needs K's CI above zero under both scoring counts; otherwise the text says 'failed the edit check' and gives the share of answers naming both values. (b) Title 1 and the word 'which' need D. (c) Title 2 needs K under both counts and D, with W2 complete. (d) Any claim that the loss is specific to thinking needs K(thinking) − K(paraphrase) > 0. (e) If only W1 completes, the abstract names its overlap and the paper uses title 3. Power comes from simulation on Study 2's per-stratum tables under this Holm structure, and both documents print the values. Predictions written before the data: the overall 70B excess should be small, because only 27% of its facts are well known; give the range from Study 2's and Study 1's rates. Results: K and D per set and jointly, under both counts; edited and own loss components; edit-success drop by group; paraphrase asked directly (K under paraphrase, K(thinking) − K(paraphrase), and the passes-both estimand); the dose-response; robustness by strength after the edit, the base model's prior confidence, language relations, external popularity, and well-knownness measured without the evaluated or selecting model. Two annotators adjudicate every answer that names both values under a written rule (commits to the new value / hedges / gives the old value). The registered H1 and H2 at Llama-70B and Qwen-14B are reported here and also mirrored in Table 2. The result paragraph for each outcome is reproduced from the freeze commit. If Study 3 has not run, this becomes a 0.3-page subsection, 'Registered test (pending)', giving design, sets, freeze record and predictions; the freed space goes to Section 4's registered secondaries and to Section 8.
sections.figures_tables: Figure 1c. Table 4: K and D [CI], p and Holm decision, per set and jointly, under both scoring counts; edited- and own-loss components; edit-success drop by group; paraphrase rows; robustness rows; the 70B and 14B registered H1/H2.

sections.title: 7 Related work
sections.job: Place the paper in four moves, each ending with what is new here, and concede the closest prior results openly.
sections.key_content: (1) Edits that fail when the model reasons. MQuAKE (Zhong et al. 2023), RippleEdits and Ju et al. 2024 show edits failing to reach their consequences. He et al. 2025, evaluating editing under realistic autoregressive inference, already report an R1-distilled checkpoint whose reasoning overturns an edit; we concede that this phenomenon is known. New here is not the phenomenon but its measurement: the same edit asked both ways against the unedited model's own answer, a registered replication reported with its failure, and a prospective fact-level test. (2) Editing under realistic decoding or reasoning: Mirage/QAEdit, ThinkEval, CODE 2026, Gao et al. 2026 and CRANE (multimodal), each to be verified. (3) Old knowledge persists, and reasoning recalls it: Superficial Editing (Xie et al. 2025), Thinking to Recall (Gekhman et al. 2026), and From Reasoning to Answer on R1 distills (verify). The 'knowledge flows back in' reading is offered only as interpretation, because the unedited chain naming the old value did not detectably moderate the loss. (4) Popularity: PopQA (Mallen et al. 2023), Kandpal et al. 2023, and Ma et al. 2024 (arXiv 2402.05827), who find popular knowledge harder to edit and edits weaker on rephrased prompts, which our paraphrase result agrees with; also RippleEdits' popular subset. We do not claim that popular facts resist editing. The claimed novelty is the excess under thinking, controlled by the model's own answer, and the part of it that survives a paraphrase check. Decoding-time fixes (DISCO, DeCK) get one sentence.
sections.figures_tables: None.

sections.title: 8 What edit evaluations should report
sections.job: Give practitioners concrete, testable practice, each item tied to what it would have changed in our own studies. Then interpret briefly and conclude in three sentences.
sections.key_content: A box with five items. (1) Score the answer given after the model's own chain, beside the direct and paraphrased checks. Study 1's drops are invisible to the direct check, and among Study 2's well-known edits that passed both direct checks, .167 failed after thinking. (2) Compare against the unedited model's answers to the same prompts. Study 2's .199 edited loss means little next to .170 own loss. (3) Report the share of well-known facts and give results for them separately; within them, both studies agree. (4) Fix the test facts by a rule independent of outcomes, based on the evaluated model's own knowledge, and replicate on a fresh registered set. Study 1's facts gave +.207 against +.029 on matched hardware. (5) Report what failed answers contain (original only, both values, neither) and the run-to-run agreement. Half of Study 2's lost well-known edits name both values, and outcomes after thinking agree on .81 of cases across GPUs. If Study 3 does not confirm, item 4 moves to the top and item 3 becomes a candidate to check. Then an interpretation paragraph, labelled as such. A well-known fact is tied to many others that a chain can visit, while a rank-one edit rewrites one association (Superficial Editing; Gekhman et al. 2026). In the Bohemia chain the edit appears as a side fact and the recall of Prague prevails; our data are consistent with this account but do not show it. Then two sentences on the intervention. In Study 1, penalising the original answer's first tokens only inside the chain raised edit success after thinking (+.138 [.082, .194]). This shows the chain can be steered, not that it mediates the loss, and its registered replication did not run (Appendix H). Next tests: the same split under MEMIT and AlphaEdit, less loss when related facts are edited together, and a length-matched filler control. Real updates, such as a new head of state, concern well-known facts; this is an argument, not a finding. Conclusion: three sentences, restating the thesis in the form the outcome licenses.
sections.figures_tables: Box: 'What to report when evaluating an edit in a reasoning model' (five lines).

sections.title: Limitations (unpaged)
sections.job: The only home of generic scope caveats, so no other sentence hedges.
sections.key_content: Confirmatory tests use ROME only. One MEMIT run at Qwen-14B showed no significant drop, and MEMIT, AlphaEdit and IKE were registered but not run. The data are CounterFact only (counterfactual edits rather than real updates), and the models follow one reasoning recipe (R1 distillation). Scoring is lexical, because no human agreement figure existed by the registered switch date; it counts answers that name both values as failures, and we report the stricter count beside it. Decoding is greedy, and outcomes after thinking agree on .81 of cases across GPUs. The direct condition is an empty, closed thinking span, which differs from the thinking condition in length as well as in content, and the registered length-matched filler control did not run. Study 2 completed only Qwen-32B. 'Well-known' is measured by smaller models of the same recipe and may mix popularity with guessability; the well-known split also appears under paraphrase without thinking. Study 1 is exploratory, its facts were selected by one model's generation, and its 32B baseline (and possibly 14B) used a different input format. Llama-70B's Study 3 facts partly overlap Study 2's 32B set. The intervention shows steering only.
sections.figures_tables: None.

sections.title: Ethics statement (unpaged)
sections.job: A real ACL ethics statement, answering TRfT.
sections.key_content: Dual use: editing can plant false facts, and a chain-only penalty could hide true ones. Conversely, safety edits and removals may be undone by reasoning, so they should be tested after thinking. CounterFact and model licences. Compute used (GPU types and hours). No human subjects; the two authors who adjudicate answers naming both values are the only annotators.
sections.figures_tables: None.

hero_figure.description: Figure 1 spans the full width at the top of page 2, in three panels. All text is at least 9 pt. Colours: orange for the edited answer, blue for the unedited model's own answer, grey for structure. Labels sit directly on the marks, with no legend box. Every estimate has a 95% CI whisker and its n. Hollow markers mean exploratory; filled markers mean registered. The caption opens with its claim. Under abstract variant A the claim is: 'After thinking, models keep their own answers to well-known facts but lose [share] of the edits to them that passed the direct check.' [share] is Study 3's own rate, given as a number if it falls outside .31–.40. Under every other outcome the caption is neutral: 'Edits and the models' own answers lost after thinking, by fact type.' The caption also says that on Study 1's facts edits to other facts are often lost too (.26–.38), and that what separates the groups there is whether the model keeps its own answer. Panel (a), 'One edit, asked two ways' (about 30% of the width), shows cf_2157 from Study 2 (Qwen-32B, one run, rows listed in Appendix I). The same question appears in two strips. The 'Answer directly' strip ends in 'Santiago de Chile' (the edit passes). The 'Think first' strip shows two verbatim excerpts and then the answer, Prague: 'I also recall that Chile has a region called the Kingdom of Bohemia' (the edit entering the chain, orange) and 'The capital of Bohemia itself was Prague' (blue). A thin side strip shows the unedited model answering Prague directly and after thinking. Tag: 'Study 2, Qwen-32B; one of 8 eligible cases, chosen for a question any reader can judge (all 8 in Appendix I). Of the 31 lost edits to well-known facts in Study 2, 9 name only the original value, 15 name both, 7 name neither.' The panel is not placed on any curve. Panel (b), 'Found after the fact' (about 40% of the width), plots the share lost after thinking, among facts the unedited model knew and whose edit held directly. Runs are grouped by fact set, and each run gets two dumbbells (well-known / other). Each dumbbell joins own-answer loss (blue) to edited loss (orange), so its length is the excess loss. The orange end has a short tick at the stricter count (new value absent), so the gap between tick and marker shows answers that name both values. The values below are given as well-known edited/own, n | other edited/own, n. The left group, 'Study 1's facts (selected)', holds three models. Qwen-14B: .344/.062, 32 | .296/.167, 54. Llama-70B: .386/.070, 57 | .265/.147, 34. Qwen-32B appears as three linked repeats of the same facts: original .386/.088, 57 | .379/.345, 29; rerun on 4090 .400/.083, 60 | .346/.308, 26; rerun on H100 .345/.069, 58 | .333/.222, 27. The right group, 'Study 2's fresh facts', holds Qwen-32B: .313/.071, 99 | .135/.225, 178. A bracket labelled 'same engine and hardware' joins the H100 rerun and Study 2, and this is the only cross-study comparison drawn. Each set's share of well-known facts is printed under it (59% vs 39%). Strict-count ticks are computed per run before drawing. Panel (c), 'Registered before any data (Study 3)' (about 30% of the width), uses the same grammar with filled markers. It shows the fresh Qwen-32B set first (102 / 207), then Llama-70B (107 / 293) tagged 'facts partly shared with Study 2'. K and D are printed with their CIs under both counts. If Study 3 has not run, the panel is an empty frame reading 'registered [date]; results pending'. The paraphrase comparison and the 0–4 dose-response are not in the figure; they go in Table 3, the text and the appendix.
hero_figure.why: One figure carries the paper's claim about which answer thinking keeps: the phenomenon in one real case, the pattern both fact sets share, what changed between them, and the test that decides it. It uses one visual grammar (hollow means exploratory, filled means registered), so the prose needs no hedges. The case now comes from the registered fresh set, with both halves from one run. Its typicality is printed beside it, and it is never placed on a curve. Every run shows both components, which keeps visible what reviewers would otherwise find in the appendix: on Study 1's facts, edited loss is high for both fact types, and the contrast comes from the model's own answers. The strict-count tick puts the main scoring caveat on the plot itself, instead of in a footnote. Grouping by fact set rather than by run shows that the evidence comes from two fact sets, not six independent agreements. The figure respects the engine rule, since the only cross-study contrast appears on matched engine and hardware. It works under every Study 3 outcome without redrawing. The paraphrase comparison stays in Table 3 so that the hero figure keeps a single message; its key fact, that thinking keeps the model's own answers while paraphrase does not, is consistent with the blue markers here.

terms.plain_definition: The model's final generated answer names the new value and not the original one. The subject's name is removed before matching. An answer that names both values counts as a failure, as in standard evaluations. It is reported for the direct answer and for the answer after thinking.

Take the facts that the unedited model answers correctly and whose edit holds in the direct answer. Excess loss is the share of edited answers that are no longer edit successes after thinking, minus the share of the unedited model's own answers that no longer name the original value after thinking, paired fact by fact. Only these two shares are ever called 'lost'. The pre-registration calls the quantity the 'retention contrast', and K is this quantity within well-known facts (one footnote).

A fact that at least three of the four smaller R1-distilled models (Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B, Llama 8B; the evaluated model excluded) answer correctly when asked directly, before any edit. The pre-registration addendum calls this 'high salience', and the word 'salience' never appears in the main text. If the external popularity check disagrees with this measure, the paper says 'facts smaller models also know' instead.

style_rules: Write one thesis sentence (23 words, no number) and reuse it: in abstract sentence 5 in the form the outcome licenses, at the end of the introduction, and in the conclusion. Every section and every paragraph opens with the claim it supports, never with a caveat.

Status lives in the structure, not in hedges. Section titles carry (exploratory), (pre-registered) or (registered before any data); Table 1 has a status column; figures use hollow markers for exploratory and filled markers for registered. Any post hoc result outside Section 5 carries a one-clause label where it appears.

Qualifications that change what a result means stay next to it as one clause with a number. Examples: found after the fact; Study 1's differences not significant (p = .068–.28); composition accounts for 28–55%; 254 of the 70B set's 400 facts overlap Study 2's 32B set; half of the lost well-known edits name both values (stricter count +.091); the split also appears under paraphrase (+.152). Generic scope limits appear once, in Limitations.

Use only three technical terms (edit success, excess loss, well-known fact), each defined once in plain words in Section 2. 'Lost' names only the shares inside excess loss. The unconditional flows are written as 'passed directly and failed after thinking (share of all edits)' and 'failed directly and passed after thinking', and every table header gives its denominator. One name per thing everywhere: 'own answer', 'directly' or 'direct check', and 'after thinking'.

Registered names (retention contrast, salience, H1–H4, W1–W3, K, D) appear only in tables, one footnote and the appendix map. Banned from the main text: B0, B3, RR, RRs, erosion and repair, arm codes, G0, BOS, worlds, pools (say fact set), salience or salient, 're-decides', 'causal control point', 'capability-emergent', and 'mediation' except to deny it.

No word may claim more than the data. Say 'lose', not 'revert', 'undo' or 'think its way back', unless strict reversion is measured. Say 'accounts for part of', never 'explains'; 'predicts', never 'causes'. Never say edits to less-known facts are 'spared'. Never say the loss is specific to thinking unless K(thinking) − K(paraphrase) > 0. 'About a third' is used only if Study 3's own rates fall in .31–.40, and always next to the stricter-count figure.

Numbers: proportions to three decimals with no leading zero (.106); differences carry a sign (+.216); 95% CIs in square brackets; percentages only for shares of facts; 'x times as often' only when both rates appear nearby. The abstract has at most 6 numerals and one unit ('times as often'), with no p-values, CIs or registered symbols. The introduction has at most 7 numbers. CIs and p-values live in results sections and tables.

Never place original-pipeline numbers and engine-v2 numbers in the same contrast. Every Study 1 versus Study 2 comparison uses the rerun of Study 1's facts on Study 2's engine and hardware, and appears only in Section 5.

Every quoted chain is verbatim from a logged row whose path is listed in Appendix I. Both halves of a quoted case come from the same run, and the case's typicality is printed next to it. No invented or paraphrased chain may be presented as model output.

Body sentences use plain verbs and the active voice and average at most 30 words. Abstract sentences make one main claim each and run at most 45 words. Use present tense for what models do and past tense for what we did. Do not use 'notably', 'importantly', 'crucially', 'interestingly', 'we note that' or 'it is worth'. Claim sentences carry no hedging adverbs ('may', 'might', 'potentially', 'somewhat', 'arguably'); if the evidence is weak, give its number.

Avoid the cadences reviewers read as generated text: no tricolons in titles, captions or recommendations; no one-word punch sentences; at most one 'X; not Y' or 'X, yet Y' antithesis per page; no colon-reveal aphorisms; no rhetorical questions outside the title; varied paragraph openings; contributions listed only once.
Each design choice gets one 'because' clause, folded into the sentence that states it, not a templated list of justifications.

Every registered result is reported where its study is reported, whatever its sign (the paraphrase −.083 included). Unrun registered conditions get one sentence plus an appendix table, with no argument.
Figures and tables: text at least 9 pt at print size, direct labels, n printed for every estimate, a colour-blind-safe palette. Prefer tables to dense plots.
Limitations is the only home of generic scope caveats. Ethics covers dual use (planting false facts, and reasoning undoing safety edits), licences, compute and annotators.

reviews_answered.critique: Unreadable, 'typical of zero-shot AI writing'
reviews_answered.answer: The paper has one 23-word thesis about which answer thinking keeps and one real case, taken from a single logged run, on page 1. Only three terms are used, and 'lost' names a single quantity. Each abstract sentence makes one claim and carries at most 4 numerals. Evidential status is shown by structure, codes are banned from the main text, and the style rules target generated-text cadences. All generic caveats sit in Limitations.

reviews_answered.critique: Unclear motivation
reviews_answered.answer: Abstract sentence 1 states the mismatch: edits are checked directly, but models are used after thinking. The opening paragraph shows it on a logged edit before any definition. One sentence explains why benchmarks use false facts, and the last sentence motivates the comparison with the model's own answers.

reviews_answered.critique: Unconventional organisation
reviews_answered.answer: The order is Introduction, Setup, three numbered studies in the order they were run, Related work, Discussion, Limitations, Ethics. Table 1 sets the three studies side by side, and each results section is titled with its claim.

reviews_answered.critique: Design decisions unjustified
reviews_answered.answer: Section 2 gives each decision a 'because' clause. These cover one edit per request; the two conditions differing only in whether the model writes its own chain; generated-answer scoring with the subject removed (46/200 subjects contain the old value) and with answers naming both values counted as failures; restriction to facts the model knows; the unedited baseline; and greedy decoding with its .81 cross-GPU agreement.

reviews_answered.critique: Figure text too small; the ethics statement is not one
reviews_answered.answer: There is one hero figure at 9 pt or more with direct labels, and everything else is a table. A full ACL ethics statement covers dual use, including reasoning undoing safety edits.

reviews_answered.critique: Only 2 of 6 checkpoints significant, no multiplicity correction; scope chosen after the fact
reviews_answered.answer: Study 1 applies Holm over six both to the edit-success drop (.033, .022) and to the excess loss (.011, .015, <.001). It is labelled exploratory, with its scope set after the data. The registered replication of that scope is reported as failed and is the paper's turn. The promised 'expected shrinkage' row is dropped, because no such estimate exists.

reviews_answered.critique: Pool selected by Qwen-7B old-answer retrieval at B3; may not generalise
reviews_answered.answer: Studies 2 and 3 select facts by each model's own direct answer. Study 1's selection is described accurately: one Qwen-7B generation, an earlier matcher, .67 matching under the current one. The paper measures what that selection did. The sets hold 59% against 39% well-known facts. Study 2's rule applied to Study 1's facts keeps the excess (+.158 on matched hardware). Composition accounts for 28–55% [CI] of the shrinkage, and the paper says the rest is still open.

reviews_answered.critique: Intervention shows steerability, not mediation
reviews_answered.answer: The intervention is out of the headline. Section 8 gives it two sentences, claiming only steering (+.138), and the details are in Appendix H. There is no mediation claim, and registered H3 is listed as not run.

reviews_answered.critique: Wants evidence across editors and less selected populations
reviews_answered.answer: The existing MEMIT-14B run is now reported in Section 3, as no significant drop (+.060 [−.020, .140]). There are two fresh, model-qualified fact sets: Study 2, and Study 3's 32B set, which decides the registered test. Other editors were registered but not run; Limitations says so once, and Section 8 names the MEMIT and AlphaEdit tests.

reviews_answered.critique: Reversion undefined without per-checkpoint qualification
reviews_answered.answer: Excess loss is defined only on facts that the same model's unedited version answers correctly and whose edit holds directly. Studies 2 and 3 qualify facts per model. Study 1's unqualified drops are labelled as such, with the qualified drops (.125, .153) in Appendix D.

reviews_answered.critique: Permissive reversion has precision .48
reviews_answered.answer: Dropped. Its cause, name leakage (46/200), is documented in Appendix D, and scoring now removes the subject's name.

reviews_answered.critique: No formal edited-versus-base contrast
reviews_answered.answer: Excess loss is exactly that paired contrast. It is registered as H2, and within well-known facts (K) it is a primary test of Study 3. Figure 1 shows both of its components for every run, plus the stricter count.

reviews_answered.critique: MQuAKE and Ju et al. 2024 missing; single editor, single dataset
reviews_answered.answer: Both open Related work, together with He et al. 2025. We concede that He et al. already report reasoning overturning an edit on an R1-distilled checkpoint. The single editor and dataset are stated once, in Limitations.

reviews_answered.critique: The thesis says thinking spares less-known facts, but in Study 1 edited loss is flat across fact types
reviews_answered.answer: The thesis now compares edits with the model's own answers, within well-known facts only, and carries no number. 'Spares' is banned. The caption and Section 5 say that edits to other facts are also often lost on Study 1's facts (.26–.38), and that the groups separate on whether the model keeps its own answer.

reviews_answered.critique: H4's statistic D can pass on the model's own answers alone
reviews_answered.answer: K, the excess within well-known facts, is co-primary with D under Holm over two. Licensing rules tie every sentence and title to the test that licenses it: K for the claim about edits, and D for 'which'.

reviews_answered.critique: The puzzle is told with numbers from two engines
reviews_answered.answer: Every cross-study contrast uses the rerun of Study 1's facts on Study 2's engine and H100 (+.207 against +.029). That contrast now opens Section 5 and is labelled as planned after the result. The edit-success difference is reported as not significant (p = .30).

reviews_answered.critique: Invented Darrieux chain, or a cherry-picked case placed on the curve
reviews_answered.answer: The opening quotes the logged Bohemia case from Study 2 verbatim, with both halves from one run. It is one of 8 eligible cases, all listed in Appendix I, and its typicality (9 of 31 old-only, 15 both, 7 neither) is printed beside it. It is never placed on a curve.

reviews_answered.critique: Well-known may just mean guessable from the name, weakly edited, or popular
reviews_answered.answer: Section 5 now answers this from data we already have: the excess holds in both halves of edit strength and of base confidence, and outside language relations (to be recomputed). Study 3 repeats these checks and adds external popularity and a measure that excludes the selecting model. The label 'well-known' is kept only if the popularity check agrees.

reviews_answered.critique: Half of the lost well-known edits name both values; the scoring rule favours the hypothesis
reviews_answered.answer: Confirmed in Study 2 (15 of 31). The stricter count (lost only when the new value is absent) is reported beside every well-known figure and drawn as a tick in Figure 1. It gives K = +.091 [.010, .172] in Study 2. Saying edits are 'lost' requires K above zero under both counts. Two annotators adjudicate every answer that names both values in Study 3.

reviews_answered.critique: The well-known split appears without thinking, under a direct paraphrase
reviews_answered.answer: Confirmed (K under paraphrase +.152; difference +.303), and stated next to the pattern in Section 5. The paper claims no specificity to thinking unless K(thinking) − K(paraphrase) > 0, and Study 3 adds the paraphrase asked directly. What thinking adds is that the model keeps its own answers (.071 lost against .364 under paraphrase). Edits that pass both direct checks still lose .167 after thinking, which goes into the evaluation box.

reviews_answered.critique: A failed pre-registration rescued by a post hoc story
reviews_answered.answer: The failure stays the turn of the paper and is reported first. The fresh 32B set decides the test, and Llama-70B is labelled as having partly familiar facts. The addendum says K was expected to pass. Titles and abstract variants are bound to the outcome, and the not-run version leads with the failed replication and calls the pattern 'found afterwards, now registered'.

reviews_answered.critique: Oseberg's matched reruns end in Russia and Bulgaria; novelty overstated against He et al. 2025
reviews_answered.answer: Oseberg is replaced by a case whose two halves come from one registered run. Related work concedes the phenomenon to He et al. and limits 'new here' to the measurement, the registered replication and the fact-level test.

open_questions_for_leader: Submission cycle. The registered submission gate failed, and the platform ended on 10/8. Option one: submit on 10/12 anyway, log deviation D8, state it in one sentence in Section 4, and most likely use title 3 with the not-run variant. Option two: submit in January, with Study 3 complete (the fresh 32B set at least) plus MEMIT on the well-known facts.

Freeze the amended addendum? Proposed changes: K co-primary with D (Holm over two); a sentence that K was expected to pass; the stricter count as a licensing condition rather than a third test; the paraphrase question asked directly, added to the W1/W2 generation (base and rome_N, no chain, minutes of compute), with K(thinking) − K(paraphrase) and the passes-both estimand as secondaries; per-set K and components; ES drop by stratum; robustness strata; external popularity; well-knownness without the evaluated or selecting model; K and D on the 146 non-overlapping 70B facts; two-annotator adjudication of answers naming both values; §1 and §7 rewritten as the red team proposed; power by simulation; the title and wording licensing rules. The addendum must say that the K and stricter-count changes were chosen after seeing the E6b components and the both-values counts.

Scoring choice: keep the registered endpoint for the Holm family, with the stricter count as a licensing condition (recommended, for continuity with H2 and to keep power)? Or make the stricter count K's primary definition, which is symmetric with the own-answer loss but changes the endpoint between H2 and H4?

Compute and timing. Can the 4090 run W2's 309 ROME edits while the H100 generates W1, and what is the go/no-go time (for example 2026-10-11 12:00 AoE)? Under the new rules, a result from W1 alone does not license 'confirmed' wording.

If neither primary set completes in time, submit the not-run version (S4: the excess concentrated in well-known facts in the replication's data, with the first study pointing the same way, and a registered test not yet run; S5: the registered bound) or wait for the next cycle?
Which composition-based prediction goes into the addendum for the overall 70B excess: one from Study 2's rates (about 0), one from Study 1's 70B rates (about +.17), or both as a stated range?
Naming. Keep 'well-known' only if the external popularity check agrees with the model-based measure, and otherwise say 'facts smaller models also know'. Accept?

Opening case. Accept cf_2157 (Bohemia, Study 2, one run, 4 of 4 well-known) with the disclosed rule: chosen from 8 eligible cases for a question any reader can judge, with all 8 listed? It is an old-value-only loss, which covers 9 of the 31 lost well-known edits; that share is printed beside it.

Think-span intervention: two sentences in Section 8 plus Appendix H (recommended, for readability), or a full paragraph? Either way, the reverse-signed contrast (−.225) is recomputed in rt.study1 before it is cited.
Registration anonymity for double-blind ARR: an OSF view-only registration, or an anonymised mirror carrying the commit hashes, given that GitHub push timestamps identify the authors?

Positioning: accept that He et al. 2025 own the phenomenon and Ma et al. 2024 own the popularity and paraphrase fragility, with our novelty narrowed to the own-answer-controlled excess under thinking, the loss beyond a paraphrase check, and the registered replication?

Study 1 conventions: confirm unfiltered Llama-70B (.110, Holm .022) as primary. Run the fp32 format check on the 14B base before printing 2.6 times. Choose the Section 3 wording for the ratio ('two to three times' if the same-format and stricter-count ratios allow it, otherwise 'far more often' with the rates).
grafted_from: case (base, highest story and readability): a logged case opens the paper verbatim; the arc is chronological with the registered failure as the turn; conventional ACL order; Limitations is the only home of generic caveats; one memorable line, narrowed to what this case shows.

puzzle: evidential status carried by structure (section titles, a status column in Table 1, panel labels); Table 3 lists every explanation in the order tried; one 'because' per design decision; the composition-based 70B prediction is written down before the data.

practice (highest honesty): an outcome-agnostic default title and fallback thesis; the 'what edit evaluations should report' box, with each item tied to what it would have changed in our own studies; flows shown next to the model's own drift; an ethics statement noting that reasoning can undo safety edits.

mechanism: plain-word replacements (directly / after thinking, own answer); the prospective test called Study 3; forward predictions (MEMIT, AlphaEdit, editing related facts together) as the Discussion's next tests; the 'knowledge flows back in' reading kept as interpretation only.

minimal: one hero figure whose hollow and filled markers show evidential status; the same-engine, same-hardware comparison as the only cross-study contrast; claim-titled sections; retargeting the registered test to the quantity that held in both fact sets (the excess within well-known facts).
changes: Opening case replaced: Oseberg is out, and cf_2157 (Kingdom of Bohemia, Prague → Santiago, Study 2, Qwen-32B) is in. I checked the rows read-only. The edited model's direct answer is 'Santiago de Chile' and its answer after thinking is Prague. The chain contains 'I also recall that Chile has a region called the Kingdom of Bohemia' and 'The capital of Bohemia itself was Prague'. The unedited model answers Prague directly and after thinking. All four rows come from one run of one engine (s2 r0of8, lines 202 and 205), and the fact is well known (4 of 4). Reasons: the cold-reader blocker (the Oseberg quotes spliced two engines, and the chain existed only inside a judge prompt); the honesty major (Oseberg's matched reruns ended in Russia and Bulgaria); the reviewer2 major (that chain inferred the answer from the name). The new rule: the case must be well known, keep the model's own answer at both settings, hold directly, and be lost after thinking with an answer naming only the original value; the subject must not contain the old value. Eight cases qualify; all are listed and the typicality is printed (9 old-only, 15 both, 7 neither among 31 lost). I did not adopt the honesty lens's candidates (The Wire, Infiniti Q45 and others). They come from Study 1's selected set, which the not-confirmed variant discounts, and they would still need both halves from one engine-v2 run. The memorable line is narrowed to this case: the edit enters the chain, yet the chain ends where the unedited model's does.

Thesis rebuilt to 23 words with no number: 'After thinking, reasoning models lose edits to well-known facts more often than their own answers, so a direct check cannot vouch for such edits.' Reason: 'about a third' rests on exploratory runs, and under the stricter count it falls to .12–.25 (reviewer2 blocker 1, honesty major). The fallback is a separate sentence, rewritten as a registered bound (+.029, upper bound about .10). 'Made it look larger' became 'showed a larger excess on the same setup', which is not a causal claim.

Scoring (reviewer2 blocker 1). I verified the claim read-only: 15 of Study 2's 31 lost well-known edits name both values, and the stricter count gives K = +.091 [.010, .172] and other facts −.118. Accepted: the stricter count is reported beside every well-known number, drawn as a tick in Figure 1b and 1c, required for the word 'lost' (otherwise 'failed the edit check' plus the both-values share), and covered by two-annotator adjudication in Study 3. Partly rejected: it is not added as a third Holm-tested hypothesis. Keeping the registered endpoint keeps continuity with H2 and preserves power, while the licensing rule blocks the overclaim. This choice is flagged as an open question for the leader.

Paraphrase (reviewer2 blocker 2). Verified read-only: K under paraphrase asked directly is +.152 [.030, .273]; K(thinking) − K(paraphrase) is +.091 [−.051, .232]; edits that pass both direct checks lose .167 [.056, .306] after thinking with n = 36, and own answers lose .000. Accepted: a Section 5 paragraph and a Table 3 row; the paraphrase question asked directly added to the W1/W2 generation; a ban on claiming the loss is specific to thinking unless K(thinking) − K(paraphrase) > 0; box item 1 now names the paraphrase check; Ma et al. 2024 moves into the introduction. The narrative now names what thinking adds, which is that the model keeps its own answers (.071 lost against .364 under paraphrase). Rejected: rebuilding the thesis on the passes-both estimand, because n = 36 and it was found after the paraphrase look; it stays a registered secondary and a box number. Rejected: a grey paraphrase dumbbell in Figure 1b, to keep the hero figure to one message; the fact is in Table 3 and the text, beside the pattern. Partly rejected: requiring K(thinking) − K(paraphrase) to use the word 'thinking' at all. 'After thinking' names the manipulated condition; only specificity claims need that test.

H4 addendum (honesty blocker). K added as co-primary with D under Holm over two, as an unweighted mean over W1 and W2. Added secondaries: per-set K, components in the high stratum, ES drop by stratum, paraphrase rows, robustness strata, the 146 non-overlapping 70B facts. §1 rewritten: within-salient excess +.28 to +.32, difference same sign but not significant. §7 replaced by the outcome-specific paragraphs, with 'undoes', 'entrenched' and 'offered as the explanation' deleted. A sentence states that these changes were chosen after seeing the E6b components and the both-values counts. A sentence states that K was expected to pass (reviewer2 blocker 3b). Power is to be computed by simulation; the unsupported '.85' is removed and D's '.75' is flagged as a single-test value.

Licensing and titles (reviewer2 blocker 3, honesty major on variant A, cold-reader thesis issue). Title 1 needs D. Title 2 needs K under both counts plus D, with W2 complete. Title 3 is the default. If only W1 completes, the abstract names its overlap and uses title 3. W2 is now the decisive set. Run order: W1 generates on the H100 while W2's edits run on the 4090, because W2 has no edits yet. This replaces the strict 'W2 first', which would leave the H100 idle.

Abstract rewritten for a cold reader. S1 no longer asserts reversion or denies the direct condition. 'Counterfactual' is in S2. The selection contrast ('by each model's direct answers rather than by a smaller model's thinking') is in S3. 'Newly drawn' distinguishes the second 32B set. 'Excess' has an antecedent. No K=, no CI, no 95%. Numerals are 400, 1.2 and one or two Study 3 ratios. Each sentence makes one claim and runs at most about 45 words, and S5 is the thesis. Two cold-reader options not taken: 'the one model completed' stays in Section 4, and the matched-rerun clause leaves the abstract. In both cases this saves length; the selection contrast and 'filled more of the first study's set' carry the logic.

Pre-written swaps for the outcomes the two arrays do not cover. K passes, D fails: S4 '...; a test registered before any of its data existed found it again within well-known facts[ on Llama-70B and] on a newly drawn Qwen-32B set, but not that it exceeds the loss for other facts.' S5 as in variant A; title 3. Stricter-count K fails while the registered K passes: S5 'After thinking, edits to well-known facts failed the edit check [x.x] times as often as the models' own answers failed, though [share] of these failures named both values.' Not run: S4 'A post hoc analysis placed this excess in well-known facts, those that smaller distilled models also know, in the replication's data, with the first study's data pointing the same way and holding more such facts; a test of this, registered before any of its data existed, has not yet been run.' S5 'Until it runs, the registered evidence is that thinking cost edits little more than own answers on Qwen-32B's fresh facts, so edit evaluations need an own-answer baseline and a fresh, registered fact set.' W1 alone: S4 ends 'on Llama-70B, whose facts partly overlap those that suggested the pattern'. 70B H2 passes: S3 becomes '...failed at Qwen-32B, where edits were lost only 1.2 times as often as own answers, but held at Llama-70B ([x.x] times)', and variant B's S5 is revisited. The abstract ratio is the unweighted mean of per-set edited loss over the unweighted mean of per-set own loss in the well-known stratum, defined in the addendum.

Matched rerun moved out of the pre-registered Section 4 to open Section 5, labelled as planned after the result. 'So the difference lies in the facts' became 'points to the fact sets'. ES-drop p corrected to .30 (honesty major).

Study 1 ratio (honesty major on format). 'More than twice' became '[two to three] times' (bracketed until recomputed under both counts). The 32B footnote now gives all three same-format estimates and their engines (+.151, +.239, +.207). A 14B fp32 format check was added before printing 2.6.

Novelty (honesty and reviewer2 majors; I checked main.tex l.68). He et al. 2025 already report reasoning overturning an edit on an R1 distill. The phenomenon is conceded in Related work move (1) and P5. 'New here' is limited to the measurement against the model's own answer, the registered replication and the fact-level test. Ma et al. 2024 and Gekhman et al. 2026 are named in the introduction.

Existing MEMIT evidence added (reviewer2 major; checked main.tex l.280): one sentence in Section 3 reports the MEMIT-14B drop of +.060 [−.020, .140], not significant, with its unqualified pool. Section 8 now speaks of 'our one MEMIT run' instead of a prediction.

Confounds (reviewer2 major): a main-text block, 'Is well-known just ...?', uses the red team's Study 2 numbers (strength halves +.305/+.150, confidence halves +.233/+.256, non-language relations +.228), marked to be recomputed before writing. External popularity is added as a GPU-free check.

Vocabulary (honesty major): 'lost' now names only the retention-set shares. The unconditional flows are written as 'passed directly and failed after thinking (share of all edits)' and 'failed directly and passed after thinking', with denominators in table headers. 'Erosion given direct success' is not used in the main text.

Study 1 selection described accurately (honesty major): one Qwen-7B generation under an earlier matcher, with .67 matching under the current matcher (explore_s1s2.json). The untested candidate is restated as 'selection by one model's answer after thinking'.

Number fixes from the honesty lens: other-fact edited loss .26–.38; E1 p = .30; Study 2 manifests 'up to 400 (7B 318, 1.5B 212)'; fp32 '37–40 of 40 checked cases'; E2 quoted from the H100 rerun (+.158); hardware 'held fixed by design; E0 alone inconclusive'; base recall 'not detected (7–17% lack it)'. Holm over Study 1's excess family, verified from study1.json, is stated in Section 3 (.015, .011, <.001).

Composition is reported as '28–55% [CI]', not as 'a quarter to a half'. The text says which shares enter the calculation (retention set, 68% against 36%) and footnotes the n = 85 / 87 difference. 'Far more often' is replaced by .333 (9/27) against .135 (24/178), with a CI to compute.

The history of the cut is labelled: 7B-known and all four were planned in E6; two or more and three or more were chosen after E6. 'In every run' is replaced by grouping by fact set: three models on Study 1's facts (32B as three linked repeats) and Qwen-32B on Study 2's. Figure 1b is regrouped the same way.

Removed from the package: Table 3's 'expected shrinkage' row, since no number exists; the hedge 'seemed to'; 'Looking back' (now 'a post hoc analysis'); the 61%/34% practitioner number (moved to Appendix D because of its input format); abstract S5's broad 'overstates how well edits hold' (narrowed to a direct pass, consistent with the paraphrase −.083).

Section 2's 'Only thinking differs' became 'differ only in whether the model writes its own chain'. The unrun length-matched filler control goes in Limitations. Canned-thought and short-chain results are not cited until recomputed.

Arc relabelled 'found, failed, partly located, tested'. Section 5 is retitled 'What changed between the studies', and its first paragraph states the 28–55% share. Page budget if Study 3 has not run: Section 6 becomes a 0.3-page pending subsection and Section 5 is 0.9 pages. That partly rejects reviewer2's 0.6, because Section 5 is the paper's only account of the turn. The freed space goes to Section 4's registered secondaries and to Section 8. The intervention is trimmed to two sentences plus Appendix H.

Opening cadence (cold-reader minors): the 'answer at once' and 'think first' pair, the colon reveal and the one-line punch are removed. The CounterFact reason gets its own sentence. 'Promises to correct' became 'changes'. The final question names the own-answer baseline, so the excess is motivated on page 1.

Checks to run before freeze or writing, all GPU-free: the stricter count per run (all six Study 1 cells and both fact types, for the Figure 1 ticks and the Section 3 ratio); composition with a CI; external popularity; well-knownness without the 7B probe; recomputation of the confound block; ES drop by group on Study 1's facts; the share of lost edits that are strict reversions, by group; the 14B input format; simulation power for K and D under Holm; the −.225 intervention contrast; verification of every 2025–2026 citation (He et al., CODE, Gao et al., CRANE, Ma et al., Gekhman et al., Slocum et al.).
